#10095. Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism

Long-context training — including pretraining and post-training, has become a foundation of frontier AI models. Longer native sequence lengths give large language models (LLMs) the working memory to read a whole code repository or ingest hours of video, and reason through multi-step agentic tasks. In three years, context windows have grown from 128K–200K tokens to 1M–2M, and models trained toward 10M tokens are arriving. Training at those lengths, not just serving them, is where the system limits show up.

In particular, efficient training at multi-million-token sequence lengths runs into the following bottlenecks:

Today, we are excited to announce long-context training support in MaxText, Google Cloud's open-source JAX training framework. MaxText enables this by supporting four context-parallel strategies on Cloud TPU: All-gather, A2A (DeepSpeed Ulysses), P2P (Ring Attention), and the A2A + P2P hybrid (Unified Sequence Parallelism, or USP), combined with load balancing and sequence packing. All four use the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel. Combined with the 3D inter-chip interconnect (ICI) ( supported on TPUs such as TPU 5p or TPU 7 (Ironwood) ), this lets one sequence span an entire slice while communication overlaps compute and memory per chip stays flat. In our benchmarks, Llama 3.1 8B (25 head dim, 16 query heads) demonstrates exceptional long-context efficiency, achieving 70% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) on TPU 5p for sequence lengths up to 4 million tokens. Across both TPU 5p and TPU 7, context can be seamlessly extended to 14 million tokens—with TPU 7 consistently maintaining 50% MFU across all sequence scales below 6 million tokens.

This functionality is available today in MaxText v0.2.4(doc).

Context parallelism splits a long sequence across chips, so no chip holds the activations of the whole sequence. Context parallelism can be combined with data and tensor parallelism, and the smallest context-parallel size that fits your sequence in HBM is usually the right one. This also holds for sparser attention variants which cut attention compute but not the activations of every other layer.

Attention is the one global operation where every token needs the keys and values of every preceding token, so each context parallel strategy has to bring those keys and values back together. Each makes a different tradeoff between memory (how much KV a chip holds), communication (how much moves per layer, and whether it overlaps compute), and model shape (how many attention heads to split).

All-gather: Each chip keeps its chunk of the sequence and, at every layer, gathers the keys and values from every other chip. It is the simplest option. However, because causal masking causes later tokens to attend to larger prefixes, All-gather requires balancing compute load across devices.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

All-to-All (Ulysses): Gathering keys and values makes every chip hold the whole sequence, so attention memory never shrinks no matter how many chips you add. All-to-All changes what each chip owns instead. Attention is independent across heads but not across tokens, so the head axis is free to shard and the token axis is not. An All-to-All before attention rotates the sharding from one onto the other: each chip gives up the heads it is not responsible for and receives the tokens it was missing for the heads it keeps, ending up with the full sequence for a few heads instead of a few tokens for all heads. This is also why Ulysses does not need token load balancing. Attention then runs as ordinary single-chip attention with standard kernels, and a second All-to-All rotates the output back. KV per chip shrinks by the context-parallel factor, but you cannot split across more chips than the model has heads — and tensor parallelism shards that same dimension, so TP × CP is capped by the head count (under GQA, by the KV heads: eight for Llama 3 8B). The all-to-all itself, though, does not overlap with compute — attention cannot start on a partial sequence, so every chip waits for data from every other chip before any of them begins.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

P2P (ring attention): Ulysses' ceiling is the head count; ring attention removes it by never leaving the token axis. Keys and values never materialize in full. KV chunks travel around a ring of chips one hop at a time, neighbor to neighbor. Each chip attends its queries to the chunk it holds while the next one is in flight, and merges the partial results as it goes. A chip holds its own chunk and one visiting chunk, never the full sequence, and the communication overlaps compute. However, dividing attention computation into smaller chunks can reduce local kernel efficiency, and unlike All-to-All Ulysses, ring attention requires explicit load balancing.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

A2A + P2P (USP): A2A + P2P (USP): Neither strategy scales on its own — All-to-All stops at the head count, and a long ring accumulates hops while thinning the overlap that makes it work. Unified sequence parallelism composes them on two axes of the chip mesh, so the context-parallel degree becomes the product of the two: All-to-All along one axis, sized at or below the KV-head count, and a ring along the other to extend past it. Because each All-to-All group has already pooled its tokens, a ring step now carries a chunk larger by the All-to-All factor, and the ring is correspondingly shorter — more compute per hop to hide the transfer behind, and fewer hops to accumulate latency and causal imbalance. On Cloud TPU the two map onto two axes of the slice's chip mesh.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

These strategies cover the attention variants in today's major models, from multi-head and grouped-query attention to DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention.

Splitting the sequence only pays off if the attention compute on each chip stays efficient. All four strategies run on Splash Attention, the block-sparse flash attention kernel from Tokamax, Google's open-source library of TPU kernels. It skips fully masked blocks and handles packed sequences without padding. P2P calls it once per ring step, on the local queries and the KV chunk that has just arrived, while the transfer for the next step runs underneath, in the forward and backward pass alike. Each chip does the same fused, block-level work it would do without context parallelism, with the communication hidden behind it.

P2P (Ring Attention) is the primary workhorse for very long-context training, whereas All-Gather is the standard baseline for most other cases where the KV can fit. These are the primary CP strategies to use in practice. We compare how far each can push context length on a fixed 64-chip TPU 5p slice with Llama 3.1 8B (256 head dim, 16 query heads) , and measure their MFUs. In ideal settings where both strategies can have large enough chunks (S/CP) and local batch size - the two major variables driving MFU on TPU 5p, we observe that P2P can outperform All-Gather almost every context length from 64K to 14M tokens, where communication becomes mostly hidden with the Ring circular transport schedule.

TPU v7x (Ironwood) takes the same recipe further. With twice the HBM per chip, P2P training of 14M tokens on 64 TPU 7 chips reached 48.7% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) compared to 37.1% on TPU 5p. We observed that ring attention performs better than other context parallelism strategies -- e.g. Ulysses and USP –- on TPU 7 chips.

The choice of context parallelism strategy depends mostly on whether the gathered KV fits in HBM, and on how many KV heads the model has:

For all CP strategies, when you run low on memory: Offload before you recompute. MaxText can move saved activations, optimizer states, and parameters to host memory tensor by tensor. At long context lengths, these transfers are hidden behind compute, making offloading effectively free. Offload attention outputs first, followed by optimizer states, layer inputs, parameters, and finally remat as a last resort. MFU stays flat through the offload steps while all-gather falls off and eventually stops fitting. For more details, see the remat tuning guide.

Looking ahead, we see two natural extensions. The first is broader model coverage. Models that mix sliding-window and global layers, such as Gemma, would run the window layers with a short exchange between neighboring chips while the global layers use the ring. We also plan to support linear attention mechanisms such as Gated Delta Net (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). The second is performance, with further tuning of the Tokamax kernels and the P2P backward pass to narrow the remaining gap to all-gather at short context, and recipes by model and context length for TPU 5p and 7 chips.

Context parallelism is available today in MaxText v0.2.4 on PyPI, the corresponding Docker images and on GitHub main. Sample recipes are available here for TPU 7 and TPU 5p. Pick a strategy with context_parallel_strategy (ring, ulysses, or usp), set the context-parallel size, and keep the rest of your run the same. The sharding guide has the flags and constraints for each strategy, and the release notes link to the pull requests behind this work. We can't wait to see what you train.

#10093. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL now supports direct querying of Apache Iceberg and Parquet data in your data lake

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing a new capability for Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL that you can use to directly query operational data together with data stored in your data lake in Apache Iceberg and Apache Parquet formats, using your existing PostgreSQL applications and tools. By eliminating the need to extract, transform, and load (ETL) structured data from data lakes into your operational database, you can reduce operational complexity and simplify application development. You can also use Aurora PostgreSQL to query data from data lakes managed in Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC)-compatible catalogs, giving you access to data across a breadth of analytics systems without moving or duplicating it. Whether you’re powering real-time dashboards, enriching transactions with historical context, or building AI agents that reason over both live and archived data, you can now do it all through a single, familiar interface.

Previously, if your application needed to combine recent transactional data in Aurora with historical records stored in Amazon S3, a common approach was to build reverse ETL pipelines that duplicated data, increased infrastructure costs, and required ongoing engineering effort to keep everything synchronized. This challenge only grows as you increasingly embed AI agents into your applications, where it is impractical to predict and pre-replicate every dataset an agent might need.

DuckLabs, the team that maintains the DuckDB project, recently joined Amazon, and this capability is an example of how the efficiency of DuckDB is being integrated into our services. DuckDB is now embedded directly within Aurora PostgreSQL, so you can query live operational data (including uncommitted writes) alongside your data lake in a single query. Query processing stays within Aurora, with no additional network hops and no ETL pipelines that duplicate data. You can query Apache Iceberg tables managed through the AWS Glue Data Catalog, as well as Parquet and Iceberg data stored in Amazon S3 and S3 Tables. You do all of this using familiar PostgreSQL syntax and your existing applications and tools.

We’re excited to bring the speed and simplicity of DuckDB directly into Aurora PostgreSQL, so you and your agents can query and combine operational and Iceberg data using the familiar PostgreSQL applications, tools, and endpoints already in use. By building this capability around DuckDB, future improvements to the open source engine can continue to bring performance and functionality gains to Aurora and other AWS services.

What is newThis capability is supported on two Aurora PostgreSQL major versions: 17 (starting with 17.11) and 18 (starting with 18.6). To use it, you create an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster, attach an IAM role with the AuroraAnalytics feature, and enable the aurora_analytics extension. The IAM role is what gives Aurora access to your data in Amazon S3 and the AWS Glue Data Catalog. You then create foreign tables that point to your Iceberg or Parquet data in the data lake, and query them using familiar PostgreSQL syntax. You can complete this setup through the Amazon RDS console, or with any PostgreSQL client such as psql. The process is well documented in the Aurora PostgreSQL documentation.

You can query data across external IRC-compatible catalogs through AWS Glue Data Catalog federation. You register the external catalog once with Glue, and then create foreign tables for the tables you want to query, the same way you would for any Glue-native table. A single query can then join data stored in Aurora with Iceberg tables registered across multiple catalogs, so applications get a unified view without moving data or replacing your existing catalog investments.

Aurora also applies optimizations such as predicate pushdown and column pruning so that only the relevant data is read. This keeps queries efficient even as the underlying data grows. Frequently accessed data is also cached in your Aurora instance, so subsequent queries against the same data return faster. You can inspect this behavior per query using aurora_analytics_stat_statements(), which reports metrics such as rows scanned, bytes read from Amazon S3, and cache hits.

To see how direct querying works, I connected to my Aurora PostgreSQL database using psql and created the extension:

For my walkthrough, I set up a simple financial scenario. I have a recent_transactions table in Aurora with the last 7 days of customer transactions, and a Parquet file in Amazon S3 containing 5 years of historical transaction data. To make Aurora aware of the historical data, I created a foreign table pointing at the Parquet file in S3:

Notice the empty parentheses in the CREATE FOREIGN TABLE statement. Aurora automatically reads the schema from the Parquet file metadata, so you do not need to define columns manually. For workloads with many tables, you can skip creating them one at a time: a single IMPORT FOREIGN SCHEMA statement bulk-creates foreign tables for every Iceberg or Parquet table in an AWS Glue Data Catalog database, inferring schemas automatically.

With both tables in place, I ran a single query that combines the recent operational data in Aurora with the historical data in S3:

The result shows both recent and historical transactions in a single result set. The 7 most recent rows come from Aurora, and the rest come directly from the Parquet file in S3. DuckDB handles the analytical scan of the Parquet data under the hood, while Aurora handles the operational data. That single query would have previously required a pipeline to move the historical data into the database first.

If a query pattern needs single-digit-millisecond latency, you can materialize data from the data lake into a native Aurora PostgreSQL table using familiar commands such as CREATE TABLE AS SELECT, INSERT INTO ... SELECT, or MERGE INTO. The materialized table lives in Aurora and is queried like any other PostgreSQL table, giving you a low-latency path for hot data without operating a separate ingestion pipeline. The read queries can run on any Aurora PostgreSQL instance in your cluster, whether the writer or a read replica, so you can offload analytical scans from your operational workload. The materialization commands write data into Aurora, so they run on the writer instance.

Get started today Direct querying of Apache Iceberg and Parquet data from Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL is available today in all commercial AWS Regions and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, at no additional charge. You pay only for the incremental Aurora compute the queries consume and Amazon S3 request costs for reading data lake files.

To learn more, visit the Amazon Aurora features page, read the Aurora PostgreSQL documentation, or try it in the Amazon RDS console. We welcome your feedback through AWS re:Post or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Esra Kayabali is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS, specializing in analytics, including data warehousing, data lakes, big data analytics, batch and real-time data streaming, and data integration. She has more than ten years of software development and solution architecture experience. She is passionate about collaborative learning, knowledge sharing, and guiding community in their cloud technologies journey.

#10091. London hotel put admin login for booking website on whiteboard behind the front desk

Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where all the victims are self-owned. This week, we welcome you to a London hotel where you could check out its admin credentials for a booking website just by walking past the front desk.

Our story comes courtesy of Neycho Tepavicharov, co-founder of Flashcloud, a Delaware-based web hosting company. He was staying at a hotel in London when he noticed a shocking breach of basic security protocols by management, who were a little too hospitable with their credentials.

As he was passing through the lobby, Tepavicharov noticed that the door behind the front desk was open and, inside that back room, there was a whiteboard. On the whiteboard, written in plain English, were the hotel’s Booking.com administrative username and password.

Anyone near the desk could clearly see the login information, and if they didn’t have time to write it down, they could have snapped a picture for later use. As Tepavicharov explains, there’s plenty of mischief you could perform with these credentials.

“With that login, someone could change or cancel reservations, see guests’ names and contact details, or message guests pretending to be the hotel,” he said. “Fake 'please confirm your payment' messages sent from compromised hotel accounts are a well-known scam.”

An attacker could potentially exploit that access to disrupt hotel operations or target guests with convincing scams. Whether the exposed credentials alone would have been enough to access the account would depend on its security settings.

Tepavicharov decided to play the role of good samaritan and warn the hotel’s manager that the business was endangering itself by showing everyone its password.

Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request.

“I asked to speak with the manager and showed him what I’d seen. He was mortified and very grateful,” Tepavicharov said. “Nobody on staff had thought of it as a risk. It was just the easiest way for the whole team to share one login.”

After Tepavicharov talked to the manager, not only did the hotel change its ways, but it also moved its website to his hosting service, Flashcloud.

Tepavicharov notes that there are plenty of takeaways from this incident. Most important: give each user dedicated credentials with their own separate login, and use multi-factor authentication.

“The lesson is an old one, but it keeps happening,” he said. “Shared logins end up written somewhere convenient. Give each staff member their own login, turn on two-factor authentication, and keep passwords in a password manager, not on the wall.”  ®

#10089. Amazon S3 Vectors now supports metadata pre-filtering for higher recall on filtered searches

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing metadata pre-filtering for Amazon S3 Vectors, which delivers higher recall on filtered queries by evaluating your metadata filter before the similarity search. You can filter on attributes such as tenant, category, status, or time, and pre-filtering adds prefix matching with $startsWith for paths, URLs, and hierarchical keys. Each vector carries up to 2 KB of filterable metadata, and a single query supports up to 100 filter constraints. There is no additional cost, no re-ingestion, and no change to your queries.

Most applications never search a whole index. They search the part of it that belongs to a particular user, account, or category, and they express that scope as a metadata filter. Semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and agentic applications all need the same thing from a filtered query: a similarity search that covers the vectors matching the filter, and returns the closest of them. With pre-filtering, a filtered query returns more of the relevant matches your index contains, giving you higher recall on filtered searches.

Common use cases Pre-filtering applies wherever results have to be both relevant and correctly scoped:

How pre-filtering works Each vector in an S3 Vectors index can carry application-defined metadata, and a query can filter on those fields.

Every vector index has an index mode. On an index whose index mode is ENHANCED, S3 Vectors resolves your filter first, then searches only the vectors that match. On an index whose index mode is CLASSIC, S3 Vectors performs the vector search and filter evaluation in tandem, validating each candidate vector against your filter as it searches. Existing indexes use CLASSIC until you update them.

Consider a support knowledge base of 8 million tickets, where an agent searches one customer’s history for a recurring error. If that customer accounts for 400 of those tickets, resolving customer_id first means the similarity search runs across all 400 of them, so the agent sees that customer’s prior occurrences. Before the index was updated, the same query drew its candidates from the full 8 million, and the result set contained fewer of that customer’s matching tickets.

On highly selective filters, pre-filtering returns up to 5x more of the matching vectors than the same query returned before on CLASSIC indexes.

Getting started Before you start, make sure your IAM policy grants permissions for the new actions.

You can get started in three steps. The walkthrough below builds a small product-catalog index and runs a selective filter against it, the same pattern you would use for a multi-tenant RAG store or a document search scoped to one client.

The dimension must match the output size of your embedding model, and distance-metric should match how that model was trained (cosine is common for text embeddings). Second, write vectors with the PutVectors API, attaching up to 2 KB of filterable metadata to each vector:

Each vector carries the attributes your application filters on. In this example, tenant_id scopes results to a single customer, category narrows by document type, created_date records when the document was created, and active is a boolean flag. By default every metadata field is filterable, so you can query on any of them without declaring a schema up front.

Third, run a filtered similarity query with the QueryVectors API. The filter uses a compact JSON syntax where a bare key-value pair is an equality match, and operators such as $and, $or, and $gt combine or refine conditions. Pass --return-metadata so the query returns each vector’s metadata:

The expected result is a single vector, doc-001, the only one matching all three filter conditions (tenant_id, category, and active):

S3 Vectors first narrows the search space to vectors matching all three filter conditions, then returns the 50 most similar vectors from that subset. Because the filter is applied before the search, those results are drawn from across all the vectors that match it.

Prefix matching with $startsWith Pre-filtering adds a prefix match operator for filtering on paths, URLs, and hierarchical keys. A document store that encodes case and folder structure into a document ID can scope a search to a subtree in one condition:

$startsWith joins the existing operators: equality, numeric range, set membership, existence checks, and boolean logic with $and and $or.

Turning on pre-filtering for existing indexes Call UpdateIndexMode on an existing index to turn on pre-filtering:

Pre-filtering takes effect in place. Your existing vectors are not re-ingested, your queries do not change, and the new filter operators are available immediately.

Here is the difference on the same index and the same query. Before the update, a query scoped to one tenant returns two of the ten results requested:

After the update, the same query returns a full result set drawn from across that tenant’s documents:

Rolling out across your indexes Once you have validated pre-filtering on an index, set the default index mode on the vector bucket so that new indexes use ENHANCED without a follow-up call:

To bring the rest of your existing indexes across, list them and check the index mode on each one, then call UpdateIndexMode on the ones still using CLASSIC:

Now available Metadata pre-filtering is available at no additional cost in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available, and in the AWS China Regions. You pay standard S3 Vectors pricing for storage, PUT requests, and queries. For full pricing details, visit the Amazon S3 pricing page. For regional availability, visit Amazon S3 Vectors Regions and quotas.

Whether you’re scoping a RAG application to one tenant, scoping an agent’s searches to one user’s documents, or narrowing a catalog search to a licensing window, pre-filtering lets you apply those filters without trading away recall. To learn more and get started, visit the Amazon S3 Vectors documentation. Send feedback to AWS re:Post for S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#10087. Amazon S3 Tables now support all Apache Iceberg V3 data types

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Amazon S3 Tables now support all data types in the Apache Iceberg V3 specification. You can create V3 tables or upgrade existing V2 tables to take advantage of V3 features like deletion vectors, row lineage, and new data types such as variant, nanosecond timestamps, unknown, geometry, and geography.

Apache Iceberg has become the open standard for managing large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data in open Parquet files in data lakes on object storage like Amazon S3. Amazon S3 Tables offer storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with fully managed features like automatic compaction, maintenance, replication, and Intelligent-Tiering.

Teams running analytics on Apache Iceberg V2 tables often hit the same limits as their data grows. A compliance request to delete 50,000 user records from a 2-billion-row table leaves behind positional delete files that slow queries until compaction runs. Semi-structured events land as JSON strings that every query has to parse. Geospatial coordinates and nanosecond-precision timestamps get encoded as strings or integers. Each workaround adds storage cost, query latency, and pipeline code. With V3, Iceberg solves these challenges by offering native support for semi-structured and geospatial data, faster row-level operations, and built-in row lineage for data governance.

Starting today, Amazon S3 Tables support all V3 data types, including variant, nanosecond timestamps, geometry, geography, and unknown, along with deletion vectors and row lineage. You can create new V3 tables or upgrade existing V2 tables in place, and S3 Tables continue to run compaction and maintenance for you.

Apache Iceberg V3 V3 is the latest version of the Iceberg specification. Among its many improvements, V3 introduces capabilities that address the most common pain points in V2. This includes:

Deletion vectors replace V2’s positional delete files with a compact binary format. That 50,000-row compliance delete now writes a single deletion vector file instead of thousands of small deletes, significantly reducing compaction time and delete file overhead.

Row lineage adds _row_id and _last_updated_sequence_number to each record automatically. Your downstream pipelines can query these fields to find changed rows without scanning the full table.

New data types let you store semi-structured, geospatial, and nanosecond-precision data natively instead of encoding it as strings or integers:

Variant data type stores semi-structured data in columnar format. During writes, the engine shreds variant data into hidden columns and collects statistics. At query time, those statistics enable file pruning that significantly reduces I/O compared to parsing JSON strings.

The following sections walk through how to use these V3 capabilities in practice, with examples that show how to create tables, work with the new data types, and manage data at scale.

Getting started A retail analytics team tracks user behavior across web and mobile apps. Each event has a different structure: page views include URLs and duration, purchases include items and amounts, and searches include query terms and result counts. With V3’s variant type, you store all event shapes in one table without predefined schemas:

Insert events with different payload shapes without worrying about schema evolution:

Now query the variant column directly, without PARSE_JSON at read time. With Amazon EMR Spark, use variant_get:

To enable deletion vectors for write operations, configure merge-on-read mode:

Now when you run a compliance delete, V3 writes a small deletion vector instead of rewriting data files:

S3 Tables compaction handles these deletion vector files automatically on the next maintenance cycle.

Upgrading from V2 AWS provides backwards compatibility for both versions to minimize disruption during migration to V3. Existing V2 readers continue to work on upgraded tables until you’re ready to fully adopt V3 features. For more details, see the S3 Tables Iceberg V3 documentation. Upgrade an existing table atomically without rewriting data:

On the next compaction cycle, S3 Tables remove old V2 delete files. New modifications use deletion vectors automatically. Row lineage fields initialize on the first data modification after the upgrade.

This is a one-way operation. The Apache Iceberg specification does not support downgrading from V3 to V2. Verify that all engines accessing the table support V3 before upgrading.

Using row lineage for incremental pipelines After your table has V3 data, use row lineage to build efficient incremental pipelines:

This returns only rows modified after sequence number 42. Your downstream jobs can checkpoint this value and process only new changes on each run, instead of scanning the full table.

Compatibility across AWS analytics services AWS offers the broadest native Apache Iceberg support of any major cloud provider, with Iceberg-compatible services at every layer of the data stack: ingestion, storage, catalog, and analytics. You can store and automatically optimize V3 tables in Amazon S3 Tables, write data with Amazon EMR Spark, integrate and manage data with AWS Glue, and run analytics with Amazon Redshift. To learn more about AWS analytics support for V3, see the Apache Iceberg on AWS prescriptive guidance.

Both S3 Tables and AWS Glue Data Catalog support the Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) API, enabling interoperability across engines regardless of the catalog endpoint.

Now available Amazon S3 Tables support for all Apache Iceberg V3 data types is now available in all AWS Regions where S3 Tables are supported. Apache Iceberg V3 support is available at no additional charge; standard S3 Tables pricing applies.

To get started, visit the Amazon S3 Tables documentation or create a table bucket from the Amazon S3 console. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. Send feedback to AWS re:Post or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#10084. On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery

Today, we are introducing on-device Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities in Google AI Edge Gallery. Voice is often the most natural way to interact with AI on phones and wearables. Recent advances in compact speech architectures now make it possible to run accurate, multilingual ASR and expressive TTS models entirely on device, all within a small memory footprint, with low latency, and completely offline. By pairing these lightweight speech models with on-device small language models (SLMs) like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4, developers can build apps that stream live transcriptions as the user speaks and synthesize natural spoken replies locally.

This release brings together major advancements across both Google’s system speech models and the open-weight ecosystem:

Below, we’ll explore how this local voice pipeline powers the new XR (Extended Reality) Language Teacher showcase, upgrades AI Chat in Google AI Edge Gallery, and how you can build with these APIs and models today.

Learning a language while traveling happens in the real world, often in underground stations, busy markets, or abroad where Wi-Fi and roaming data may not be available. To show how vision, language, and speech models can work together 100% locally on your phone with no network connection needed, we built the XR Language Teacher showcase in Google AI Edge Gallery. Simply point your camera at an unfamiliar object or menu, ask "What is that, and how do I ask for one?", and immediately hear an explanation in your language alongside authentic pronunciation in the local language.

Link to Youtube Video (visible only when JS is disabled)

With inference running locally on a paired phone, the same experience works standalone on a phone and extends naturally to hands-free smart glasses. To see how we adapted Language Teacher for intelligent glasses check out our recent talk at Android Dev Summit: Building Audio-First Experiences for Intelligent Eyewear with Gemini Nano.

Beyond the XR Language Teacher showcase, we also built ASR and TTS directly into Google AI Edge Gallery’s main AI Chat feature, giving on-device SLMs like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 a natural, offline voice interface while on the go.

Link to Youtube Video (visible only when JS is disabled)

While multimodal models like Gemma 4 can process audio inputs directly, we provide a modular solution for cascading language models with separate, lightweight voice models for latency optimization and flexibility. Depending on your target devices and model requirements, our open-source code on GitHub shows you the optimized and recommended solution for Android using ML Kit, as well as MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform coverage and open model support.

For developers building for Android devices, ML Kit’s GenAI Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech APIs provide a standardized, platform-integrated path out of the box. With the underlying speech models managed through AICore and Google’s on-device speech services, developers get production-grade quality without having to manage model downloads or worry about APK size bloat. Your app also benefits automatically from hardware acceleration across NPU and TPU backends (when available) and seamless background model updates.

Integrating ASR and TTS into cross-platform applications usually requires handling low-level audio framing, Voice Activity Detection (VAD), and complex decoding pipelines. MediaPipe Task simplifies this by providing unified, turnkey ASR and TTS APIs across iOS, macOS, Windows, Linux, and Web that abstract away manual pre-processing, audio stream routing, and platform-specific audio management into simple, high-level interfaces:

Under the hood, ML Kit and MediaPipe Tasks are powered by LiteRT, Google’s high-performance on-device AI inference infrastructure. Cross-platform applications requiring even more fine-grained control over speech processing or custom model architectures can also build on it directly.

Speech models often rely on multiple subgraphs and auxiliary assets, such as encoder/decoder subgraphs and tokenizers for ASR, or phonemizer dictionaries, voice embeddings, and vocoders for TTS. All required components for each model are packaged into a single .litertlm file for easy deployment. The app ships with ready-to-use .litertlm models, including Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 (multilingual ASR), PocketTTS 100M (multilingual TTS), Phonon 31M (ultra-lightweight English TTS), and Kokoro-82M (multilingual TTS). Beyond these, the vibrant Hugging Face LiteRT Community with over 10K+ followers offers a growing catalog of open-weight models, like Whisper, Qwen3-ASR and Moonshine for ASR, or Qwen3-TTS and Matcha for TTS. For developers seeking custom implementations or support for additional open-weight voice models, LiteRT provides a rich set of multimodal model examples to help you get started, with more on the way.

Adding a local voice pipeline takes on-device SLMs beyond typing-based chat interfaces, enabling natural, voice-first interactions that work anywhere, completely offline. All the building blocks to try these experiences or integrate them into your own apps are available today:

We'd like to extend a special thanks to our significant contributors for their work on this project:

Alice Zheng, Ajay Dudani, Alex Kanaukou, Amy Zeppenfeld, Byungchul Kim, Cheng Yang, Chintan Parikh, Chris Parsons, Cormac Brick, David Chou, Dong Chen, Geonsun Lee, Glenn Cameron, Hriday Chhabria, Ian Ballantyne, Ireneu Pla, James O’Donnell, Jamieson Pryor, Jason Poon, Jenn Lee, Jianing Wei, Jing Jin, Jingxiao Zheng, Jingyu Shi, Karthik Thirumalai, Kristen Wright, Lu Wang, Marius Kintel, Matthias Grundmann, Miao Wang, Mogan Shieh, Na Li, Paul Hsia, Qiumin Xu, Ravi Shankar, Rishika Sinha, Ronald Wotzlaw, Sachin Kotwani, Sandeep Patil, Sebastian Schmidt, Shao-Fu Shih, Shuangfeng Li, Suril Shah, Tiger Souvannakoumane, Tzu-Ping Chen, Weiyi Wang, Wentao Tu, Yang Yang, Yi-Chun Kuo, Yishuang Pang, Yu-che Liu, Yu-hui Chen, Yuling Liang, Zhihao Yang, Zichuan Wei.

#10083. Orbit Global Menu: A working global menu addon for GNOME

We love this, but suspect this is the Marmite of GNOME extensions

A new extension brings a working global menu bar to the GNOME desktop, even for some apps that don’t have menu bars at all.

Orbit Global Menu is a new GNOME extension that gives the GNOME desktop a feature it was intentionally designed without, and one that some users miss very badly – this vulture being one of them. It adds a working global menu bar to the GNOME top panel. We suspect this is something that will cause strongly contrasting opinions among many GNOME users: some will by puzzled why anyone would bother, while others may think "at last!" and rush to try it.

There have been other attempts to do this before, and the Reg FOSS desk has tried several of them, but we never found one that worked with the majority of applications. Our fondness for this UI feature was visible in the two-part series we wrote in September on how to customize Xfce and then in part two how to get the global menu working with more apps.

The problem is getting worse over time, as in recent versions (since GNOME 40 and Gtk4), the GNOME human-interface guidelines encourage smartphone-style hamburger menus, replacing the traditional horizontal menu bar. It is tricky to add global menu bar support to apps that lack a menu bar, but Orbit's developer "Unmade" found a rather labor-intensive solution. The menu bar applet contains maps of keyboard controls for 292 different apps, so it can show a menu all on its own and then send those apps simulated keystrokes to operate it. It's not the programs' full menu trees, just a subset of them, but it works.

It's also not the most elegant solution, but it is a solution and it works. We tried it on Ubuntu 26.10 and every app in the full install worked to at least some extent. If you are willing and able to build and install a small additional connector, it lets the global-menu applet talk to lots more applications.

The GNOME shell is unusual among open source desktop environments, to an extent that we have criticized before. GNOME Shell was designed with a distinctive look and feel of its own, unlike almost all other desktops. It has a minimalist, stripped-down layout that doesn't look or work quite like anything else, and it's intentionally not very customizable. To change how GNOME works means writing new Javascript code, then packaging it as an extension that users can install from the GNOME Extensions website. This requires both a browser extension and a "native host messaging" connector to be installed into the underlying OS – or a purpose-written app. By default, the desktop comes with neither.

The end result is that GNOME lends a visual identity to the Linux desktop, one that is clear and distinct from either Windows or macOS. (Back in 2013, this vulture argued that when Microsoft threatened to sue multiple Linux vendors over infringing Windows UI patents, some 20 years ago, this UI fragmentation was just what the company wanted.) GNOME 2 was the Linux world's default desktop. GNOME Shell was controversial in its early days, and lost pole position, but it has since won it back. Today, GNOME is the default desktop on all the major distros: Ubuntu, Fedora and Red Hat Enterprise Linux and the RHELatives, as well as Debian and SUSE, all default to GNOME.

GNOME does away with a lot of features that are significant functional parts of other graphical desktops. For instance, it has no desktop icons, no system tray or defined place for status indicators, and neither GNOME nor GNOME-compliant applications have menu bars, either inside windows (Microsoft style) or in the top panel (Apple macOS style). This is disorienting and confusing for those used to controlling software mainly using their menus – but now, that's mainly older hands. This design suits those who grew up on smartphones and tablets, or who feel more comfortable with their stripped-back keyboardless UI than a full desktop WIMP, which can be overwhelming to newbies and non-techies.

If you've followed the evolution of graphical desktops for some 40 years, as this gray-plumed vulture has, some trends are very apparent that aren't so clear if you came in once evolution was underway.

Apple introduced the first global menu bar in the Lisa, and improved on that in the Macintosh. DR GEM copied it very early on, but Apple sued and DR changed the PC version of GEM to be less Mac-like. Microsoft's Windows came along after this, and moved menu bars inside windows instead. When Apple acquired NeXT in 1996, it moved NeXTstep's patent-avoidant vertical menus back to a global bar at the top, along with the clock and some status indicators. There they remain, 30 years later. In 2007, it launched the iPhone, containing a very cut-down OS based on OS X, replacing the Finder with a cut-down version of the Dashboard layer from OS X 10.4. The panel remained, shorn of its menus, which were too fiddly for a small screen.

As The Register mentioned in 2017, in its preliminary releases, Android started out as a keypad-driven Java phone that looked and worked very much like BlackBerry. When the iPhone appeared, Google changed course. The new Android UI resembled iOS, complete with that top panel, still without menus. GNOME 3.0 was not far behind: in 2009 the team promised a revamp of the user experience, and in 2011, launched GNOME 3.0. It too has the fixed top panel — now huge on a laptop or desktop landscape screen – and mostly empty.

Now that top panel regains its original 1983 function. We're rather impressed by the Orbit global menu. It does the job, and it even works with apps that don't have menu bars. It's not perfect: for instance, over-long menus have to scroll, and may fail to do so if new submenus appear.

The GitHub repository has extensive instructions, including how to build and install the optional connector module that lets more apps export their real menus to the extension. It also tells you how to instruct some apps, notably Firefox, that there is a global menu for it to use. We are saddened to note that, as is so often the case, Wayland gets in the way here.

It works rather well with some other extensions, too. With a menu bar, GNOME's strangely centered clock seems out of place, but several extensions, such as Frippery Move Clock, shove it over to the right where we still feel it belongs. If you prefer a lighter-colored panel and dock, it also plays nicely with Blur my Shell. ®

#10082. Announcing AWS Well-Architected Agent, an AI-powered intelligence to optimize your cloud environment (preview)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing the public preview of AWS Well-Architected Agent, an AI-powered service that analyzes your AWS environment to deliver targeted, contextual recommendations for improving your applications’ cost, security, performance, and resilience. The AWS Well-Architected Agent analyzes your infrastructure, understands unique business goals, and delivers contextual recommendations with ready-to-implement fixes. It delivers context-aware optimization without relying on manual audits or generic checklists.

The agent evaluates your environment as an experienced cloud architect would. It automatically correlates utilization metrics, resource configurations, and application topology, and analyzes against Well-Architected best practices across 65+ AWS services. It generates recommendations aligned to your declared business goals, delivers implementation packages with every finding, and surfaces cross-pillar trade-offs making it simpler to remediate the findings.

Here are the three main features of this service:

AWS Well-Architected Agent in action To get started, create an agent profile to define the scope of what Well-Architected Agent can access and provide recommendations on, complete the IAM role setup to access resources, conduct architecture review, and remediate recommendations.

Create an agent profile In the AWS Well-Architected console, choose Get started with Well-Architected Agent. You can define an agent profile that specifies which AWS accounts and applications to monitor, which optimization pillars to focus on, and the permissions required.

You can choose AWS accounts or AWS Regions to monitor and optimization pillars that matter most to your business. You can also set goals for each pillar: cost optimization, performance, resilience, and security.

To give access to the agent for your AWS environment, provision customer-managed IAM roles the agent uses to read resource configurations, utilization metrics, and application topology. To learn more, visit the IAM prerequisite for AWS Well-Architected Agent.

When you choose Get Started, the agent creates your agent profile. Resource and application recommendations will be generated within 24 hours after profile creation.

You can conduct an architecture review on pre-deployment workloads by uploading an IaC project in Terraform, AWS CloudFormation, or AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) to be analyzed. Choose Conduct architecture review in the dashboard, upload a.zip file containing IaC project or repository file, and select which Well-Architected lens to use for reviewing your infrastructure.

You can define your applications to add context which will enhance the relevancy and further contextualize recommendations. Choose Add application context in the dashboard, add your applications with AWS accounts, AWS Regions, AWS services, tags if you want to narrow the scope to specific resources, and the details of applications.

Review prioritized recommendations and start remediating Now you can see generated prioritized recommendations generated by the agent across your resources and applications, selected pillars, ranked against your declared goals, with automation-ready remediation included.

When you choose the specific recommendation, you can see the details, insights into why the agent are suggesting the recommendation, impacts and trade-off, and recommended fixes across affected AWS resources.

Choose Start remediation to address recommended fixes. You can choose the console, updated IaC template, CLI commands to remediate by the resolution type. It provides detailed step-by-step instructions and you can roll out this instruction and verify the result.

When you choose Using updated IaC template, the agent provides the code changes needed to update your existing IaC templates such as the CDK function shown above which you can copy directly into your codebase.

You can also configure API access to integrate recommendations directly into your existing development and operations workflows. To interact with the agent programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the AWS Well-Architected Agent documentation.

Things to know Here are some things that you should know about the Well-Architected Agent.

You can still use existing AWS Well-Architected Tool to manually evaluate your cloud architecture with user-defined lenses that measure your workload using your own best practices.

Join the preview Access to the AWS Well-Architected Agent and its recommendations is available in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon). You can onboard workloads from any AWS commercial Region. AWS Well-Architected Agent is delivered by AWS Support and available to AWS customers with an AWS Support plan.

Give it a try today in the AWS Well-Architected console and send feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Channy is a Lead Blogger of AWS News Blog and Principal Developer Advocate for AWS Cloud. As an open web enthusiast and blogger at heart, he loves community-driven learning and sharing of technology.

#10078. Rockstar workers vote on union recognition as GTA VI launch looms

UK staff get their say while a separate union-busting dispute heads towards its conclusion

More than 1,600 Rockstar Games employees in the UK will begin voting on union recognition on Thursday, with the ballot kicking off just a week before the long-awaited launch of Grand Theft Auto VI.

The ballot, which opens on November 12 and runs until November 26, will determine whether Rockstar formally recognizes the Rockstar Game Workers Union, part of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB). Nearly all UK employees below director level are eligible to vote.

If successful, the union would become the largest recognized union in the UK games industry, giving workers a collective voice.

The proposed recognition agreement follows four months of negotiations between Rockstar management and employees. It would allow workers to negotiate over pay, overtime, pensions, bonuses, leave and other employment conditions, while securing consultation rights over HR policies and AI.

The vote comes at a particularly busy time for Rockstar, with GTA VI finally due to arrive on November 19, more than 13 years after its predecessor. The game is expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches in history, although the people responsible for making it have rather more immediate concerns than sales records.

"I am incredibly proud of the work we've put into making this game. I'm also proud of the union we've built here. For me, those two things are connected," said Nestor Uriate, an animation programmer and Rockstar Game Workers Union representative.

"We care deeply about the games we make, and we want to make sure we can continue doing that work in an environment where we're respected, have a meaningful say over our conditions and can feel secure about our futures."

The vote follows a year of bad blood between Rockstar and the IWGB. The union accused the GTA developer of union busting after it fired 31 members in October 2025, claiming they had been singled out for taking part in a private Discord group.

Rockstar denied the allegations, insisting the workers were dismissed for gross misconduct rather than their union activities.

The dispute subsequently reached an employment tribunal, where Rockstar unsuccessfully attempted to have blacklisting allegations struck from the case. Closing submissions are expected on November 17 and 18, meaning the legal proceedings will reach their final stages just as GTA VI prepares to hit shelves.

Despite the ongoing dispute, Rockstar's head of publishing, Jennifer Kolbe, recently indicated that management would respect the outcome of the recognition vote, telling Bloomberg: "We go where the team goes. So if they want a union, they will have a union."

The union campaign has also attracted support from elsewhere in the games industry, including SAG-AFTRA and the Communications Workers of America (CWA), which represents workers at Blizzard.

Alex Marshall, president of the IWGB, said the vote was an opportunity for Rockstar employees to take greater control over their working conditions.

"What happens at Rockstar matters beyond the studio. Workers across the games industry are watching, and this ballot is an opportunity to show what can be achieved when people come together, organize and build the collective power to shape their own working lives."

For Rockstar, November was already shaping up to be a big month. By the time GTA VI has been in players' hands for a week, the company should also know whether its UK workforce has voted to secure a formal seat at the negotiating table. ®

#10076. European tech buyers add digital sovereignty to cyber shopping list

Sales from EU HQ'd vendor rocket in two years. The Trump affect? Yes but NIS2 and DORA are factors too

European tech buyers are increasingly choosing cybersecurity vendors from their own continent in a bid to reduce their reliance on American technology.

Digital sovereignty isn't only prompting enterprise customers to question their clouds of choice, it is also reshaping other parts of the industry too, and the shift is marked.

According to sales figures compiled by Context, distributor sales in EMEA of cybersecurity products from EU-headquartered vendors jumped 35 percent in the two years to calendar Q3 2026. Total cybersecurity sales grew up 10 percent over the same period, and sales by US-run companies went up just 8 percent.

That growth is from a relatively small base, though EU vendors gained nearly three percentage points to reach 15 percent of tracked sales by value. There is still a long way to go as US-headquartered vendors accounted for 62 percent.

The trend coincides with a loss of trust in the Trump administration among customers outside of America, after it cosied up to autocratic rulers while criticizing and punishing allies with tariffs and more.

Context stopped short of assigning blame. It said organizations are reviewing their reliance on third-party tech in light of EU compliance  regimes: the NIS2 Directive and Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA).

NIS2, transposed into national law in October 2024, requires organizations in the bloc to raise their common level of security in the face of digital threats and risks to critical infrastructure. DORA, introduced in January last year, is designed to strengthen cyber security in the financial sector.

"Digital sovereignty is becoming a buying decision. As customers and resellers get clearer about what it means in practice, they're asking who holds the encryption keys, who can access sensitive logs and where that data is stored," said Context veep of research Joe Turner.

"We're seeing a measurable shift in the EMEA channel. EU vendors gained nearly three points of sales share in two years. An organization can keep its existing identity platform and still choose a European supplier to manage its security logs. That's the kind of decision that gives European vendors an opening."

The stats indicate that EU-HQd vendors comprised 92 percent of tracked sales in security awareness training, 82 percent in vulnerability management, and 52 percent for SIEM and log management. US-headquartered companies held into 74 percent of identity and access management sales and 54 percent of cloud security sales.

The Reg has asked Context for UK-specific figures to see whether British customers are also voting with their wallets for European alternatives. That certainly isn’t the case for tech purchases in the British public sector, despite Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s professed desire to buy British.

Data released yesterday by the Institute for Public Policy Research showed just £1 in every £6 spent by government with the biggest technology suppliers goes to Brit businesses.

Still, Burnham only came to power in July so there is time yet for him to put his money where his mouth is.

Sovereign AI is another area of concern for enterprise customers. Analyst Omdia said last month that despite the marketing adjective meaning "local assets," almost a third AI providers disclose no proof of sovereignty, and some "expect enterprise to pay for audits to verify their claims."

Omdia also found that 80 percent of contracts say network resilience is "out of providers control or responsibility," and "US-headquartered AI providers offer better service transparency and contract terms than a majority of local sovereign AI providers, with providers in India a notable exception."

Sovereign services in Omdia's classification include data residency, operational autonomy, jurisdictional sovereignty, and technological autonomy.

"Local hosting is not sovereignty. Serious providers must demonstrate their credibility through transparent operations, fair contracts and proof of competence. That includes the network, because data in transit must be sovereign too," said Camille Mendler, research director for telco B2B at Omdia.

Someone should tell Microsoft and Anthropic.  ®

#10072. Microsoft admits SQL Servers might wobble after October update

Linked server connections can linger long past their welcome

Encountered some odd SQL Server connection behavior since the October update? There might be a culprit… Microsoft has admitted that a change has caused linked server queries to fail to close connections.

Linked servers via OLE DB providers have been around for years and are a useful way of, for example, using additional data sources in queries. Once a provider is added, SQL Server can open a connection to grab data, and close it again when the query is complete. Or, at least, that's the theory.

The problem is that after the October 13 (KB5126646) update, connections created by SQL Server linked server queries might remain open. According to Microsoft, "As additional queries are performed, connections to external databases can accumulate instead of closing as expected.

"This can slow or degrade server performance after prolonged run time."

You think? Administrators will likely have already noted a suspicious number of open connections to external databases on affected systems.

Microsoft said the issue affects SQL Server linked server queries that use OLE DB providers to connect to external databases. It gave PostgreSQL and Oracle as examples of connections known to be affected.

And the fix? "If idle connections can be identified, it is possible to manually close them to temporarily relieve server load.

"It is also possible to temporarily restore system stability by restarting the SQL service."

The Windows behemoth went on to state the obvious: "However, these steps can also interrupt active queries or transactions, and the problem can resurface again after sufficient operation time."

Bouncing a SQL Server to deal with connection leakage is less than ideal, although it would at least be a good failover test and, let's face it, having to restart Microsoft services regularly is something many administrators will be all too familiar with.

There is a mitigation available, although only through Microsoft support for business. Otherwise, an out-of-band update should be along within the next few days to deal with the problem.

According to Microsoft, the technical glitch affects every version of Windows except Windows 11 26H2, stretching back to Windows 10 1809 and LTSC 2019, and Windows Server from 2025 back to 2012.

Microsoft, or rather the unfortunate souls responsible for administering their server products, has not had the best time of late. The October 2026 Windows Server update left some Exchange Servers wobbling until either a Registry edit was made or a fix was applied as part of the November update. ®

#10071. All the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Amazon Prime Day 2026 was exclusively for Prime members and ran June 23–26, 2026 with millions of deals across more than 35 categories.

As part of our annual tradition of sharing how AWS powered Prime Day (2016, 2017, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025), I want to share the services and chart-topping metrics from AWS that made your amazing shopping experience possible.

Prime Day 2026 – all the numbers As always, Prime Day was powered by AWS. Here are some of the most interesting and/or mind-blowing metrics:

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and AWS Graviton – During Amazon Prime Day 2026, AWS Graviton powered up to 49% of the Amazon EC2 compute used by Amazon.com.

Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon EBS, our high-performance block storage service, peaked at over 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving over an exabyte of data daily.

AWS Lambda – AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) and Fargate – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon ECS launched an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, representing a 47.7 percent increase from the previous year’s Prime Day average.

Amazon CloudFront – Amazon CloudFront delivered over 2.1 trillion HTTP requests during the global week of Prime Day 2026, a 5 percent increase in total requests compared to Prime Day 2025.

Amazon DynamoDB – Amazon DynamoDB, a serverless, fully managed, distributed NoSQL database, powers multiple high-traffic Amazon properties and systems including Alexa, the Amazon.com sites, and all Amazon fulfillment centers. Over the course of Prime Day 2026, between June 23 and June 26, 2026, DynamoDB processed over 59 trillion requests. DynamoDB maintained high availability while delivering single-digit millisecond responses and peaking at 192 million requests per second.

Amazon Aurora – On Prime Day, Amazon Aurora, a relational database management system (RDBMS) built for high performance and availability at global scale for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and DSQL, processed hundreds of billions of transactions, stored 5,491 terabytes of data, and transferred 1,194 terabytes of data.

Amazon ElastiCache – During Prime Day, Amazon ElastiCache peaked at serving over 2.3 quadrillion daily requests and 2.1 trillion requests in a minute.

Amazon Kinesis Data Streams – Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, a fully managed serverless data streaming service, processed a peak of 988 million records per second during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) – Amazon SNS, a fully managed pub/sub messaging service for application-to-application and application-to-person communication, delivered 5 trillion messages in a single day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) – Amazon SQS, a fully managed message queuing service for microservices, distributed systems, and serverless applications, received a peak of 213 million messages per second during Prime Day 2026

AWS CloudTrail – AWS CloudTrail processes billions of API activity events per day for governance, compliance, and operational auditing. During Prime Day 2026, that volume surged to 3.6 trillion events in just four days, a 44% increase over Prime Day 2025.

Amazon CloudWatch – Amazon CloudWatch processed over 2.15 quadrillion metric observations per day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon GuardDuty – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon GuardDuty monitored an average of 14.08 trillion log events per hour, a 59% increase from last year’s Prime Day.

AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) – We ran over 44,000 AWS FIS experiments – more than six times what we conducted in 2025 – to help ensure Amazon.com remains highly available on Prime Day.

Prepare to scale If you’re preparing for similar business-critical events, product launches, and migrations, I recommend that you take advantage of AWS Countdown Premium. From retail peak seasons to major sporting events, elections, and healthcare enrollment periods, we help you deliver flawless experiences when it matters most. Our experts help you manage your infrastructure to handle massive traffic spikes while maintaining security and performance. We work alongside your team to scale infrastructure, optimize costs during demand surges, strengthen security measures, and monitor real-time demands. To learn more, visit AWS Countdown Premium for business critical events.

I look forward to seeing what other records will be broken next year!

#10069. Announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions, a new form factor that lets you run standard HTTP web applications on Lambda without rewriting your code into an event handler. You can take a standard port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or any Node.js framework, deploy it with a single command, and Lambda automatically handles scaling, multi-region distribution, and active CPU billing. No adapters, no infrastructure to manage, and no framework lock-in.

With this launch, AWS Lambda now offers three distinct form factors, each built on the same Firecracker isolation technology and designed for a different programming model.

Lambda Event Functions are what you already know as Lambda functions. They use the event-driven, single-concurrent handler model with wall-clock billing. We’re introducing the “Event Functions” name to highlight that programming model: your function receives an event, processes it, and returns a response. The event-driven programming model is ideal for event processing, queue consumers, and invocations triggered by other AWS services.

Lambda Web Functions use an HTTP-native programming model with multi-concurrent execution and active CPU billing. Your code listens on a port and handles standard HTTP requests. That programming model is ideal for web applications, API backends, and interactive HTTP workloads where multiple concurrent requests and I/O-heavy processing are the norm.

Lambda MicroVMs provide isolated, stateful sandbox environments with customer-managed lifecycles for running untrusted or user-generated code.

The three complement each other. An application might use Event Functions for asynchronous backend processing, Web Functions for the user-facing API and server-side rendering layer, and MicroVMs for interactive code execution features, all within the same AWS account and sharing the same operational model.

Why Web FunctionsModern web applications need to serve global audiences with fast, consistent response times while giving developers the freedom to use standard frameworks and iterate quickly. Building this today typically requires assembling multiple infrastructure components, configuring multi-region deployments, setting up latency-based routing, and tuning billing models to avoid paying for I/O wait. Developers often find themselves adapting their application code to fit a specific compute model rather than deploying the HTTP server they already have.

Lambda Web Functions removes this complexity. Each execution environment handles multiple requests simultaneously (up to 128 concurrent requests per environment), which means a burst of incoming traffic can share warm environments instead of mapping each request to a new one. Web Functions meter the CPU time your code uses, so time spent waiting on a database query or an API call consumes little CPU. Memory is metered for as long as the execution environment exists. For I/O-heavy web workloads like server-side rendering, API backends, and AI inference endpoints streaming token responses, this can reduce compute costs.

Let’s try it outTo get started, I wrote a simple Express.js server. This is the same code I run locally with node index.js, no Lambda-specific adapters or wrappers required.

The only difference from running locally is the AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT environment variable, which Lambda sets to the host and port your server must listen on. To run locally, set it yourself, for example AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:3000 node index.js.

With my code ready, I deployed using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI):

One command. No prior resource setup. The CLI bundled my source, created the Web Function, published its first revision, attached a Web Function endpoint, and returned a live HTTPS URL in under a minute.

A revision is an immutable snapshot of the code I deployed. The endpoint is the HTTPS URL that routes traffic to a revision, or splits traffic across revisions. Those are the resources I use to iterate and to control how traffic moves to new code.

Next, I wanted my application to serve users in Europe and Asia with lower latency. I redeployed with multiple regions:

Lambda Web Functions replicated my code to all three regions and configured latency-based routing automatically. Each request now routes to the Region with the lowest latency for the caller, on a best-effort basis, through one global URL (.lambda-web.global.on.aws).

When I updated my code and ran the same deploy command again, the CLI detected the existing function, uploaded the new revision, and pointed the endpoint at it. Total turnaround from code change to live: seconds.

For production workflows that require a more gradual rollout, I can shift traffic between revisions with a single API call:

This sends 90% of endpoint traffic to the current revision and 10% to the new one, giving me a canary deployment without additional tooling.

Better together with Amazon CloudFrontFor applications that combine static and dynamic content, Web Functions works well alongside Amazon CloudFront. You can select a Web Function endpoint as the origin for your CloudFront distribution. Static assets are served from the cache while dynamic requests route to your Web Function, giving you CDN performance for static content with serverless compute for the dynamic parts.

Web Functions improves the private-origin experience with CloudFront. With this launch, you attach CloudFront origin access control (OAC) to a Web Function endpoint instead. CloudFront signs requests to the origin, and the endpoint allows only your distribution to invoke it. You get the same private-origin pattern CloudFront already provides for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), without exposing the endpoint or adding custom authorization to your app.

Now availableAWS Lambda Web Functions is available today in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). Web Functions run Node.js 24 (nodejs24.x) on Arm64 at launch and support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC.

To get started, deploy your first Web Function in under a minute:

For pricing details, visit the AWS Lambda pricing page. To learn more, see the Lambda Web Functions documentation.

#10068. The latest FreeBSD report is here, and the AI debate is ongoing

Only a minority want to ban it. Plus plenty of updates on 16 projects

The FreeBSD project's status team has published FreeBSD's third status report of 2026, showing plenty of ambitious work underway and a community still undecided on how to treat code from AI coding assistants.

The FreeBSD Status Report Third Quarter 2026 is a substantial document, with 51 entries from five teams covering 16 projects, plus six other sections with more detailed reports.

There are updates on the progress of the Sylve project, which is an attempt to bring a smooth polished GUI for managing FreeBSD virtualization hosts – something akin to Proxmox for FreeBSD. We mentioned this when we looked at the new Daemonarchy project last month. Another covers the new AppJail effort – a containerized app distribution system for FreeBSD, including for GUI apps, which aims for something broadly comparable to Snap, Flatpak and AppImage on Linux.

In other words, interesting and quite radical stuff is happening in the FreeBSD space.

What this particular LLM-skeptical vulture was most interested to see, though, was an update on the internal discussion about how to handle code generated by AI coding assistants in the project. We first reported on this vexed subject back in September 2025 and no final answer has yet been published.

NetBSD banned AI-generated code in 2024 and although the bot-boosters say this will doom it to irrelevance, as we reported last month, the project is thriving. Also back in October, we looked at OpenBSD 8.0, whose launch materials are full of mockery for AI users.

Under the FreeBSD Core Team section, there is a subsection headed "FreeBSD Developer AI survey." The survey was created by Baptiste Daroussin, and received 140 responses. Although the percentages show that there is some resistance to AI, there are hints here as to why it’s taking so long. Some project committers are against it, yet many more are proponents. Since there are only seven bullet points, we thought we would quote them in full:

Policy: 88 percent want the Project to adopt a policy, either a formal, written policy (49 percent) or light guidance and best practices (39 percent). Six  percent said that AI should be explicitly discouraged, and three percent that the existing contribution rules are sufficient.

AI-assisted code: 35  percent said it must be disclosed, 25 percent that it must be reviewed more strictly than human code, 22 percent that it should be treated like any other contribution, and 16 percent that it should be rejected outright.

Safeguards: mandatory human review (78 percent) and mandatory disclosure (69 percent) were requested most often, followed by provenance or licensing documentation (47 percent) and mandatory testing (39 percent).

Disclosure: 84 percent want AI use disclosed, either always (48 percent) or when its involvement is significant (36 percent). 79 percent want AI-assisted commits marked in the commit log, and 56 percent prefer a tag that names the tool.

Concerns: the main concerns about quality are correctness and subtle bugs (39 percent, licensing and provenance (26 percent), and maintainability (21 percent). 75 percent are somewhat or very concerned about copyright and licensing.

Principles: accountability, meaning that a human remains responsible (91 percent), and transparency (78 percent) were selected most often, and preserving code quality was the top-ranked goal for a policy.

Other uses: 65 percent would allow AI-generated documentation with human review. 54 percent would allow AI tools on Project infrastructure, most of them with restrictions, and 29 percent would not.

Only six percent for explicit discouragement, 16 percent for outright rejection,  and 35 percent against LLM-generated documentation. This plus the usual sort of calls for responsible use and disclosure, concerns about copyright issues, and so on.

The Reg is strongly reminded of the Debian developer poll we reported on in August. This had no fewer than four slightly different AI-refusal options out of eight, and despite the Condorcet voting method it uses, the result was giving permission to use bots.

With such relatively weak opposition, we suspect that FreeBSD will go the same way as Debian: tell developers to be careful, but allow bot usage, resulting in LLM-extruded code being committed into the project. ®
