#10044. Why Specialization Is Inevitable

Those who follow Dharma AI already know that we view specialization as one of the defining principles of effective AI systems, shaping everything from cost and performance to reliability and sovereignty. Few papers have articulated that case as rigorously as the 2026 work by Goldfeder, Wyder, LeCun, and Shwartz-Ziv.

In this article, we explore and interpret ideas from AI Must Embrace Specialization via Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence (Goldfeder, Wyder, LeCun, & Shwartz-Ziv, 2026). The paper's convergence case — spanning optimization theory, biology, organizational economics, and machine learning — provides both the evidential structure and the intellectual foundation for the discussion that follows. The framing, organization, and editorial synthesis presented here are Dharma's.

The conventional expectation is reasonable: as AI systems grow more capable, they should also grow more general. Greater capability and broader applicability seem like natural companions — more resources, better methods, and expanded training should produce systems that approach more tasks with increasing confidence.

The pattern that actually appears is different. The systems that achieve the most significant results in any given domain tend to be the ones most narrowly focused on it. The breakthrough in protein structure prediction came from a system engineered for a single scientific task. The historical milestones of AI, examined closely, reflect intense domain targeting rather than expanding generality.

This pattern recurs. It recurs across domains, across decades, across architectural choices that have almost nothing in common. A pattern this consistent suggests a common cause — one that does not originate inside AI research at all.

In 1997, Wolpert and Macready proved something that rarely surfaces in discussions of AI architecture: no single, general-purpose optimization algorithm outperforms all others across all possible problems (Wolpert & Macready, 1997). The proof is mathematical, not philosophical. Averaged across every conceivable problem a learner might face, every algorithm performs equally well — and equally poorly. An algorithm that gains on one distribution of problems necessarily concedes on others. The performance is redistributed, not multiplied.

The practical implication is direct: “an algorithm wins by being a good fit for the target problem” (Goldfeder et al., 2026). The theorem does not say generality is impossible — it says generality is not a performance advantage. The consistent structural path to outperformance is concentration: trading breadth for fit.

This becomes sharper when finite resources enter the picture. Any real system operates under constraints — finite compute, finite data, finite development time. Given finite energy, an approach that directs available resources toward learning a finite set of tasks will outperform one that distributes those same resources across an unlimited range. The arithmetic is unforgiving: as the task set expands without bound, the resources available per task shrink toward zero. Universal coverage and meaningful performance are, under finite resources, in direct tension.

The conclusion the theorem points toward is not that generality is bad. It is narrower and more operational than that: as the paper states, "universal generality is a theoretical concept, but in practical terms it is a myth" (Goldfeder et al., 2026). What survives contact with real constraints is not the system that tries to do everything — it is the system that fits its target.

The mathematics establishes this as a prediction, not a preference. Whether that prediction holds in the world beyond optimization theory is a different question.

Two other domains arrived at the same prediction before optimization theory gave it a name.

As the paper describes the biological case: every performance gain in one niche comes at a cost elsewhere. A generalist carries traits suited to many environments but optimal for none — competence spread too thin to dominate any particular condition. There are no performance gains without trade-offs; the resources invested in one capability are unavailable for another. Selection favors designs matched to local conditions over those optimized for uniform coverage across all possible environments. The organisms that survive to reproduce are not the most generally capable — they are the most specifically matched. The result, accumulated over evolutionary timescales, is not generalists dominating — it is specialists filling niches. As the paper states: "Specialization is not an accident of biology; it is a predictable consequence of limited resources, competing objectives, and environments that reward performance on a small subset of evolutionarily relevant challenges" (Goldfeder et al., 2026).

Competitive markets follow the same dynamic through different means. Organizations and strategies that fail to meet performance thresholds are eliminated — not through extinction, but through exit, defunding, and replacement by better-matched alternatives. Competition acts as a selection mechanism: it amplifies effective strategies and eliminates ineffective ones. The mechanism has nothing in common with biological selection — no inheritance, no mutation, no evolutionary timescale. The unit of selection is not the organism but the organization, the product, the strategy. Yet the structural pressure is the same: finite resources, performance requirements, and the systematic removal of entities too broadly distributed to excel where it counts. Concentrated capacity outcompetes distributed capacity when performance standards are clear and consistent.

Evolution and markets operate through entirely different mechanisms — different timescales, different units of selection, different inheritance mechanisms. Yet both produce the same outcome under resource pressure: fit over breadth. The theorem predicts this. Biology and markets arrive at it independently. When a third domain arrives at the same finding through different means entirely, the pattern ceases to look like a theorem and begins to look like something more general about how constrained systems behave.

The same pattern has emerged inside machine learning — not derived from optimization theory, but arrived at through the accumulated experience of building systems and watching what improves them.

The clearest form is negative transfer: a measurable degradation that occurs when a system trained on multiple tasks suffers because those tasks compete rather than cooperate (Ruder, 2017). When tasks share structure, training together helps. But when tasks compete for representational capacity, or impose conflicting gradients during training, performance on individual tasks falls below what a dedicated system would achieve. The gain from breadth becomes a cost to depth. It is a documented consequence of dividing finite capacity across tasks that pull against each other. The specialist, facing no such competition, does not pay this cost.

The architecture of frontier models offers a different form of evidence. Mixture-of-experts systems achieve their breadth not through uniform generality across all parameters, but by routing each input to a specialized subset of the network — activating different experts for different tasks. The paper's authors read this as a structural concession: a system designed to be general achieving its results by recovering specialization internally. This is an argued interpretation, not a demonstrated theorem — these architectures were designed for computational efficiency, and what they imply about generality's limits is a reasonable inference rather than a stated intent. But it is a notable one: the most capable general-purpose systems reach their performance by doing internally what specialist systems do by design.

The clearest historical example follows the same logic. AlphaFold achieved a step change in protein structure prediction by targeting that specific task with task-specific architecture and training choices (Jumper et al., 2021). Its gains came from narrower focus, not broader coverage. The paper uses AlphaFold as an archetypal case — not as evidence that all specialized systems achieve equivalent gains, but as an unusually clear illustration of the mechanism. That mechanism has appeared repeatedly: the history of AI milestones, the paper notes, frequently reflects intense domain targeting rather than broad competence, even when the results look like demonstrations of general intelligence.

Three distinct places. Three different mechanisms. The same finding.

The picture would be incomplete without addressing one of AI research's most cited observations. Sutton's Bitter Lesson holds that methods relying on domain knowledge are consistently outperformed by methods that scale computation (Sutton, 2019). On its face, this appears to complicate the case for specialization: if scale and generality win, perhaps specialization is only a useful heuristic under resource constraints that will ease as compute becomes cheaper.

The objection rests on a conflation between two distinct concepts. Domain knowledge refers to hand-coded features, engineered priors, and rules designed to give a system insight into a particular area. The Bitter Lesson targets this — and it is correct to do so. Systems that encode explicit domain knowledge have been consistently outperformed as scale increases.

Domain specialization is different: the decision to direct a system's resources, architecture, and training toward a bounded set of tasks rather than distributing them broadly. This is not the encoding of knowledge about a domain. It is a decision about scope.

The paper draws the distinction precisely:

"The diminishing usefulness of domain knowledge is distinct from the usefulness of domain specialization. As scaling progresses, we will need to know less about proteins to build a system that does protein folding; however, such a system still benefits from focusing specifically on proteins." (Goldfeder et al., 2026)

Scaling changes what systems can learn from data. It does not change whether concentrating resources on a finite task set outperforms distributing them across an unlimited range. The Bitter Lesson and the specialization argument operate on different dimensions — one describes how knowledge should be acquired, the other describes what a system should be pointed at. Both can be true simultaneously. Scaling changes the mechanisms by which systems learn; it does not dissolve the constraint that makes fit more valuable than breadth.

Across four analytical traditions, the same pattern emerged through different paths. This is not a coincidence that demands explanation. It is the evidence.

When finite resources meet selection pressure — in an optimization problem, an ecosystem, a market, or a training run — fit consistently beats breadth. The specific mechanisms differ. The timescales differ. The units of selection differ. But the structural dynamic is the same, and it produces the same result.

The theorem does not cause this pattern in biology. Biology does not cause it in markets. Neither causes it in machine learning. They all face the same underlying constraint: performance under scarcity requires concentration. What the theorem establishes mathematically, evolutionary history confirms empirically, competitive markets demonstrate institutionally, and machine learning rediscovers architecturally.

Specialization is not a preference. It is what emerges when finite resources meet the requirement to perform.

If you're evaluating how domain focus affects AI performance in your organization — or building the case internally for a specialization strategy — we'd like to hear about your context. Get in touch with Dharma AI.

Forister, M.L., Novotny, V., Panorska, A.K., Baje, L., Basset, Y., Butterill, P.T., & Dyer, L.A. (2012). Global distribution of diet breadth in insect herbivores. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 109(2), 418–423.

Futuyma, D.J. & Moreno, G. (1988). The evolution of ecological specialization. Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics, 19, 207–233.

Hannan, M.T. & Freeman, J. (1977). The population ecology of organizations. American Journal of Sociology, 82(5), 929–964.

Loasby, B.J. (1983). Knowledge, learning and the firm. As cited in Goldfeder et al. (2026).

Ruder, S. (2017). An overview of multi-task learning in deep neural networks. arXiv:1706.05098.

Where the No Free Lunch theorem establishes why specialization is structurally predicted, this piece examines the evidence that it outperforms in practice — and why it remains underweighted in most AI procurement decisions.

I would add that in the era of AI Agents, deploying a new hyperspecialized agent with a very narrow domain and less prompts/context, would lead to less hallucinations and less token comsuption. It's cheap and convenient, so is the most probable path in my opinion.

The top line thesis — specialization beats generality — is (forgive me) something of a PGIO (penetrating glimpse into the obvious). I do appreciate the distinction between domain knowledge and domain specialization. They're not the same axis, and conflating them is a common mistake. Regretably, the authors stop right where things get interesting. Domain knowledge's value-add is described as diminishing as scale increases, with no stated floor. Specialization's value-add is described as persisting; not growing, just not eroding the way knowledge does. That's a decline running against a flat line, not two things moving in the same direction at different speeds. The authors never say where that decline runs out, or when investing further in expert content stops paying off — compared to just narrowing scope. A distinction this precise about what specialization is deserves precision about when to stop chasing knowledge and start chasing focus. How much is enough? 10K hours worth (a la Malcolm Gladwell)?

Great point, and I agree that this is where the discussion becomes most interesting.

It is not possible to say where the decline bottoms out, since neural networks learn representations through superposition rather than assigning individual neurons or subnetworks to specific domains. In other words, it is not possible to isolate parts of the network and claim that they are responsible for domain X or domain Y, as these domains are encoded through overlapping representations. What we can affirm is that it depends on the relationship between breadth of domains in the knowledge base and the number of parameters of the model (the greater the parameters, the greater the capacity to retain knowledge). To answer this question, we would need some way of measuring the amount of domain knowledge contained in the training data, as well as the degree of overlap between those domains in the latent space learned by a highly non-linear neural network. I believe this question is currently intractable.

Regarding the point at which investing in specialized content ceases to pay off, I believe that this only happens when the objective is to build a genuinely more general-purpose model. If the goal is to use the available resources (parameters) to provide shallow responses across a broad range of topics, then it makes more sense to train on a dataset with broad coverage but relatively little depth in each domain. On the other hand, if the objective is to build a model that solves a finite and relatively small set of tasks, more specialized data will always be the better choice. Naturally, as you increase the size of that task set, you eventually return to the first scenario of wanting a general-purpose model.

The same reasoning applies to the question of when we should pursue greater focus: whenever the scope of the application is itself focused. It is fundamentally a design choice. If you are training a model for open-ended tasks that may receive any type of input, it is better to have a model that responds superficially across many topics than one that responds deeply to only a few. Conversely, if the application has a well-defined scope, it will always be better to train a model specialized for that scope, making more efficient use of its resources instead of spending them on knowledge that will never be required.

That said, these are very relevant questions, and we hope to address at least part of them through mechanistic interpretability, which is one of the research areas within our R&D efforts. The techniques in this field allow us to observe internal circuits within models, sparsely used neurons, neurons that activate under specific conditions, and other internal mechanisms. This may help us better understand how models work internally and answer some of your questions more directly.

#10043. AWS Weekly Roundup: GPT-6.1 Terra on Bedrock, Step Functions as agent tools, and more (November 2, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

The agentic launches that stayed with me last week had nothing to do with how capable a model is. They were about reach. AWS Step Functions, which already orchestrates over 220 AWS services, can now be handed to an agent as a tool, so workflows teams already trust became callable without a rewrite. In the same week, the AI blog published how one engagement platform exposed roughly 400 internal API operations the same way. Neither story involves rebuilding anything, only describing what exists and letting the agent find it.

The other thread was cost. OpenAI’s newest Terra model reached Amazon Bedrock priced well below the model beside it, and two post-quantum launches landed for a deadline nobody can put on a calendar yet. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesOpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, and what interests me is where it sits rather than what it tops. Terra is the everyday-workload line of the GPT-6 family. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than both. Those are OpenAI’s figures, not an independent test. The price is what I would check first: input and output tokens are at least 50% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It takes up to 1 million input tokens with text and image input, and you can reach it from the Bedrock APIs or ChatGPT Work and Codex.

AWS Step Functions workflows are now available as AI agent tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, which connects agents to tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The division of labor is the idea: the agent decides when to run a workflow and what input to pass; Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. A support agent can trigger a refund, and the eligibility check, the manager approval, and the credit still happen in that order every time, because the ordering was never the model’s to improvise. Your existing Standard and Express workflows qualify as connector targets, and agents can also look up runs. It’s available in all Regions where AgentCore Gateway is, at standard rates.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation – You can now establish a shared secret with a post-quantum algorithm using AWS KMS keys, with private keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs. All three NIST FIPS 203 parameter sets are supported through Encapsulate, which produces a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext, and Decapsulate, which recovers it. The threat is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary records today’s key exchange and recovers the secret once quantum computers are powerful enough. It’s available everywhere KMS runs except the Middle East (UAE and Bahrain) and China Regions. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL added post-quantum TLS key exchange the same week, on versions 18 and higher.

AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation – You can now carry a user’s identity with their request to AWS services in another Region. This removes a genuine architectural constraint: trusted identity propagation used to require every service accessing that identity to sit in the same Region, which left two unappealing options, broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users, or consolidating all your services into a single Region. Now the identity travels with the request automatically, so you grant access by user and group membership and audit who accessed what. It’s available at no additional cost everywhere IAM Identity Center runs.

Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) – You can now run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU, the practical answer to work that only ever uses a fraction of one, like small-model inference and multi-model serving. You declare the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally cap its share of GPU compute, and ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale, with no code changes. It works on ECS Managed Instances and ECS on Amazon EC2, and on Managed Instances it watches the MPS control daemon and replaces the instance if it turns unhealthy. It’s available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances – You can now have AWS Lambda fetch only the files needed at each stage of startup instead of pulling a whole container image first, which AWS puts at up to 70% off container startup time. You create a SOCI index, push it to Amazon ECR, point the image URI at the indexed tag, and Lambda detects it automatically. The technique also reached Amazon SageMaker AI training and processing jobs, with benchmarks: lazy loading held at 3 to 11 seconds regardless of image size, against a median 3 minutes 42 seconds for a 13.2 GB image, a range they report as 8x to 46x.

Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports Kubernetes Gateway API – You can now declare how traffic reaches your applications with Gateway and HTTPRoute resources on Amazon EKS without installing a separate controller, and EKS Auto Mode provisions and manages the underlying AWS load balancing infrastructure. You get HTTP and gRPC routing, cross-namespace routing, weighted traffic splitting, header-based routing, and automatic TLS certificate discovery through AWS Certificate Manager. Existing Ingress workloads keep working alongside them, so this is additive rather than a migration. Gateway API support is included with EKS Auto Mode; standard load balancing charges apply.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

How Nubank automated disaster recovery with the AWS DevOps Agent – Nubank serves more than 140 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, and classifies over 300 business flows as critical, each tested on a regulator’s schedule. Nubank reports that handing evidence collection and report writing to the AWS DevOps Agent cut a test cycle from about 4.3 hours to roughly 40 minutes, and quadrupled flow coverage in 2026 to more than 160. One execution terminated more than 900 EKS instances under synthetic traffic with AWS Fault Injection Service, producing the evidence its regulator needed.

How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway – Roughly 400 internal REST API operations, built by 25 teams, sitting in private VPCs across seven Regions, with tenant identity that could never become a parameter the model gets to set. MoEngage estimates the managed path saved about six months of platform engineering. The detail worth stealing: a full tool listing would have crossed 20,000 tokens per connection, so agents search for tools by describing a task instead of receiving the catalog.

Reducing petabyte-scale S3 storage costs with evidence-based lifecycle rules – The hard part isn’t deciding to act, it’s knowing which data has gone cold and where it can safely live. This uses S3 Storage Lens groups and Storage Class Analysis to prove access patterns before moving anything. In the engagement described, 5.8 PB of logs in Amazon S3 Standard at approximately $241,000 per month showed an access ratio below 0.1% past 90 days, and a 90-day transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval cut the bill by roughly 70%, a figure the author ties to that workload.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, with more than 2,200 sessions. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders. The 2026 season is winding down as re:Invent approaches, so check the hub for what’s still on.

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

#10042. Software Samaritan revamps borked Indian certs to block smart TV ads

A little tinkering can black hole obnoxious Samsung TV ads and some tracking, until a firmware fix ruins the fun

eMudhra's private key exposure has been a security disaster, but it also means that you can block those annoying ads on smart TVs if you’re so inclined.

Luckily for those with some know-how and a hatred of smart TV ads, Czech software developer Daniel Vrátil has done the work for you and published his project on GitHub for anyone who wants to take a stab at it - and do the legwork to add support for their own ad-riddled television.

Vrátil said he’d been blocking ads on his Samsung smart TV using a Pi-hole (DNS-based ad-blocking software that can run on a Raspberry Pi, for those unfamiliar), but right around the time the eMudhra certificate leak mess unfolded, he had messed something up while tinkering with his home lab and the ads were back.

First, here's a bit of background on the eMudhra mess. The company, based in India, operated a publicly trusted HTTPS certificate authority and says it has issued more than 60 million digital certificates. As we learned last month, eMudhra wasn't doing its best to keep its cryptographic keys safe: Eight intermediate CA private keys were found to be absurdly weak, with one being the number four and the others consisting of two- or three-digit numbers that could be guessed with little effort.

eMudhra has since left the CA racket, saying that it wasn’t a big deal to it since issuing certs was a small part of its business. The company has blamed a bad software script put in place to generate keys that its hardware couldn’t handle as the root of the issue.

What all that means, in a practical sense, is that anyone could forge an eMudhra certificate to spoof a website and do something malicious. It also means that security researchers who were able to get their hands on devices that still trust eMudhra certificates could have a field day learning how their communications work, which is exactly what Vrátil took advantage of.

eMudhra private keys were added to the open source mitmproxy service - a fully interactive HTTPS proxy that can be used for good or bad - shortly after they were exposed. Pair that with a 2022 Samsung smart TV that still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates, and you have a way to inspect its HTTPS traffic and redirect selected requests to a server of your choosing.

By Vrátil’s account, swapping out annoying ads for pictures of his family on his TV’s main screen was a pretty simple task.

“Luckily for me, Samsung did not yet release an update for my TV that would revoke the certificate,” Vrátil explained in his writeup. “This allowed me to route all traffic from the TV through mitmproxy and get a list of all the domains and endpoints that my TV talks to, but also see the structure of the requests and response payloads.”

The advertising traffic flow was pretty basic, it turns out: Activity on the TV is relayed to an ad server, which serves up ads on the home screen based on a JSON response. By generating a certificate for Samsung's advertising domains using a compromised eMudhra signing key, and configuring his router to direct requests for those domains to a server on his home network, Vrátil was able to replace ads with family photos served from his NAS. He also added code that tosses other requests to those advertising domains, including tracking data, into a black hole rather than forwarding them to Samsung's servers.

As mentioned above, it’s on GitHub for those who want to trick their TV, if it still supports eMudhra certificates, but you’ll have to do the legwork to dissect how your device is getting ads and tweak the code to work.

“It's not exactly a one-click setup,” Vrátil told The Register in an email. He’s invited people to try it out, but no one has bothered to submit a pull request to add support for their own device to his public repo.

It’s also worth noting that this is only going to work as long as vulnerable devices keep trusting eMudhra certificates, which hopefully means you need to act fast. That said, smart TVs that are out of support may never receive such an update, leaving them exposed to the certificate weakness even if their owners block the ads.

“The compromised eMudhra certificates open up a lot of opportunities for understanding and spoofing network requests from embedded devices, especially those that no longer receive security updates,” Vrátil told us. “And while replacing ads on a TV's home screen with pictures of my family is fun, there are also countless much more sinister applications of this vulnerability.”

As for Vrátil, he’s still trying to figure out how to block the firmware update that may eventually render his method obsolete, even though that, as he points out, is a security risk in and of itself.

“I want to run the traffic through a proxy that would validate the connection against an up-to-date trust store to at least mitigate anyone intercepting traffic from my TV, or spoofing responses, like I do with my little project here, but it won't protect me from other potential security risks, so there's a trade-off,” he explained.

We suppose at this point you can take your pick of abuse. You can use a vulnerability to block ads and some tracking while leaving your TV exposed to potential interception, or let the manufacturer serve up ads and collect data about your viewing habits. There are safer ways to block ads than relying on a TV to keep trusting a compromised CA. ®

#10041. ScarfBench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Enterprise Java Framework Migration

Modernizing enterprise applications is one of the largest and most expensive software engineering activities organizations undertake. Teams migrate applications across frameworks to improve maintainability, cloud readiness, developer productivity, and access to modern capabilities.

Recent advances in coding agents have sparked excitement around AI-assisted modernization. But an important question remains:

Can AI agents reliably modernize real-world enterprise applications?

Existing software engineering benchmarks have demonstrated impressive progress in bug fixing and code generation, but framework migration presents a fundamentally different challenge. Success requires not only translating code, but also preserving behavior, adapting build systems, and navigating runtime dependencies.

To address this gap, we introduce ScarfBench (Self-Contained Application Refactoring Benchmark), an open benchmark for evaluating AI agents on cross-framework migration tasks in Enterprise Java.

ScarfBench focuses on migrations across three major Java ecosystems:

Unlike traditional benchmarks that compare generated code against reference implementations, ScarfBench evaluates whether migrated applications actually build, deploy, and preserve behavior.

Framework migration is much more than replacing annotations.

A simple repository migration can require changes across dependency injection, persistence configuration, queries, and framework descriptors. Small mistakes in any of these pieces can prevent successful deployment.

Figure: Spring → Jakarta Migration Example

Framework migration requires translating framework semantics, not just source code.

ScarfBench provides a systematic way to evaluate AI agents on enterprise Java framework migration tasks.

This provides a much more realistic measure of modernization quality.

ScarfBench includes both focused migration tasks and whole-application migrations.

Starting from a JSR-based enterprise Java taxonomy, expert migrations create verified implementations across Spring, Jakarta EE, and Quarkus.

We evaluated several state-of-the-art coding agents on ScarfBench.

Despite strong performance on traditional software engineering benchmarks, framework migration remains difficult. Success rates vary considerably across framework pairs and whole-application migrations remain particularly challenging.

Figure: Compile → Deploy → Test Progression

Compile success consistently exceeds deploy success, which in turn exceeds behavioral success. Build success alone significantly overestimates migration quality.

Figure: Migration Outcomes by Target Framework

Migration difficulty depends strongly on the target framework, with Jakarta EE proving particularly challenging.

Beyond measuring success rates, ScarfBench helps us understand how agents behave during modernization.

A migrated application is only useful if it actually builds and runs.

We therefore compared agent-reported outcomes against independent build verification.

Claude Code reported successful builds for 29 out of 30 whole applications.

Only 22 of those applications actually built successfully.

Meanwhile, the single application classified as failed by the agent ultimately built correctly.

This suggests that agent self-assessment should not be treated as a reliable signal of migration completion.

Independent build and test validation remains essential.

Framework migrations rarely affect a single file or layer.

Changes in configuration, services, databases, and web components often cascade across the application.

This suggests that migration is an iterative dependency-resolution process rather than a simple source-to-source transformation.

We used layer revisit frequency as a proxy for migration effort. Layers that required repeated visits typically involved debugging, dependency resolution, or framework adaptation.

Rather than proceeding linearly, agents repeatedly returned to configuration-related artifacts while resolving framework differences and dependency issues.

Not every migration issue originates from source code.

Agents frequently struggled with environmental issues, including:

These operational concerns often delayed validation even when the source-code migration itself was largely complete.

Modernization failures span build systems, deployment environments, dependency injection, databases, endpoints, assertions, and infrastructure.

The biggest challenge in framework modernization is not translating Java code.

It is managing the web of dependencies across configuration, infrastructure, and runtime environments.

While frontier agents can automate substantial portions of the migration process, reliable validation and architectural reasoning remain critical for achieving successful outcomes.

ScarfBench helps expose these challenges and provides a standardized way to measure progress toward truly autonomous application modernization.

ScarfBench is designed as an open resource for researchers and practitioners.

Researchers can compare agent architectures and techniques. Practitioners can use ScarfBench to evaluate modernization solutions before deploying them in production environments.

https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-research/ScarfBench

https://huggingface.co/spaces/ibm-research/ScarfBench

Framework migration remains one of the largest unsolved problems in AI-assisted software engineering. We hope ScarfBench helps the community measure progress and accelerate the next generation of AI-assisted application modernization.

We invite researchers, practitioners, and framework communities to evaluate their agents, contribute new migration scenarios and help advance the state of the art.

#10040. Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing a simple, cost-effective path for data lake modernization. Amazon S3 Tables now support managed migration of your Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg. Migration works with Parquet tables in Amazon S3 that are registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and allows you to upgrade your data lake with no pipelines to build or compute to provision, while production workloads keep running.

Apache Iceberg has become the open standard for large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data open and queryable with any Iceberg-compatible engine. Amazon S3 Tables offer fully managed storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with features like automatic maintenance, optimization, replication, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering built-in.

What is new Previously, migrating Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg could take weeks of engineering work to build and manage the required infrastructure. Converting data types and building rollback capabilities added operational complexity. Now, this is available as a managed, API-driven operation.

S3 Tables handle the entire migration workflow, including data validation, compatibility checks, type conversions, file recompression, and compaction. Before copying any data, S3 Tables identify every source object in scope and generate a compatibility report. You can sync as many times as you need without stopping writes to your source table, except for a few minutes during cutover. Once you are ready, you can complete the migration, minimizing time that tables are offline.

Compared to self-managed approaches, S3 Tables managed migrations are cost-effective because you pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the Hive-to-Iceberg conversion, and source objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering stay in their current access tier.

A first look at the migration To migrate an AWS Glue Hive table, choose your destination table bucket in the S3 console, then choose Create table from migration.

Create a namespace and table name for your destination Iceberg table. The destination table is created using recommended default settings tuned for query performance and storage efficiency.

When you start the migration, S3 Tables validate the source table, generate a compatibility report, and begin copying data. The destination table is read-only during the migration. Once you complete migration, the destination table is promoted to read-write.

You can begin working with your data right away using a direct integration with Amazon Athena and Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio in the AWS console, or use any tool compatible with the Apache Iceberg REST API to directly query the tables. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables migration documentation.

You can also use AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, or the Agent Toolkit for AWS. For example, set up migration jobs and call the start-table-migration command.

To catch up the destination table with changes in the source, call sync-table-migration as many times as you need before you complete the migration. Each sync copies only what changed.

If you’re using coding agents like Kiro, the migrating-hive-tables-to-s3-tables skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS provides step-by-step migration guidance with safety guardrails for agents. The skill can:

To learn more, visit the GitHub README page for the skill.

Now available Amazon S3 Tables managed migration is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo), and Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, Stockholm) Regions. At launch, the capability supports AWS Glue-registered Hive tables stored in Parquet format within the same AWS account and AWS Region. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, or troubleshoot about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

Try it in the Amazon S3 console today and send feedback to AWS re:Post for Amazon S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#10039. Hugging Face and Cerebras bring Gemma 4 to real-time voice AI

For voice AI, latency is a critical parameter. Developers have made tremendous progress in model quality, but the user experience is still often limited by response times. Hugging Face and Cerebras are changing that experience. Today, we demonstrate what becomes possible when an open, modular voice AI architecture is paired with industry-leading inference speed.

The result is a speech-to-speech experience that feels dramatically more natural. Instead of waiting for an AI to respond, conversations flow with the responsiveness users expect from human interaction.

The demo is built as a real-time speech-to-speech pipeline. Each part of the system is modular, open, and replaceable, making it easy for developers to adapt the stack for different assistants, robots, products, or research projects.

This creates a fully open speech-to-speech loop:

The architecture brings together the strength of the open-source AI ecosystem: Cerebras for fast inference, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4 31B for the language model, and Qwen for text-to-speech. Every layer can be inspected, modified, and extended by the developers

Today, some production systems see a reasonable median latency while still experiencing frustrating multi-second delays at the P95. Those delays become even more noticeable when tool calls or multimodal steps require multiple turns.

Cerebras helps solve one of the most important bottlenecks in the stack: the language-model response time. By making inference dramatically faster and more stable, Cerebras allows the rest of the Hugging Face pipeline to shine.

That stability is especially important at the long tail. Many systems can deliver acceptable median response times, but occasional slow responses still make conversations feel unreliable.

This same Hugging Face speech-to-speech pipeline already powers Reachy Mini robots, with more than 9,000 robots in the wild. For robots, voice assistants, and embodied AI, responsiveness is not a cosmetic improvement. It is what makes the interaction feel alive.

The motivation to use Cerebras is therefore not simply cost reduction. It is low latency, predictable performance, and the ability to create real-time experiences that feel natural at scale.

This collaboration reflects a shared belief that the future of AI will be both open and performant. Open-source models, open infrastructure, and breakthrough inference speed together create a foundation for the next generation of conversational AI.

We invite developers to explore the demo, experiment with the code, and help shape what comes next for real-time voice AI.

We even crossed 10k Reachy Minis in the wild 😄

It's exciting to see how Hugging Face and Cerebras are pushing real-time voice technology forward. Fast responses make conversations feel much more comfortable and engaging, and that's exactly what users have been hoping for. 😊 When the delay is reduced, interactions become smoother and more natural, making voice experiences feel less like talking to software and more like having a real conversation.

What I appreciate most is the focus on an open and modular approach. That gives developers more flexibility to build solutions that fit different needs instead of being locked into a single ecosystem. The combination of strong model quality with impressive inference speed could help unlock many practical applications across education, customer support, accessibility, and beyond. 🚀

The emphasis on latency is absolutely the right direction because speed directly shapes the overall experience. Even the smartest system can feel frustrating if every response takes too long. Bringing that waiting time down creates a much more fluid interaction, and it's great to see innovation focused on something users notice immediately. 👏

Looking forward to seeing how this evolves over the coming months... Faster conversations... Better responsiveness... More natural interactions... Exciting progress for developers and users alike... 🌟🙂

#10038. How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write

AI agents now read email, book travel and move money for the people who use them. Every tool call also pulls in text that someone else wrote, and whoever controls that text can try to steer the agent. OWASP calls this agent goal hijack and ranks it first in its Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026).

In September we announced Agent Anomaly Detection in Private Preview on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It reads your agents' traces and logs asynchronously, without adding latency, and flags sessions where an agent acts outside its intended boundaries. We tested this feature against benchmarks for this top risk of agent goal hijack.

Security tools tend to look good on tests their own team wrote, so we ran five non-Google-written, public agent-security benchmarks through Agent Anomaly Detection without changing anything. In four of them, the harmful instruction hides in data that a tool returns. In the fifth, the user asks for harm directly.

The model itself didn't follow about half of the harmful instructions it read. It refused three in four direct requests for harm, and ignored or failed at about 30% of the instructions hidden in tool output. Of the ones that were executed, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 87% for post-execution review. It raised false alarms on 2% to 16% of benign sessions, depending on the tools the agent uses. Poisoned memory is the clear gap: when instructions planted in the agent’s long-term memory made it act, Agent Anomaly Detection caught 4 of 18.

We ran each benchmark case through an agent built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) using gemini-2.5-flash, on the benchmark's simulated apps. The agent sent its traces and logs to Agent Anomaly Detection, as a customer's agent would. Then the benchmark's own Python check read the final state of the apps, such as whether money left the account, and labeled the session. Deterministic code decides the label, not a model, so an injected instruction can't mislead the grader, and Agent Anomaly Detection cannot cheat the benchmark. Each agent first ran at least 300 benign sessions, because Agent Anomaly Detection learns how each agent usually behaves.

We also recorded whether a tool returned the harmful instruction to the agent. In many cases, the agent never opens the email or file that holds it. So each harmful session ends one of three ways:

In AgentHarm, the user sends the request, so the agent always reads it.

The five benchmarks are AgentDojo (NeurIPS 2024), InjecAgent (ACL 2024 Findings), Agent Security Bench (ASB, ICLR 2025), AgentDyn (2026) and AgentHarm (ICLR 2025). ASB plants the instruction in the agent's long-term memory. In all, Agent Anomaly Detection scored 1,774 sessions.

Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 87% of the harmful instructions that the agent carried out, and raised a few false alarms on ordinary office work. It's strongest on goal hijack and tool misuse, and weakest on poisoned memory.

Each finding carries a threat category, and four of Agent Anomaly Detection’s five categories align with the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications. We graded each OWASP category on what this study showed, not on what Agent Anomaly Detection is designed to catch.

Public benchmarks concentrate on goal hijack and tool misuse, so our evidence is strongest there. We did not find public benchmarks with labeled agent traces for cascading failures or for identity and privilege abuse. Shared benchmarks for those categories would help the whole field.

By benchmark, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 85% of the carried-out harmful instructions on AgentDojo, 87% on InjecAgent, 99% on AgentDyn and 81% on AgentHarm. Over all harmful sessions, including the ones that the agent never read or resisted, it flagged 45% to 62%. In the 141 sessions where the agent never read the instruction, nothing happened, and it flagged just 1.

Results held across the apps. In 8 of the 11 apps, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged at least 95% of the carried-out harmful instructions. The lowest rate was in AgentDojo's Slack app, at 63%. Many of those instructions ask for one small action, such as a page visit, which looks like normal browsing.

Agent Anomaly Detection also flags many requests that the agent refuses. In AgentHarm, the agent refused most requests and carried out 108 of 412, and Agent Anomaly Detection still flagged 55% of the refused sessions, because the request sits in the user's own message, which it reads. When the agent didn't follow an instruction hidden in tool output, it flagged only 11% to 25%, because the instruction sits deep inside a tool result.

False alarms were rare on ordinary office work: on the three injection benchmarks, whose benign sessions are office tasks, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 2% to 4% of benign sessions. On AgentHarm it flagged 16%. Those benign tasks are twins of the harmful ones, so they post to social media, run terminal commands and download files. High-impact tools in normal use look more like misuse.

Agent Anomaly Detection did less well in five areas. It flagged only 11% to 25% of the instructions that the agent resisted, because a resisted instruction changes little in how the agent behaves. It missed more small actions, like single page visits, because they look like normal work. And it raised more false alarms for agents whose everyday work uses high-impact tools. If your agent is one of them, expect more findings at first, and triage them by severity and threat category.

The other two areas are new agents and poisoned memory. Some Agent Anomaly Detection methods need a few hundred sessions of history: on AgentDyn, it flagged 33% of carried-out harmful instructions when each agent had about 220 benign sessions, and 99% with 360. And it caught only 4 of the 18 sessions where poisoned memory made the agent act.

Protect your agents with defense in depth. Use controls that stop harmful actions before they run, and Agent Anomaly Detection to find what gets through.

We used one agent model and simulated apps, and the benchmarks' benign tasks are likely simpler than your production traffic, so your false-alarm rate can differ. Agent Anomaly Detection returned no result for about 6% of the sessions we sent; counting those as misses lowers the overall rates by 1 to 2 points.

Agent Anomaly Detection is in Private Preview. To request access, read the Agent Anomaly Detection overview.

#10037. Palantir’s Karp takes a sharp left turn, says he and the company’s products are actually ‘progressive’

Trump donor says he privately questioned deportation tactics. Shame about the privately bit

With tech CEO roles, a certain level of shamelessness comes with the job description. Yet Alex Karp, head honcho of Palantir, seems set to raise the bar with a conspicuous display of political flexibility following the Democratic wave in the US midterms.

In December 2024, Karp gave $1 million to the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc.

But it does not take cutting-edge AI and data analytics – in which Palantir claims to have unique power – for Karp to understand on which side his bread is buttered. The man with the distinctive verbal diarrhea is now stressing his progressive credentials – and those of Palantir's products.

The CEO told Politico that he is now open to voting for the Democrats come 2028.

"I've been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir – all of our products are essentially progressive," Karp reportedly said.

Karp's explanation for his political generosity was an apparent desire for balance.

"My giving is equal, Democrat, Republican," Karp told the publication. "I can tell you, without going into things I'm not gonna disclose, I'm very balanced, and everyone in the political arena knows it. And I'll tell you what, I'm also not the village idiot."

All of which raises the question of whether, in avoiding idiocy, it is necessary to eschew any principled stance whatsoever. If only the Germans of the Weimar Republic had thought to fund both sides. Apparently, all Europe needed was a more balanced political donations portfolio.

Such is Karp's sensitivity towards the topic that he once claimed: "I love when I'm getting yelled at in cities in Europe... Keep yelling at me... the only reason why someone's not goose-stepping between me and you is my product. Say thank you."

They have not said thank you. In fact, across Europe, governments are looking to reject Palantir, while the EU has instigated a sovereign tech and AI policy to escape the clutches of the US tech giants.

Karp has a talent for holding two seemingly contradictory positions. He has talked about the need for democratic societies to exercise hard power, and, elsewhere, about founding a company that could "power the West to its obvious innate superiority."

At the same time, he has presented Palantir as a force for peace. "We see ourselves as the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement," he wrote in his shareholder letter.

It is his company's association with a longstanding customer, the controversial US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), that has drawn the most criticism. In Minnesota earlier this year, federal immigration officers shot and killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in incidents captured on video. It has detained US citizens, and critics argue it has shown scant regard for due process.

Karp denied that Palantir's association with ICE should reflect badly on the company.

He told CNBC: "If you are critical of ICE, you should be out there protesting for more Palantir. Our product, actually, in its core, requires people to conform with Fourth Amendment data protection."

In the Politico interview, Karp said he was "really happy to hear" President Trump, a driving force behind ICE's expansion, acknowledge after the midterm elections that ICE deportations have been too tough.

"And I'm glad he's saying in public now what I've been saying in private," Karp told the news outlet.

Karp has no shortage of public opinions on goose-stepping or innate Western superiority. Why, then, reserve his concerns about deportations for private conversations? A public intervention from a Trump donor and ICE supplier might have carried some weight.

Maybe he doesn't care so long as people are still writing about Alex Karp. But anyone who cares about more than that might feel the need to take a hot shower and scrub off the associated trauma. ®

#10036. 🤗 Kernels: Major Updates

In our previous post (From Zero to GPU), we introduced the 🤗 Kernels project, which aims at standardizing how custom kernels are packaged, distributed, and consumed. We want the project to be frictionless and secure, while making it as Hub-friendly as possible.

Over the past few months, we have worked towards this goal. In the process, we also almost completely redesigned the project. This post will summarize the major updates we have shipped and what’s coming.

We have introduced a new repository type on the Hub called "kernel". This enables us to cater to users with compute-related specificities. For example, a user can get a sense of which accelerators, operating systems, and backend versions are supported for a given kernel:

One can browse all available kernels on the Hub here: https://huggingface.co/kernels.

Making these kernels first-class citizens of the Hub also benefits the AI ecosystem. Users can now see trends across kernels, models, and the applications that use them. The kernels become more discoverable to users.

Kernels run native code with the same privileges as the Python process that loads them, so a malicious kernel can do real harm. Therefore, security has always been of utmost importance to the Kernels project.

This is why we focused early on reproducibility: you should be able to recompile a kernel yourself and verify that it matches the publicly available source. We use Nix to make this possible, since it keeps builds pure through hermetic evaluation of the build recipe and a strongly isolated sandbox. We further improve provenance by embedding the source Git SHA1 into the kernel itself.

In recent months, we have added additional layers of defense: trusted kernel publishers and code signing.

With the new repo type, we also introduced “trusted publishers”. Since kernels execute code on a machine with the same privileges as the Python process they are used in, an attacker could compromise machines by uploading a malicious kernel and coaxing you to use that kernel. To help you avoid such malicious kernels, the kernels package will now only load kernels by trusted publishers by default. A trusted publisher is an organization that is trusted by the community to act in good faith.

We still want to support loading kernels from organizations or users that are not trusted publishers, but you have to explicitly opt in using the trust_remote_code argument when loading a kernel from the Hub:

By default, users cannot publish kernel repositories on the Hub. They have to request to be a kernel publisher. Users and organizations can request for access from their account settings. This gives us time to treat these requests on a case-by-case basis.

An additional layer of security that we are adding is code signing. Code signing protects against the scenario where an attacker uploads a malicious kernel to a kernel repo from a trusted publisher whose Hub credentials were compromised. In code signing, a kernel is signed with a private key known only to the kernel developer and validated with a public key that is generally available. In the Hub compromise scenario, an attacker cannot sign the malicious kernel since they do not own the private key needed for signing.

To further improve security, we use Sigstore’s cosign to sign using ephemeral private keys. Since these signing keys are only valid for a limited time, an attacker typically cannot use the private key, even when it is leaked. We also verify that the kernel was signed by a trusted GitHub workflow from a trusted GitHub repository.

Kernel signing is already supported by kernel-builder and we have provided the kernels verify-signature to verify a kernel. Kernels does not verify the signature upon loading a kernel yet, since we would like to test this new functionality more before fully rolling it out. Preliminary notes on setting up code signing for your own kernels can be found in the kernels 0.16.0 release notes: https://github.com/huggingface/kernels/releases/tag/v0.16.0.

Previously, a bunch of utilities were intertwined between kernels and kernel-builder. We have established a better separation of concern between the CLI of kernels and kernel-builder. The mental model here is that kernels is a library for loading and preparing kernels for use. Therefore, it should not include anything related to “building” kernels.

As a result of this, both kernels and kernel-builder are now much leaner and more specific. Refer to the documentation to learn more about this:

This improved CLI experience also lets us cater to the rise of agentic kernel development in a better manner. More on this later.

We have extended support for frameworks, the most visible changes are:

kernel-builder and kernels complement the rise of agentic kernel development wherein an agent is leveraged to come up with an (optimized) kernel from scratch. Together, they support a workflow in which agents can scaffold, build, benchmark, and iteratively optimize kernels.

Agentic kernel development is still nascent, and the right development loops will continue to evolve. That makes simple, clear fundamentals especially important where the tools should be easy to compose into whichever agent workflows or frameworks people choose to use.

kernel-builder helps enforce a structure in how kernel source code should be scaffolded and used to perform reproducible builds. This gives agents a predictable project layout and repeatable workflow to operate within. Its CLI is also meant to be agent-optimized. For example, this can mean non-interactive commands and outputs that are straightforward for an agent to interpret programmatically. To this end, we also have backend-specific skills to help agents navigate the idiosyncrasies of different backends. These skills can capture backend-specific toolchains, compilation paths, and performance considerations.

Building a kernel successfully isn’t the only goal, we need to ensure that it delivers actual speedups over a baseline on the target hardware. A successful build is therefore only the first validation step. Usually, this target hardware can include many different accelerators, even different families of the same accelerator.

This makes it important to evaluate results across hardware vendors and generations where relevant. Our tight integration with HF Jobs can make this benchmarking process easy. Agents can use this integration to run benchmark suites, collect performance results, and compare them against a defined baseline.

This way, agents can run tests across different hardware configurations to get reliable feedback on the performance of the generated kernels and identify what needs to be done. That feedback can then inform the next optimization iteration.

Below are some examples of agent-augmented kernels. These illustrate the kinds of kernels that can be developed and evaluated through this workflow:

The environment setup for building kernels with kernel-builder can be daunting. To make it easier for users, we now have an installation script for setting up an environment in one click. If you prefer working with ephemeral instances, our Terraform setup guide is worth following.

After the kernels are built, we create a system card for each kernel to expose useful information, including how to use it and its exposed interfaces. When the kernel is pushed to the Hub, this system card becomes the front matter for the kernel:

Is a question one would ask multiple times to plan things better. Use the has_kernel() method for this purpose:

It returns a bool. If you’re looking for more explanations around why a given kernel isn’t supported then use get_kernel_variants():

It should print (depends on the machine you’re on):

Kernel-builder has targeted manylinux_2_28 almost since the beginning. We used to target manylinux by using a modern gcc toolchain compiled with glibc 2.28. To avoid compatibility issues with older versions of libstdc++, we statically linked libstdc++.

However, this approach recently resulted in some issues. Some libstdc++ functionality uses global initialization. This can lead to corrupted data when multiple libstdc++ versions come into play, such as the libstdc++ that is linked dynamically by PyTorch and the libstdc++ that is linked statically by a kernel. Some recent kernels use functionality (e.g. C++ regexes) that trigger global initializations, leading to such corrupted data, causing segfaults and other issues.

To solve this issue, kernels now link libstdc++ dynamically. To ensure compatibility with old libstdc++ versions, we now compile kernels with the official manylinux_2_28 toolchain.

Our goal with the Kernels project is to serve both kernel developers and users of custom kernels. We’re always keen on receiving feedback from the community on how we can improve it. Don’t hesitate to contribute!

Acknowledgements: Thanks to Aritra for reviewing the post.

#10035. AWS Weekly Roundup: AgentCore Runtime V2, Amazon DynamoDB bulk put items, and more (November 9, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Most of the cost of adopting something new isn’t the new thing, it’s the move. Moving a Hive table to Apache Iceberg has typically meant weeks of engineering work. Last week, Amazon S3 Tables turned that into three steps: start, sync as often as you need, complete. The source stays writable except for a few minutes at cutover. The same week, Amazon DynamoDB started loading data from S3 into tables that already exist.

The pattern I like is that neither one asks you to stop what’s running. That’s also the way to read the agent news this week. The new Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime is a single field on the runtime you already have, and Web Answer is a tool you attach to a gateway you already run. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesThe new AgentCore Runtime: elastic, optimized, and consistently fast starts – If you run agents on AgentCore and haven’t tried the new runtime since it became generally available, it’s worth a look. It changes two things. First, memory: sessions start small, page in more on demand, and give memory back when it goes cold instead of holding the peak, so you pay for what your agent uses. Second, cold starts: AgentCore prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores the snapshot for every new instance. In the team’s tests, that kept P75 cold starts at about 2 seconds for images from 200 MB up to 2 GB, while the original runtime rose from roughly 5.4 seconds to nearly 30 seconds as images grew. The per-unit rate is higher, but you use far fewer GB-hours, so the team expects most agents to see a lower bill, though that isn’t guaranteed.

To opt in, you set platformVersion to V2 when you create or update a runtime. Create and update take several minutes while the snapshot is prepared, and your container must report healthy on /ping within 120 seconds, so report health only after initialization finishes. The docs cover how to optimize your agent for V2. V2 is available in 10 Regions, and committed baseline pricing is coming soon.

Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg – You can now migrate Parquet tables registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog into S3 Tables without building a pipeline or provisioning compute. S3 Tables validates the source and produces a compatibility report covering every object in scope. Each sync copies only what changed, so production keeps writing until cutover. Afterward you can query the table with Amazon Athena, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, or any engine that speaks the Iceberg REST API. You pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the conversion, and objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering keep their tier. At launch it works within the same account and Region, in 10 Regions.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

Amazon DynamoDB now supports bulk put items – You can now load line-delimited DynamoDB JSON or Amazon Ion files from Amazon S3 into existing tables as a managed, asynchronous job. Each record can carry its own condition expression, so one file can mix plain, insert-only, and version-guarded writes. Writes use dedicated system capacity and cost less than the equivalent per-request writes. An Accelerated tier handles deadline-bound jobs. The Database blog post gives illustrative Accelerated times of less than 1 hour for 100 million 1 KB items. One thing to know before you start: canceling doesn’t roll back items already written.

Announcing Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – You can now give an agent a single tool call that returns a synthesized, cited answer to a natural-language question, instead of building your own search, retrieval, and citation pipeline. Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, and decides when it has enough evidence. You attach it as a target on AgentCore Gateway and call it over MCP, and you can limit it with domain include and deny lists and publish-date filters. It’s available in US East (N. Virginia). The getting started post explains when to use it instead of Web Search, which returns ranked results for your own model to synthesize.

AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources – You can now process records from a single Kafka partition across many parallel AWS Lambda invocations. Classic consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count. Queue mode uses Kafka share groups and needs Kafka 4.2 or later with share groups enabled. It works with self-managed clusters and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. You give up ordering and get at-least-once delivery, so your functions need to be idempotent. The Compute blog walkthrough covers poller scaling and when to keep stream mode.

AWS announces AWS Interconnect – last mile preview with Equinix – You can now set up a private, managed connection from Equinix’s network of 282 data centers to AWS without ordering cross-connects or configuring routers. Capacity is quad-redundant across two locations and four links, with BGP and VLANs configured for you, a 99.99% availability SLA, and MACsec by default. You pick a Region, bandwidth, and AWS Direct Connect gateway, then paste the activation key into Equinix Fabric. The preview covers the San Jose metro and, as of last Thursday, Northern Virginia, with 1 Gbps connections at no charge.

AWS Security Hub now provides an SBOM inventory for your compute resources – You can now see every software package installed across your organization’s Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon ECR images, and Lambda functions in AWS Security Hub, with each package’s version and how many resources run it. That’s the list you want the next time a widely used library has a vulnerability. The inventory builds on the SBOMs that Amazon Inspector already generates, so it fills in automatically wherever Inspector is enabled. It’s included in Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

Serverless ICYMI Q3 2026 – Julian Wood’s quarterly recap is a quick serverless catch-up before re:Invent: Lambda SnapStart for container images, a 90-minute timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, Lambda MicroVMs in 10 Regions, 1 MiB payloads in Amazon SNS, and the new AgentCore Runtime.

AWS contributes a large-transaction binary log optimization to MySQL – With binlog on, a huge transaction holds a global commit lock while its events are copied, blocking every other commit. The optimization, which Amazon Aurora MySQL has run in production since 2019, promotes the spill file into the binlog instead of copying it. In AWS’s tests, commit latency for a 50 GiB transaction dropped from about 7 minutes to about 2 to 2.5 seconds. It has now shipped to community MySQL.

How OrderServ achieved up to 64% cost savings with multi-tenant ECS – Cognizant’s food-ordering platform went from one Amazon ECS cluster per brand on AWS Fargate to a shared cluster on EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools. The 64% applies to a 3-year Compute Savings Plan (47% with a 1-year plan). Scaling time also fell from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, with a few more before the year ends: Belém, Brazil (November 14), JAWS FESTA 2026 in Akita, Japan (November 17), and Port Harcourt, Nigeria (December 12).

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#10034. Jensen Huang's self-sabotage sends Nvidia into a midlife crisis

The competition is circling like vultures

Nvidia CEO and founder Jensen Huang has been ousted after nearly two weeks of controversy that, at times, felt more like a soap opera than reality: a wealthy businessman, reported affairs, and an alleged Chinese spy and GPU smuggler.

For Nvidia’s board, it seems there was no question Huang had to go. The man behind what was recently the most valuable company in the world proved too big a liability to retain in any capacity. He was too toxic even for a demotion from CEO to chairman, a vantage point that would have retained Huang as the face of the company even if he could no longer be trusted to run it.

Replacing him won’t be so easy. Nvidia now faces an identity crisis. Huang, who has led the company for more than three decades, has no clear successor. The GPU slinger has no shortage of brilliant engineers, but executives capable of wrangling one of the biggest and most influential brands in the world, not so much.

Ian Buck, father of CUDA and Nvidia’s VP of hyperscale and HPC is currently favored by many to be Huang’s successor. Buck has taken on a more public role within Nvidia in recent years headlining keynotes at events like Supercomputing and the AI Infra Summit.

CFO Colette Kress, a bean counter who’s kept Jensen’s ambitions grounded for more than a decade, now takes the reins as interim CEO while the board searches for its next figurehead.

And while Kress fights to contain the chaos, others will no doubt capitalize on Huang’s controversial choice of consorts to advance their own agendas.

One need only ask a few inconvenient questions to cast doubt on Nvidia’s loyalties. How deep does China’s influence in Nvidia go? Can Nvidia’s hardware still be trusted? You get the idea.

It certainly wouldn’t be the first time Nvidia’s and, by extension, Huang’s loyalties have been called into question. In late 2023, Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman blasted rival Nvidia for supplying GPUs to China in spite of US export controls, calling the behavior “un-American” and likening the graphics titan to an AI arms dealer.

Nvidia has also faced criticism from US government officials, including former commerce secretary Gina Raimondo, for failing to take a hint and trying instead to limbo under US export controls in order to continue selling chips to the Middle Kingdom.

After the Trump administration's short lived blockade of H20 sales early last year cost the company some $10.5 billion, Huang spent much of the 2025 lobbying the Trump administration to reverse export bans on the sales of older Hopper generation GPUs to China, an endeavor which ultimately proved successful.

One could make the case that Huang’s ongoing efforts to sell Nvidia’s chips to China were financially motivated. But that argument is undermined by Huang admitting to having an extramarital affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang (no relation), a woman that US intelligence has accused of moonlighting as a Chinese spy and helping to smuggle GPUs into the country.

When technology and politics collide, the appearance of impropriety is often more damning than the impropriety itself.

Uncle Sam has forced Chinese companies out of the United States for the mere possibility that they could be coerced into planting back doors in critical infrastructure. Just ask Huawei whether the truth counts for anything once Washington has decided that you’re a national security threat.

Huang’s affairs may not just cost him his job, but could cost Nvidia key government contracts and make the company’s hardware less attractive, particularly in highly-regulated and notoriously risk-averse industries.

Rival chipmakers will no doubt capitalize on Nvidia’s bad optics if Huang’s departure doesn’t pop the AI financing merry-go-round bubble first – Nvidia's stock lost about 25% of its value in the few days after news about Huang started breaking, only recovering slightly after his ouster. Regardless, with Nvidia’s reputation marred and its future shrouded in uncertainty, once loyal customers may be more willing to explore alternative providers.

There are certainly plenty to choose from. Amid a surge in custom AI chips from the likes of Broadcom, Marvel, and others, Nvidia’s main advantage wasn’t so much technological as it was simply considered a safe bet.

AMD is the most obvious winner here. As we reported earlier this year, the House of Zen’s GPU tech has already surpassed Nvidia’s, at least on paper. What’s more, the company has a long and unblemished relationship serving the US government. AMD’s chips now power two of the Department of Energy’s three largest and most sensitive supercomputers.

Meanwhile, hyperscalers with sufficient cashflow – think Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta – may seek to insulate themselves from Huang’s fallout by investing more heavily in homegrown silicon and offering it to customers.

Then there's the threat from the man himself. Huang's ambitions and influence are such that he's unlikely to fade into obscurity. He may disappear from the spotlight while things blow over, but it’s a pretty sure bet that he’ll pop up at a new company eventually, and will still have enough sway to poach some of Nvidia’s top engineers. ®
