The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

Agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this issue.

Good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

Taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

That's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

#9974. You could have invented transformers from memory

[code][interactive app][slides][X post][Hacker News][机器之心]

Large language models today can recall obscure facts from every corner of the world. Most recently, I was running late for a friend’s board game night, so I asked Astra to remind me the rules to Dune: Imperium. It gladly narrated them to me as I drove over and helped me remember the rules well enough for me to play again. We’re so used to asking models about anything that we take their vast knowledge for granted.

How do models remember so much information? And how much can they store?

In this post, I’ll go through an intuitive way to look at linear maps, MLPs, and self-attention as different kinds of memory stores. From this intuition we can derive some heuristics for how much memory each layer can store.

The key property that characterizes a “good” memory store is its ability to recall what it stored. After all, even if we could store infinitely many facts, it’s not very helpful if we can’t recall them when we need to. The more memories we store, the more they interfere with each other when we try to recall one. So throughout the post we’ll focus on one quantity, the interference-to-signal ratio, which measures how much the other memories get in the way during recall. The number of memories a store can hold before the interference grows as large as the signal is its capacity.

We’ll develop this perspective and show how you can go from a linear layer to something better, an MLP, which improves both capacity and recall, and then all the way to self-attention, which has very good recall and can store a potentially unbounded number of memories. With 64-dimensional keys, that’s a jump from about 64 memories, to about 2,700, to over a million.

Here are the terms we’ll use throughout. A memory store is a function $f$ that holds $M$ memories, for $i = 1, \ldots, M$. A memory is one key-value pair: a key $k_i \in \reals^{d_k}$, used for lookup based on similarity, and a value $v_i \in \reals^{d_v}$, which is what we want to retrieve. To use $f$, we query it with an input $x$, and it recalls an output $f(x)$. A good memory store recalls $v_i$ when we query it with $k_i$, or with another vector similar to $k_i$. In the literature, a memory store that recalls by similarity is called an associative memory.

The most basic memory store is linear: it simply accumulates memories via outer products,

where the rows of $K \in \reals^{M\times d_k}$ and $V \in \reals^{M\times d_v}$ are the keys $k_i\transpose$ and the values $v_i\transpose$.1

To store a new memory $(k, v)$, we simply add $vk\transpose$ to the existing weights.2

Take a linear layer $y = Wx$ inside a network with a scalar loss $L$, and let $\bar y = \grad L(y)$ be the gradient of the loss with respect to the layer’s output. The gradient with respect to $W$ is $\bar y x\transpose$, so a step with learning rate $\eta$ is

This recurrence is a memory update: it updates the weights with a new memory with key $x$ and value $-\eta\bar y$. For more on this view, see Irie, Csordás & Schmidhuber, who express a linear layer trained by gradient descent as attention over all of its training inputs.

To query the memory store with an input $x$, we multiply the input by the matrix:

So recall is a lookup by similarity to the stored keys: we compare the query with every key, and return the sum of the values weighted by those similarities.

So storing memories is easy: just keep adding outer products to the weights. But what happens when we try to recall one?

Let’s assume for simplicity that every key is normalized to have length 1, i.e. $k_j\transpose k_j = 1$. Then

meaning we get back the value of the target memory, the one whose key we queried with, plus interference from every other memory whose key is similar to the query.

If the keys were all orthonormal, the interference would be zero and recall would be exact. But $\reals^{d_k}$ only has $d_k$ orthogonal directions, so we cannot get perfect recall once we store more memories than the key dimension: $M > d_k$.

What is the outer-product store’s capacity? Here’s an intuitive argument. There are $M-1$ interference terms. If the keys are random unit vectors, each similarity $k_i\transpose k_j$ is about $\pm 1/\sqrt{d_k}$. If the values are random too, with similar lengths, the $M-1$ interference terms add up like a random walk, so the interference’s squared length is about $(M-1)/d_k$ times the signal’s, and

once we store as many memories as the key dimension, the interference is as large as the signal, drowning it out.

Each bar below is one stored memory’s weight in a single recall, relative to the target memory’s weight (in red). Every bar adds a bit of its value to the recall. Drag $M$ past $d_k = 64$ to watch the small bars pile up until recall fails. The other buttons switch to memory stores we’ll build later in the post.

Even below its capacity of about $d_k$ memories, the outer-product store produces significant interference during recall.3 To raise the capacity, or recall more cleanly below it, we need to reduce interference.

The brute-force way is to make the key dimension $d_k$ larger, since a linear store’s capacity grows with $d_k$. How large $d_k$ can be is governed by hardware constraints.

Alternatively, we can make algorithmic improvements. We can store memories more carefully: the outer-product store adds each memory without looking at the others, so it does nothing to cancel their interference. Or we can recall more selectively: every memory in a linear store contributes interference, even when its key has low similarity to the query, so we can improve recall by suppressing the less similar keys.

In the rest of the post, we’ll see that storing outer product memories more carefully gives us the optimal linear memory store, which has about twice the capacity. Recalling selectively via nonlinearities gives us MLPs and self-attention.

The outer-product store writes each memory without regard to the others. Instead, we can choose the weights $W$ so that recall fits all of the stored memories at once. This is a linear regression problem:4

When we store more memories than the key dimension, $M > d_k$, the least-squares solution is

This is the outer-product store $V\transpose K$ with one change: before we compare the query with the keys, we multiply it by $(K\transpose K)\inverse$, which undoes the keys’ covariance $K\transpose K$. This whitens the keys, so the store no longer overweights directions that many keys share.

When $M \leq d_k$, the regression can fit every memory exactly, as long as the keys are linearly independent. So the optimal store recalls with no interference at all, even when the keys aren’t orthogonal.

When $M > d_k$, we start to get interference, since there are only $d_k$ directions for the memory store to work with. For random keys and values, our interference-to-signal ratio becomes

so the optimal store’s capacity is twice as large as before!

When $M \leq d_k$. If the keys are linearly independent, the $M\times M$ matrix of inner products between keys, $KK\transpose$, is invertible, and

fits every memory exactly. When $M < d_k$, the problem is underconstrained and has infinitely many solutions, and this one is the min-norm solution. The rows $\tilde k_i\transpose$ of $(KK\transpose)\inverse K$ are known as the dual basis for the rows of $K$: by construction, $(KK\transpose)\inverse KK\transpose = I$, so $\tilde k_i\transpose k_j = \delta_{ij}$. Then $f(k_j) = \sum_i v_i\, \tilde k_i\transpose k_j = v_j$, so there is no interference and we have perfect recall.

When $M > d_k$. Setting the gradient of the objective to zero gives $W K\transpose K = V\transpose K$, so $W = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse$. Both solutions are $W = V\transpose (K\transpose)\pinv$, where $A\pinv$ denotes the pseudoinverse of $A$: $(K\transpose)\pinv = (KK\transpose)\inverse K$ when the keys are linearly independent, and $(K\transpose)\pinv = K(K\transpose K)\inverse$ when they span $\reals^{d_k}$.

Now we can analyze the interference of $f(k_j) = V\transpose K\,(K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$. For a stored key $k_j$, the weight on each value $v_i$ is $k_i\transpose (K\transpose K)\inverse k_j$, which is exactly entry $(i, j)$ of the $M\times M$ matrix $P = K(K\transpose K)\inverse K\transpose$:

Compared to the outer-product store’s $\sqrt{M/d_k}$, the $-1$ is the $d_k$ memories’ worth of interference that the optimal store cancels.

We can check our predictions numerically. We randomly sample $M$ memories with unit-length keys in $d_k = 64$ dimensions, query the memory store with one of the stored keys, and measure the interference-to-signal ratio:

The outer-product store reaches its capacity at $M \approx d_k = 64$. The optimal store recalls exactly up to $M = d_k$. Past that, its interference rises from zero like $\sqrt{M/d_k - 1}$, and the store reaches its capacity near $M = 2d_k = 128$, as predicted. Since it cancels a fixed number of memories’ worth of interference, the gap between the two stores shrinks as $M$ grows.

This optimal memory store is still linear in the similarities though. It must scale small and large similarities by the same factor. To do better, we need to change how the store recalls.

If we had a way to suppress the weight when $k_i\transpose x$ is small, then we can reduce the amount of interference from low similarity keys.

Let’s pass each similarity through a nonlinear function $\sigma$ before computing the weighted sum of values:

We just rediscovered a two-layer MLP from first principles! The rows of the first weight matrix are the keys, the columns of the second weight matrix are the values. Sukhbaatar et al. pointed out this resemblance between feedforward layers and memory stores, and Geva et al. found that the feedforward layers in trained transformers often work this way, with keys firing on recognizable patterns in the input.

Ideally, the gating function $\sigma$ is chosen such that when the similarity is low ($k_i\transpose x \sim 0$ or even when $k_i\transpose x < 0$), its corresponding term in the sum gets suppressed to reduce interference. A ReLU activation zeros out keys with negative similarities, and adding a bias allows shifting that threshold5. A squared ReLU activation further suppresses the keys with similarities close to zero. A similarity of 0.1 becomes 0.01, while a similarity of 1 stays 1. In fact, squared ReLUs are one of the lesser known but established-at-scale improvements to MLP activations (So et al.).

A squared ReLU MLP is a GLU MLP whose gate and input projection share weights, since $\operatorname{ReLU}(Kx)^2 = \operatorname{ReLU}(Kx) \odot Kx$. The SwiGLU MLPs in today’s language models give the gate its own weights and use a Swish activation in place of the ReLU.

In practice, MLPs store facts in superposition: many facts share the same weights, and the output is a blend of many memories. Garcia et al. build one explicitly: the hidden units of a GLU MLP compute random features $\phi(x)$ of the input, the second weight matrix is an outer-product store $\sum_i v_i \phi(k_i)\transpose$ over those features, and the MLP stores far more facts than it has hidden units. Still, trained transformers’ ReLU MLPs can activate as few as 1% of their hidden units for a given input, so each recall draws on a small fraction of the memories (Li et al.).

The original transformer paper made this connection too, but only in v2 and v3 on arXiv. There, Vaswani et al. describe the feedforward layer as “a kind of attention,” with the rows of its two weight matrices as the keys and values, and ReLU in place of softmax. They even tried replacing the feedforward layers with attention over learned key-value parameters, and got about the same translation quality: one version did slightly worse, another slightly better, though the first one trained about 30% slower. The passage is gone from every later version of the paper. We’ll get to how self-attention relates to all this below.

Squaring the similarities works because it shrinks low similarity weights much more than large ones. We can push this further with $\sigma(s) = \operatorname{ReLU}(s)^p$. The signal stays the same, since $1^p = 1$, while an interference term with similarity $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ shrinks to $d_k^{-p/2}$. The $M$ interference terms add up like a random walk, so the interference-to-signal ratio is

memories, geometrically more than before!

To check this, we run the same experiment as before for five choices of $\sigma$:

Since the interference grows like $\sqrt{M}$, the lines are nearly parallel on a log-log plot. Only their height changes, and with it the capacity, where each line crosses 1:

Raising the weights to a power increases the capacity to about $d_k^p$. But what if we could push this to the limit? Rather than pick one power, we can use infinitely many of them. Indeed, the exponential is a weighted sum of every power,

with the sharpness $\beta$ setting the weight on the higher powers. Here is the same experiment with $\beta = \sqrt{d_k}$, the value self-attention uses,6 for the exponential and its series truncated after 2, 3 and 4 terms:

With 2 terms, the capacity is about 40, below the linear store’s, since the constant term gives every key a weight of about 1. With 3 terms it’s about 450, and with 4 terms about 3,100, close to the squared ReLU’s. The full exponential stays far below the dashed line, so its capacity is past the edge of the chart.

To find the exponential’s capacity, we query with a stored key $k_j$, so the target memory has similarity 1 and weight $w_j = e^{\beta}$. Every other memory has weight $w_i = e^{\beta s_i}$, where for random unit keys the similarity $s_i$ is roughly Gaussian with mean 0 and variance $1/d_k$. With random values of similar lengths,

Setting the ratio to 1 gives a capacity of

growing exponentially with $\beta$ as long as $\beta$ is well below $d_k$, rather than polynomially in $d_k$ like before! With $\beta = \sqrt{d_k} = 8$, the capacity is about $e^{14} \approx 1.2$ million memories, nearly 20,000 times the linear store’s. A longer run of the same experiment puts the capacity at about 1.2 million too.

In practice, we may not want to naively exponentiate numbers in our implementation, since small numbers can underflow and large numbers can overflow. Fortunately, the interference only depends on the ratios between weights, as the chain above shows, so we can divide every weight by their sum without changing the interference-to-signal ratio, while ensuring numerical stability:

Unlike an MLP, whose keys and values are trained weights, self-attention computes its keys and values from the tokens in its context. Each token stores one memory, so the number of memories $M$ is the context length. That’s what makes self-attention non-parametric: its memories aren’t parameters, and the store grows with the context.

Here’s the bar figure again, starting with softmax. At $\beta = 8$, recall never fails within the slider’s range, so lower $\beta$ to 2 and raise $M$: recall fails after a few dozen memories. Each doubling of $M$ needs a bit more $\beta$ to keep recall working, which is the idea behind the next section.

Since $\beta$ determines how hard we suppress less similar keys, we can increase $\beta$ as the number of key-value pairs increases. Why not just make $\beta$ huge? As $\beta \to \infty$, softmax becomes a hard argmax that picks only the most similar key, which isn’t differentiable, and a very large $\beta$ already makes training work poorly, since the softmax saturates and the gradients to every other key vanish. So we raise $\beta$ only as much as $M$ requires. Scaling the attention logits with $\log M$ is a trick for long contexts that does this. There are a few versions of it, and each sets $\beta$ relative to a fixed reference length $L$, usually the training length, so that $\beta$ keeps its trained value when $M = L$:

Here’s how each rule does in our experiment, with $\beta = \sqrt{d_k} = 8$ at $L = 1024$ memories:

Qwen’s rule and Su’s rule coincide past the reference length $L$, where the interference-to-signal ratio falls as the store grows, to about 0.004 at 2 million memories. YaRN’s faster-growing scale pushes the ratio down to about $10^{-4}$. In each case, scaling $\beta$ with $\log M$ allows for essentially an unbounded number of memories with distinct keys to be stored.

Here are the memory stores we visited, with their capacities when we query with a stored key and the keys and values are random:

We started from a heuristic memory store, the outer-product memory, and gradually built our way up to all the standard layers we see today in modern transformers. This perspective also allowed us to estimate how they differ in their capacity, their ability to act as vector-valued key-value stores.

I should mention that this capacity estimate is only one way to look at the architecture of modern neural networks. Our capacity estimate only counts how many random vectors a single layer can recall before the interference dominates the signal. In fact we haven’t actually considered the training data at all, which affects what actually is being represented in the keys and values! There are other works which account for the trained layers, measuring stored information in bits. Morris et al. estimate that GPT-style models memorize about 3.6 bits per parameter, and find that once a model fills its capacity, it starts to generalize and memorizes less of each training example. Allen-Zhu & Li find that language models store about 2 bits of factual knowledge per parameter, even when quantized to int8.

From here, there are many related directions which are also fascinating:

I’ve always been drawn to memory, maybe because I viscerally feel how limited my own is. Perhaps part of me hopes that by understanding how machines remember, I’ll learn something about myself too.

Sometimes this accumulation of keys and values is called “Hebbian learning”, since the strength of the synapses (weights) is increased by inputs (keys) and outputs (values) that fire together (are correlated). ↩︎

This outer-product memory store is used for the state of linear attention, also called fast weights: each token stores the memory $(k, v)$ by adding $v k\transpose$ to a matrix that later tokens query (Katharopoulos et al.; Schlag, Irie & Schmidhuber). ↩︎

This is for recalling a clean value vector. If each value only needs to point toward the right answer among a fixed set, like selecting the most likely token, a recall just has to land closer to the right answer than to the wrong ones, and a $d\times d$ matrix can hold about $d^2$ facts (Nichani, Lee & Bietti). ↩︎

We can also use this regression objective to design short-term memories that a sequence model writes during the forward pass, like linear attention and self-attention. See my work on test-time regression. ↩︎

For random keys, a ReLU reduces the interference by a factor of $\sqrt 2$. A random key’s similarity is equally likely to be positive or negative, so the ReLU zeroes about half of the weights and leaves the other half unchanged. That halves the interference’s variance, the sum of the squared weights, so the interference itself shrinks by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$. See Zhong et al. for a full derivation. ↩︎

Transformers divide the similarities by $\sqrt{d_k}$ rather than multiplying. But their queries and keys have length about $\sqrt{d_k}$, so a matching pair has $q\transpose k \approx d_k$. Our keys and queries have unit length, so a matching pair has similarity 1. Hence we scale by $\beta = \sqrt{d_k}$ . ↩︎

In transformer notation, the similarity is $k_i\transpose q$ with $q = W_Q x$, scaled by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$. I fold $W_Q$ into the keys. Keys and queries in a transformer have length about $\sqrt{d_k}$, so that scaling matches $\beta = \sqrt{d_k}$ for unit-length keys like ours. ↩︎

#9973. BOFH: The best way to stop an idea spreading is a controlled burn

The Boss mentions 'AI security,' triggering an entirely proportionate incident response

Look, off in the ether – is it a bird, is it a plane? No, it's a stupid idea, on final approach...

And look, the Boss has his office door open!

The Boss has wandered into Mission Control with something obviously on his mind. Over time, the PFY and I have learned to equate these thoughtful moments with the BAG FULL lamp of a commercial vacuum cleaner at a waxing salon. Do not open.

His presence in Mission Control is never a good sign, but his "thoughtful" presence, even more so. He'll have seen something, read something, spoken to someone, or possibly overheard something in a toilet stall that will have sounded – to him – like a great idea. Or it might have been a cheddar-frenzy-induced fever dream that he wants to run by us.

And the Boss's crazy ideas are, unfortunately, like bran flakes to his mental digestion, the output of which being delivered to the PFY and myself as a veritable slurry of poorly considered ideas.

"AI," he says, pausing for effect, once he's rolled to a stop.

He then waits patiently for one of us to ask "What about AI?" However, that will never happen. In terms of stupidity, it's up there with saying Candyman into a mirror five times, power washing a gremlin, or visiting a basement when Jason's in town.

"For the security system," the Boss teases.

I continue my intense focus on my monitors, hoping the lunacy will depart. The PFY does the same.

The PFY and I know that the only way out of this is to stall till the end of the day, at which time the Boss's overnight reset will trigger, leaving him only a vague memory of having had a good idea.

"Uh-oh," I say, reaching into my drawer for my crashtop. "It looks like one of the distribution switches on 4 has crashed."

"And not just 4 – it looks like the boardroom has gone down too."

"It could be a virus," I say, using words I know the Boss will respond to.

"I don't know. It's too soon to tell," I say, departing.

So now I'm hiding in a cramped comms room on the fourth floor while I plug the crashtop into the CCTV VLAN so I can check on the Boss's location. Luckily, we upgraded the system to an AI-integrated platform, so I only need to type IDIOT into the search field to find him.

Sure enough, he's back in his office, typing away furiously, which can only mean there's a memo on its way. And if there's a memo, there's a path to reminding him of his dumb idea tomorrow...

On the screen, the Boss looks around anxiously as his laptop fires up DBAN in full confirm mode. He then reaches for a sheet of paper and starts scribbling furiously.

The office lights switch off as the BMS system clock suddenly finds out that it's midnight.

On the screen, the Boss's phone torch comes on and he resumes scribbling.

"Hello?" the Boss asks, with a hint of feedback.

"It's the virus!" I gasp. "It's coming from inside the building!!!"

Meantime, I've messaged the PFY and advised him to pick up the shredder from the boardroom cupboard.

"It's the wireless broadband connection on the roof!" I say. "We need to disconnect it!"

"I thought you said it was coming from inside the building?" the Boss asks.

Further discussion is impossible now that his phone is erasing itself, having been marked as a stolen device...

The PFY was unable to find the shredder, as it looks to have been dumped now that board papers are no longer printed. On the plus side, he has a plan.

"So, we're clear to enter the building?" I ask the fire warden.

"Yes, you're clear, though it looks like the fire started on your floor."

"It doesn't surprise me," I say. "We're creative people. Our ideas spark innovation."

"It looks like there was some as-yet-unknown accelerant used."

"Oh," I say, thinking of the smokers the PFY occasionally chats to outside at the skip. "Well, we may never know."

"Don't you have some sort of AI surveillance system?" he asks.

"Sadly, that was the first thing to go," I lie.

"So, in review," the PFY says. "We shut down a couple of switches, put the building in night mode, trashed a laptop and a mobile phone, then set fire to the building."

"And the funny thing is, I took a look at his scribblings – and it wasn't all that bad."

"Really?" I ask, reaching for the isopropyl and a lighter, just in case it's contagious.

#9972. Baseten on Hugging Face Inference Providers 🔥

We're thrilled to share that Baseten is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub!

Baseten joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub's model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

Baseten is an AI infrastructure platform that covers serverless AI, training and more. With a catalog of many frontier models, Baseten makes it easy for developers to integrate a wide range of AI capabilities into their applications with minimal setup.

Baseten supports a broad spectrum of model types - from LLMs to text-to-speech and more. As part of this initial integration, Baseten is launching support for conversational and text-generation tasks on Hugging Face, enabling access to popular open-weight LLMs such as Kimi K3, latest DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM-5.2, and many more. Support for additional tasks will roll out soon!

See the full list of models supported by Baseten here.

Follow Baseten on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/baseten.

Baseten is available through the Hugging Face SDKs - huggingface_hub (>= 1.26.1) for Python and @huggingface/inference for JavaScript.

The following examples show how to use the latest DeepSeek V4 Flash through Baseten. Use a Hugging Face token to authenticate - the request will be routed to Baseten automatically.

Hugging Face Inference Providers are integrated in most Agent Harnesses - including Pi, OpenCode, Hermes Agents, OpenClaw, and more. This means you can plug baseten-hosted models straight into your favorite tools without any extra glue code. Browse the full list of integrations here.

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a baseten API key you're billed on your baseten account.

For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us; we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.)

Important Note ‼️ PRO users get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free users, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

We would love to get your feedback! Share your thoughts and/or comments here: https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/HuggingDiscussions/discussions/49

Discuss and provide feedback on Hugging Face Hub features

Thank you, beautiful work. I’ll take a closer look at it soon!

#9971. Don't bother patching: multiple remote code execution vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM800A

Since October 11th waves of cyber attacks have hit internet-exposed fridge controllers by Danfoss and Copeland throughout Europe, with attackers triggering defrosting operations and causing tens of millions of euros in spoilt food damages and even causing fires in some cases.While, as pointed out by SentinelOne, attribution remains open and analysts should be careful not to immediately assume all incidents are linked to the same threat actor, the impact of these incidents (in particular their psychological effect) is in sharp contrast to their technical simplicity.

While much online commentary has correctly pointed out that these kind of controllers should not be internet-exposed, remote connectivity of some sort is often a must-have due to maintenance personnel constraints and SLA or insurance requirements.As a result, many asset owners are simply content to change default credentials, apply patches for known vulnerabilities, enable strict level session control, and move on. This is insufficient and asset owners need to remove internet exposure as soon as possible (e.g. though use of a VPN, private APN, or highly restrictive IP whitelisting ACLs). We recommend against allocating scarce security resources to patching efforts and instead focus on reducing exposure.As we will demonstrate in this blogpost, Midnight Blue researcher Carlo Meijer found several pre-authentication remote code execution 0-day vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A in less than an hour with casual manual inspection.

Prior to the attack waves which started in France on October 11th, several vulnerabilities had already been documented in multiple Danfoss product lines (AK SM-800, AK SM-800A, AK-EM100) by SynAcktiv (in 2023 [1,2]), Claroty (in 2025 [3]), and DIVD/HackDefense (in 2023 [4]).

These vulnerabilities have included the much-discussed code-of-the-day authentication bypass (CVE-2025-41450), OS command injection (CVE-2023-25915, CVE-2025-41451) and path traversal (CVE-2023-25914) vulnerabilities in the AK-SM800A, as well as SQL injection (CVE-2023-22583) and OS command injection (CVE-2023-25911) vulnerabilities in the EOL AK-EM100.

All of these vulnerabilities are shockingly trivial to find and exploit, and the first public Proof-of-Concept (PoC) exploits were dropped within 48 hours of the French attacks [5, 6] - preceding the second attack wave on November 2nd.

According to Censys, there are still hundreds of Danfoss systems exposed online (though no doubt a sizeable chunk are by now honeypots) and over a 1000 Copeland and Dixell fridge controllers. In addition, controllers from similar vendors (such as Eliwell) which have not been targeted remain exposed in the hundreds as well.

All this is to say that despite the demonstrable subpar security posture of these controllers and several attack waves with serious impact, controllers remain exposed to the public internet. While this is for understandable reasons (supermarket chains sometimes risk SLA or insurance condition violations by taking away remote maintenance and restricting access through VPNs isn't a trivial systems change), we consider it of paramount importance for defenders not to fall into the trap of considering risks sufficiently mitigated by applying patches as is suggested by Danfoss guidance.

In order to demonstrate this, we investigated the latest Danfoss AK-SM800A firmware version (5.3.2 at the time of writing) and within an hour of manual investigation (no AI necessary...) uncovered 6 pre-authentication remote code execution 0-day vulnerabilities.

We are currently in a coordinated vulnerability disclosure process with Danfoss and as such will withhold technical details until disclosure is sorted, but due to ongoing targeting of these controllers we consider it important asset owners have a realistic view of the overall security posture of these devices ontrollers in order to take the appropriate measures rather than rely on piecemeal patching.

Mitigation: Restrict network exposure through VPNs, private APN, or highly restrictive IP whitelisting ACLs

Danfoss AK-SM800A firmware images can be downloaded from their website and contain 7-zip compressed ARM binaries handling application logic. Danfoss AK-SM800A controllers run Danux, a custom Yocto-based Linux distribution, on an i.MX6 processor.

Let's start by setting up an emulation environment for the firmware. The path of least resistance here is emulating the binary in userland, rather than emulating the entire system including the kernel. After mounting the filesystem, we can copy qemu-armel-static in there and run the following command to be presented with a shell:

As pointed out by Claroty, the SM800A platform consists of an NGINX reverse proxy, a bunch of CGI handlers, and independent processes handling application logic. Requests for URLs ending with .cgi suffix are forwarded to a task created by the sm_app executable.

It turns out that sm_app is a huge monolithic application that is responsible for pretty much everything that happens on the device. It is more like a mini Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) running in a userland process (a common embedded architectural choice resulting from lift-and-shift platform migrations). It has a task (thread) list consisting of 52 entries, among which are Task_Modbus_drv_task, Task_Ethernet, Task_IOHandler and Task_Web to name a few. Running the sm_app in this environment that's missing a significant chunk of the devices and drivers will almost certainly end in a crash. Applying some ad-hoc patches to the binary to avoid crashes will probably work, but potentially painful.

Fortunately, we're only interested in Task_Web, so instead of fixing up everything, I can just LD_PRELOAD my way in the binary, let it run all the initialization code until it hits main(), hijack the code flow from there, apply some hooks which I won't delve into here, and start the web server. It turns out that Danux conveniently ships with gcc:

With some additional minor fixes, we are now able to talk to the emulated web server:

The first thing to do is get a sense of the security quality of the code base through so-called code smells and anti-patterns.

The first such bad code smell is the extremely liberal use of strcpy. Use of the strcpy() function is discouraged as there is no size parameter. Instead, the function will keep copying bytes from the source buffer into the destination until it hits a null byte. This is a common source of memory corruption vulnerabilities in cases where the source buffer is provided by the user. Hundreds of strcpy invocations exist in the codebase which are part of externally reachable and unauthenticated handler functions. In fact, in earlier firmware releases each command handler is itself responsible for enforcing authentication, rather than doing so centrally. This needlessly enlarged the pre-authentication attack surface.

Next, we check for binary security mechanisms and exploit mitigations:

It turns out that stack canaries and Position Independent Executable (PIE) are not enabled. These mechanisms have been staples of memory corruption defenses for decades and enabling these features on a modern Linux distribution running on a modern ARM application processor requires no engineering work at all. It is simply a matter of setting the right compiler flag. Enabling these features became the default in Ubuntu 17.10 and there is simply no excuse for a network-facing application that was last updated a few months ago to not have them enabled.

What's more worrying, is that multiple Danfoss business units (including Climate Solutions & Electronic Controllers) received IEC 62443-4-1 certification for Secure Product Development Lifecycle and this is prominently advertised as such. In addition, Danfoss explicitly mentions IEC 62443-4-2 is a guiding framework for designing cybersecurity requirements and implementing improvements. Asset owners, system integrators, and those responsible for procurement should realize exactly how little such certifications can say about the actual security posture of a product.

The initial impression of Danfoss' security posture, combined with the nature of the historical vulnerabilities, is a worrying one. But to see just how bad this pans out, let's see what can be found in no more than one hour of manually digging through the latest version of the firmware.

We could develop a harness and subject the binary to coverage-guided fuzzing. However, that constitutes serious effort, and with the impression of the code quality that I have, I'm going to simply look into random places where strcpy() is invoked instead. One of the first functions inspected turns out to be an unauthenticated endpoint for a CGI handler having a bunch of parsing logic and strcpy invocations.

While we will not disclose the exact endpoint affected, we will show it can be trivially exploited with a oneliner:

This gives us a nice SEGFAULT showing we can probably hijack program control flow:

There's at least 5 different vulnerabilities of this kind in just the little bit of code i inspected.

Of course, remotely triggering a crash is bad in itself, but being able to leverage the buffer overflow to obtain remote code execution is much worse. Any reasonably experienced exploit developer will agree exploiting straightforward stack-based buffer overflows on ARM Linux without exploit mitigations is very straightforward. And if they don't, there's probably a frontier or open weight model out there willing to help them agree.

The only challenge (if you can call it that) left to overcome is the fact that strcpy() stops copying bytes when it hits a null byte. If we wish to gain remote code execution, we inevitably need to write several addresses containing null bytes. Thus, we need to somehow overcome this inherent limitation of strcpy() and while we won't share our approach for now it's not exactly rocket surgery. Also, the exploited application runs as root (because of course it does).

Since we have to be vague due to coordinated disclosure being ongoing, let's at least show the result of our 100% artisanal, hand-crafted, AI and gluten free exploit in action as PoC:

The exploit demonstrated above was targeted at version 3.3.0, but the bugs are present in the latest version of the firmware as well (5.3.2 at the time of writing).

In later firmware versions, however, the concepts of session control and security levels were introduced by Danfoss [1,2]. According to Danfoss, session control is an authentication rules engine for the various remote interfaces (StoreView Browser, StoreView Web, Alsense, and 3rd party XML). This session control mechanism replaces the individual handler-level authentication enforcement mentioned above.

Session control has three security levels: backward compatible, permissive, and strict. Starting at 4.0 security level strict was set as the default which:

This AKSM-auth header mechanism historically held a base64 encoded username and password as the authentication key but now needs to include a session token derived from initial authentication [3]. At the strict security level, virtually all the web-accessible attack surface is fenced off from unauthenticated users (including the bug that was used in the exploit above) which is why enabling this security control was included in CERT-FR's official mitigations.

Unfortunately, it turns out the session control mechanism also has at least one trivial pre-authentication memory corruption vulnerability.

The way this is implemented is through a separate binary: sm_fcgi_app. It acts as a Web Application Firewall (WAF) in the sense that it passes through all commands to NGINX if it believes that the user is authenticated. If not, then the only command allowed to be passed through is the getauth command, which is used to authenticate.

At first glance i spotted a potential for parser differential attacks on sm_fcgi_app which might open the entire attack surface to unauthenticated users, but decided to investigate a quicker route to success. It turns out there's another simple strcpy based pre-authentication memory corruption:

Running this against the latest AK-SM800A firmware with strict session control enabled produces a SEGFAULT which, with some additional effort, can be turned into yet another pre-authentication RCE. It goes without saying that sm_fcgi_app does not have stack canaries and PIE enabled either. I think we're done here, we've seen enough.

The last thing we want to figure out is exactly how bad this can get.

It's one thing to initiate long defrost cycles and spoil tens of millions of food once, but the typical response of defenders is to factory reset affected controllers, rotate credentials, apply patches, set strict session control mode, and possibly wall off the controllers from internet exposure. But any controllers that are hit continue to do their job in production.

Now, imagine an attacker who manages to persist on such controllers. They don't just trigger the initial payload but they leave a little implant that survives a factory reset and firmware update. With OS level access, this isn't too hard on typical Unix-like devices as shown in the SALTWATER / SEASPY malware for Barracuda devices, FIRESTARTER malware for Cisco devices, and Sonicwall malware all which survive firmware updates.

In such a scenario, an attacker could either retain remote access or leave a time-triggered payload for a 2nd (or 3rd...) strike - increasing damage by spoiling new batches of food. Alternatively, attackers could simply wipe flash memory and/or push a malformed firmware update to brick the controllers and render them permanently inoperable - requiring costly and time-consuming replacement similar to the TTPs deployed during the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid.

Both approaches seem feasible against the AK-SM800A controllers since they do not make use of the i.MX6's secure boot features as evidenced by checking some of the responsible One-Time Programmable (OTP) fuse registers.

1. Full device take-over: Through remote code execution, an unauthenticated attacker can remotely run arbitrary code at the operating system level of the AK-SM800A controller. This would allow the attacker to change parameters or initiate unwanted actions (such as defrosting operations) while hiding their activities from any system logs. In addition, the lack of secure boot functionality would allow an attacker with RCE to persistently implant controllers to maintain access or have it trigger a secondary payload at a later point in time. Without deep introspection and forensics capabilities, determining whether a device is implanted at the firmware level (even after a factory reset) is infeasible.

2. Equipment damage (bricking): Due to the lack of secure boot, an attacker with RCE could push malicious firmware that simply renders the device inoperable and irrecoverable without specialized hardware intervention (e.g. by wiping flash memory and/or causing an infinite boot loop). Such a 'bricking' or wiper approach would require full device replacement. The dangers of such a scenario to OT equipment in particular and adversary deployment of such TTPs have been highlighted in previous blogposts by Midnight Blue [1,2]. This could potentially lead to freezers being unavailable for days or longer while controllers get replaced.

In light of all of the above, we consider piecemeal patching or enabling of strict session control to be a misallocation of scarce security and personnel resources since they have minimal security ROI against such a fundamentally flawed codebase missing basic exploit mitigations and yielding multiple pre-auth RCEs with an hour's casual glance.

Instead, we strongly recommend asset owners and system integrators to take the following course of action for all Danfoss, Copeland, and Dixell controllers and preferably for similar controllers by other vendors as well:

How we found multiple RCEs in less than an hour, and why patching seems hopeless

Limitations of authentication in TETRA, and how it fails to provide integrity guarantees

#9970. Meta is back with Muse Glimmer: local, agentic, multimodal, and open source

To celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:

In addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

That means you can make it do things like, quantize itself, find quantized weights on the Hub, deploy itself to inference endpoints, and even optimize itself for specific hardware! Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as moviebox a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

I also like the architectural choices here, particularly the hybrid attention pattern, grouped-query attention, and Q-K normalization. Alternating sliding-window and full-attention layers seems like a thoughtful way to balance long-context capability with efficiency, while sharing KV heads across query heads can significantly reduce memory requirements during generation.

The day-zero ecosystem support makes the release even more compelling. Having integrations across Transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, and other tools means developers can start testing real-world workflows immediately instead of waiting for the surrounding ecosystem to catch up. Open multimodal models that are genuinely practical to run locally could be a huge part of where AI development goes next. 💡👏

#9969. Palantir adds three UK police forces to its beat with £10.1M deal

Five-year contract follows London setback as former Met chief Cressida Dick emerges as a paid adviser

Three UK police forces led by Cambridgeshire Constabulary have awarded Palantir a £10.1 million contract after London Mayor Sadiq Khan blocked a separate deal with the Metropolitan Police.

The five-year agreement covers Bedfordshire Police, Cambridgeshire Constabulary, and Hertfordshire Constabulary, despite warnings from campaigners and politicians about dependence on the supplier.

A contract award notice says the east of England police forces expect the Palantir platform to provide "an enterprise-wide data integration and analytics capability, enabling the secure ingestion, linking, and analysis of data from multiple systems and sources across the policing environment." The contract runs until October 2031, with the estimated value covering all three forces.

News of the award coincided with revelations that former Metropolitan Police commissioner Dame Cressida Dick has worked as a paid adviser to Palantir since September 2025.

A Palantir spokesperson told the Bureau of Investigative Journalism: "Dame Cressida is advising us on how our software could help improve the delivery of services in the public sector, drawing on more than 40 years of public service in a variety of roles."

Dick said her role was limited to advising on how such products could assist public services. She said she had never lobbied or advocated for Palantir, or introduced the company to her contacts.

Dick led the Metropolitan Police, the UK's largest force, between 2017 and 2022. She left after Khan said he had lost confidence in her. She later said she was "intimidated" into leaving.

Separately, Khan stepped in to block the Met from awarding a £50 million contract to Palantir. His office cited serious concerns about the procurement process. Palantir later sued the Met, but the case was settled in October.

The new police contract award follows a report from MPs warning of vendor lock-in to US suppliers, including Palantir. It said: "Our view that Palantir's increasing presence across the public sector represents an unacceptable point of weakness is not ideologically motivated or driven by concerns about the quality of their products.

"The government should retain the ability to pick and choose individual suppliers and safeguard against the risk of vendor lock-in and debilitating dependencies, particularly in areas of critical national importance such as healthcare and national security infrastructure." ®

#9968. A technical vision for the Haskell ecosystem

the technical leadership committee of the Haskell Foundation has been successfully bootstrapped!

We have spent the last few weeks discussing our vision and strategy and are now fully operational.

We’re going to actively develop initiatives and proposals that we believe need funding and execution. For that we need companies, contractors and volunteers to help. Everyone can participate, whether it’s by dropping ideas informally, writing a concrete proposal themselves or finding entities that could support or fund initiatives.

We tried to keep the community proposal process as light as possible. However, we believe that fairness and participation are vital, especially when funding is involved, so anyone who writes a proposal should be aware that we will open the floor for the community to comment or even deliver counter-proposals. The process may evolve as we make experiences and get feedback.

Below is our vision. Feel free to get in touch with us!

We believe that Haskell is awesome and that it can provide unique value to everyone, because it sits at an interesting intersection between human craftsmanship and machine automation:

There may be better languages for formal verification or for vibecoding, but there’s no better language for “human in the loop”. Haskell is where we maintain control of our work, build institutional knowledge and ship responsibly.

We’re driven to improve Haskell for everyone:

Imagine Haskell had the iteration speed of golang, the debugging capabilities of C# and the onboarding experience of rust. And all that while providing stronger guarantees and better performance!

Modern workflows require fast iteration times: compilation, interactive repl, remote dependency caching, CI and test integration. All of this affects both human and machine workflows.

While Haskell scales well in terms of code complexity… it doesn’t scale well in terms of build times. As an example, GHC’s own CI has turnaround times of 6 hours. We want to bring them down to 2.

Instead of helplessly dumping logs and binaries into LLM chats, we envision deterministic tools that allow precise and ergonomic enquiries:

And all of that in your editor/IDE as well as through powerful CLI and scripting interfaces, the latter enabling power users as well as LLM-driven debugging (natively, without requiring any custom adapters like MCP).

Debugging must be fun again, without littering Debug.Trace.trace all over your codebase.

Documentation and interactive exploration will assist newcomers in understanding all caveats of laziness and GHC and should clearly explain how to leverage these tools.

In these times of low frustration tolerance, we are going to build the best onboarding experience in the programming language ecosystem, because it is the ultimate benchmark for developer experience as a whole.

This can only be done if we commit to unix principles, which we summarize as:

Documentation should be a joy to read, written by humans, for humans.

Security and trust don’t get established by accident. Once trust is lost, it’s often irrecoverably lost.

To protect our community assets and reputation, we need to:

We should further support attempts to utilize or extend the strengths of the Haskell language to boost practical applications of secure design and architecture, such as Information Flow Control or Mandatory Access Control. We’re also monitoring the efforts of dependent types and liquidhaskell.

What if we could compile Haskell software that’s 10 years old with the latest GHC, without any source code changes?

While this might seem like an impossible goal to achieve… embarking on that journey is going to get us closer to a robust, stable and predictable ecosystem anyway.

The questions we need to answer along the way are:

Not only requires this investment in GHC and core tooling, but also potentially support community efforts to maintain stable package sets or coordinate ecosystem upgrades, make cabal more ergonomic for complex use cases, spearhead and support stability policies and gather data about what parts of the ecosystem cause churn.

We want Haskell to not only be a choice for fast moving startups, but also for large or conservative companies that do not want their workflows or software stacks disrupted. Stability will benefit both of these types of users, reduce cost and friction and build a reputation for Haskell as a modern language with a predictable ecosystem.

All of the above is an attempt to support the Haskell open source ecosystem that we love. We are committed to open source, its values and the social aspect of it. Collaboration is how we engage with and inspire each other.

We want to enable all the maintainers and volunteers who keep this ecosystem alive, many of them unknown, doing their part on a Saturday evening at the other end of the world.

We code because we love to ship products. But we also code, because we want to socialize, meet people and have a good time. We’re committed to both of these values.

Thank you @hasufell and the TLC for writing this up; it’s very inspiring to see these goals. I think this ambitious agenda will provide us with a lot of fun and profit.

#9966. Quantum Systems drones back in the air after malware scare

Germany's Bundeswehr lifted precautionary grounding after malicious update reportedly reached military servers

Quantum Systems says its drones are flying again with Germany's military after a cyberattack prompted a precautionary grounding.

The company says it spotted the attack at the end of October and reported it to the relevant authorities, but disclosed few details about the intrusion.

"The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said on Thursday.

"Through the quick measures taken and the characteristics of the incident, there is no risk in operating Quantum Systems' unmanned systems for the end users and the operators."

It added that other players in the European defense industry, and those who support Ukraine's military efforts, have faced "persistent cyberattacks for years."

The Bundeswehr grounded its Quantum Systems drones after malware was detected in an update to QBase, the company's QBase ground-control software, Der Spiegel reported, citing unnamed sources. QBase lets operators plan missions, monitor flights, and process data from the ground.

The malicious update reportedly reached servers belonging to the German military and other customers, but did not directly infect the drones.

"The fleet is operating normally around the globe – including Germany and the Bundeswehr," Quantum Systems told Reuters. "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution."

A spokesperson for Germany's defense ministry declined to comment on the attack or the reported details. The Register asked Quantum Systems for further details.

Founded in 2015, Quantum Systems has been providing drones to the Ukrainian war effort for years.

Last month, Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced funding for "several tens of thousands" of the company's interceptor drones as part of Germany's winter aid package. The new drones will be built in Ukraine and support interceptor systems already in use on the front lines.

Quantum Systems announced a $1.2 billion Series D funding round in July, valuing the company at around $8 billion. ®

#9965. Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

Knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

The distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a new, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

The standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

As a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

Dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

Offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:

The GIF below shows the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

The table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

The loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only shows up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

To see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

Distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

The efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

The student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

Want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

#9964. Oh my Word! Microsoft retires compatibility options, because who needs layouts to stay put

Admins with archives of ancient files brace for the wave of tickets from confused users

Microsoft is retiring some legacy layout settings in Word, potentially rearranging documents created or last saved in Word 2010 or earlier.

"Affected documents may show layout differences, such as text reflow, changes in spacing or page count, or images and shapes moving to another page," the Windows biz said.

The advice, if silly little things like page layout in a document matter, is to "consider exporting it to PDF before the change."

Compatibility Mode lets a newer version of Word open a document created in an older version, such as Word 2010, without changing its layout. Newer features are switched off while the document is open this way. Users can convert the document to unlock newer features, although people using older versions of Word may then have difficulty editing parts of it.

Microsoft has not identified the individual settings being retired, saying only: "We are retiring a set of compatibility options in Microsoft Word (desktop app) for documents in Compatibility Mode." The reason? "To simplify how Word handles document layout and provide a more consistent experience across platforms."

Administrators may therefore want to check older templates, forms, and other documents whose pagination needs to stay put.

The change is due to begin rolling out in the Windows version of Word from December 2026 and be completed by January 2027. The Mac version will follow in early 2027.

Microsoft Word is more than 40 years old, and its first Windows version was released as the 1980s drew to a close. The word processor has evolved over the decades and is a mainstay of Microsoft's productivity suite.

Compatibility Mode helps keep older documents from having their layouts abruptly borked the way Word does so well. Losing some of those safeguards could give administrators a fresh batch of "what the heck has happened to this document?" tickets as the change rolls out. ®

#9963. Build Low-Latency Multilingual Voice Agents: Open Weights & Full Deployment Control with NVIDIA Magpie TTS

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

By the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one users notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

Voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Supporting more languages is only part of the challenge. Developers also need the ability to:

Open models change what's possible on every one of these.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (new) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new)

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

In conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before users hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most important latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

At 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

The table above shows Magpie served as the NVIDIA NIM, measured on-prem — the optimized container running on your own GPU. The open Hugging Face checkpoint is the same model and your path for research and fine-tuning; the NIM is the tuned serving stack that produces these production latencies. Both run on hardware you control.

Because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

Low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

Local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

Together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

This release doesn't only add languages — it also improves synthesis quality across many existing ones. Compared to the previous release, Magpie shows reduced character error rates (CER) and higher speaker similarity (SSIM) on several languages, with the clearest gains on French and Spanish:

Source: Magpie TTS Multilingual model card. CER lower is better; SSIM higher is better.

The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

While objective metrics help measure progress, speech quality is ultimately perceptual. You can hear the difference yourself on NVIDIA Build or the Hugging Face demo.

Latency you can measure is useful. Latency you can control is even better.

Open weights give developers capabilities that come from owning the deployment. With Magpie you can:

For enterprises building production voice AI, this control over deployment, performance, and customization is often what matters most.

Voice AI in production is a system of models, not a single one. Magpie TTS is part of the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent Developer Example, a reference implementation showing how purpose-built speech, language, and reasoning models work together as a coordinated system — so you can build always-on voice agents, not just better-sounding speech.

The Nemotron Voice Agent developer example provides an end-to-end reference implementation that developers can clone, customize, and deploy in hours. It includes production patterns for:

Rather than assembling individual components from scratch, developers can start from a complete reference architecture and adapt it to their own applications.
