InfoQ Homepage Presentations Opening the Black Box: Critical Explainability for AI Agent Tool Selection with Kiji Inspector

Hannes Hapke shares how Dataiku’s open-source Kiji Inspector applies Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) directly to decision tokens to expose why agents pick specific tools. Moving past superficial chain-of-thought narratives, he discusses causal ablation, layer activation extraction via patched vLLM engines, and production monitoring workflows for software architects and senior engineering leaders.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

For today, we want to focus on what we call the Kiji Inspector. It is a tool that is helping you to understand how agents "Think." The fundamental problem that we have with agents is that we don't know how they actually make their decisions. We have a number of tools out there. We have prompt engineering, behavioral testing, or probably the most sophisticated processes like chain of thought. None of them are actually providing you causality, they're often just giving you plausible explanations or plausible narratives of what the root cause could be. When we were asked to figure out how can we make sure that the model that is running an agent is picking the right tool, how do we know that it's thinking about the right context, we decided that we needed to look into the model.

The way we do this is by using sparse autoencoders. Before we get there, let me start explaining what an autoencoder is. This is a concept that has been around for a very long time, probably three decades by now. Autoencoders take a set of inputs, reduce this to a smaller latent space vector, and then reconstruct them through a decoder. The whole point of that autoencoder is that you want to minimize the error between the input and the reconstructed output. In an optimal system, there would be zero error, and the output here would be exactly as the input. Then you know that the representation of your vector z here in your latent space is most optimal. This has been used many times in various things like embeddings and vector searches and information compression, dimensionality reductions of various sorts of kinds. This is a really interesting way of forcing your model to reduce the amount of information to a smaller vector space.

The cool thing about this concept is that it's self-supervised. You don't need any labeling. You use the input as the output, that's your target, and then in between, that's what you would use in production. With sparse autoencoders, you would flip this concept around a little bit. Here in this case, we wouldn't create a bottleneck for the information, but we want to go wide here, with a little catch, and I'll explain the catch. Let's say you grab an activation from a model, or a hidden state, and you pass it through the sparse autoencoder, you can go wide in the information, and that means you force the model to pick certain features to represent the information. When you take a look at the activations inside of a model, there's something that we call polysemantic representation of the context, which means that one neuron that fires can have multiple meanings or topics it would fire on.

In our feature representation, if we want to understand the model, we need to separate them and put them apart from each other, and so that's why we're going wide in the feature representations here. Then again, we try to then have a decoder where we narrow that information piece again, and we try to reconstruct the activations that we used as an input. The catch here is that in this activation function, we are then forcing the model to only use a small set of features to be actually active, and the rest of them, roughly 95%, that's the ideal number, we want to force them to be zero. In that moment, we actually force the model during the training process to just be really selective on a handful of features, and then we can be absolutely certain that those features are representing the themes and the context of the model itself, what the model was thinking in this given layer at the processing of a certain token.

Then we can go one step further. Once you have those feature vectors you generated, those indices don't mean anything to us, to humans. What we can then do is, once we have a corpus, we can grab all the documents that fire highly on, let's say, dimension 3 and dimension 6, and then we can look at those documents and say, what do they have in common? It could easily be that they say like, the first one has something to do with Python, so then over the course of the entire corpus, we could say, those two features, they represent a programming language or an API vocabulary or things like this.

What we have tried to do in this project is combining a number of things and package them up so that everybody can use them in production. The first thing that we want to do is, sparse autoencoders have been around for a number of years now, and OpenAI published some research, and Eleuther published some research on this, but they focused on the entire LLM generation. What we changed here in our approach is we were only interested in the agentic decision-making. We focused on the decision token rather than the entire prompt, and then averaging those activations across the entire prompt. Then we put a bunch of concepts together. For example, Eleuther came out with this concept of token-level fuzzing, and so we added this to our framework so anybody who wants to use that framework and trains their own models, they can use that token testing. Then also we added causal validation testing as well so that you can make sure, is it actually causal or is it just correlation?

Then the other sweet thing, what we changed here in this project, what is novel, is that we're not just training on a number of prompts, but we created those pairs, training pairs. We have a given intent — I'll show you an example later — but for a given intent, you have something that we call the anchor that's the correct answer and the correct tool use, and then there's an adversarial reply, which is very similar, but very different. It's basically like look something up in an internal database versus look up something online. Two different use cases, very similar in the prompt response, but very different outcome in terms of the tool selection.

Looking at the training pipeline, let's say we have all these pairs generated, which I will show you how we do this. We then take our target model, and little caveat here, those have to be open-source models. We can't do this with OpenAI's models because we don't have access to their weights, but you can do this with any open-source model, and that's another novelty in our framework that we're not just focusing on Gemma models from Google or Nemotron models from NVIDIA. That tool, that framework here is working with various open-source models that are out there. You pick your subject model, that's the model you want to use the explainability for, and then you run all your prompts through the model itself, grab all the activations from the particular layers you want to watch. Then with those activations, you can train your sparse autoencoder as I just showed you with putting them in, widening them up, and then forcing the decoder again to reconstruct that activation.

Then once you have the model trained, you can do a contrastive analysis, and I'll show you this later, how we then figure out through those pairs of what's actually relevant in the context or not. Or you can go to a large language model and say, tell me what those documents have in common, and then you can generate those themes. This all happens in that package where we call the Kiji Inspector. You put in your corpus, you nominate those models, and out you get a feature definition of what those features mean when you run those LLMs and agent requests.

Earlier, I just mentioned you have to pick a certain layer. There's a little bit of an art what layer to pick rather than science. There's a little bit of an explanation here that if you're early in the stack, like maybe in the first third, the model hasn't fully conceptualized all the concepts of your prompt request. You're basically activating things that are highly relevant to the prompt itself. If you're further down the stack, there's a lot of intricacies of the model itself. Here in this particular model, we're looking at the Nemotron 3 from NVIDIA. That's an MoE model. That's because every different request goes through different routings, you have crazy errors. Learning something later on is very difficult. Also, the concepts you extract are so abstract in some cases that even for humans, it's impossible to understand what's going on. Then also for the models, it's difficult.

What we wanted to do is, for our particular experiments, we picked layer 20 because it is already down the pipe. It's like the model extracted some abstract concepts. It's not too far down the pipe that it would be too non-human understandable. In our open-source models, what we're publishing, we're publishing multiple layers. You can pick wherever you want to be in your model layer setup. Again, this is another representation of the training pipeline. Basically, you have your input. You calculate those representations. Then you do the reconstruction back to, in our case, it's 2688 dimensions. Then you calculate the loss. It's a very standard autoencoder model architecture. The key thing, and we show this in the following slide, we're using a particular activation, what we call the Jump Regularized Linear Unit. I will explain this here why this is in this particular case.

Then, how do we actually focus on the decision token? The way we do this is by forcing the agent to respond to a given prompt and says, I will use blank. Whatever tool, whatever the model then responds is expected to be the tool name, because we've provided the selection of tools in the prompt itself. Then in the response, we would see what tool the model has chosen. We do this a million times. We generated a training set with a million samples, basically 500,000 pairs, good and bad examples. The pairs come in later when we try to evaluate the model. During the training process itself, we use them raw, and we have those 1 million samples. Why are we doing this contrastive pair design again? Here's a little example. Let's say you have a given intent, resolve a password issue, and you can have the request, how do I reset my password?

That would trigger the tool knowledge base. You could also say, I tried to reset my password three times, and that could be a completely different tool. It's very similar in the response or in the request, but it's a very different tool outcome in this particular case. Later on, what you will see is we will then use those pairs and figure out which of the features we generated are actually relevant for those given tools. When we generate the features for both tools, the dimensions where the features are different have mostly contributed to the decision-making between knowledge base versus ticket lookup.

I don't want to go through the math here, but there's an interesting concept regarding the JumpReLU. As you know, Regularized Linear Units basically are, anything negative is zeroed out and anything positive is the input. It's like a linear function, but it's not differentiable because of that bend. Here in the JumpReLU, that's another derivative of the ReLU activation function. It's basically the output is the input, but there's a threshold. The interesting thing here is when we train the model of, figure out which activation is actually relevant and not relevant, we can then tune that threshold during the training process as the output activation. That's another tweak we can have to teach the model which feature is relevant for which given activation. When we look at some results per layer, then we see some really interesting side effects of early on, the error is low, but the model hasn't learned much.

Later on, the error is crazy high because this is logarithmic. Then we have too many, basically we learn something, but the error is exorbitant high. That's why we ended up in our practical example, we ended up somewhere in between at layer 20. Again, if we look at some stats here, like total, I think we had like 2,600-and-something input features, we widened this to 10,000 dimensions. Of those 10,000 dimensions, a little bit above 80% of those dimensions are alive. That means somewhere through the training, they have been nonzero. Then only less than 0.2% are completely dead, meaning those features have never been used through the entire training process. Then when we do the testing later on, we actually figured out that out of those 10,000 features, 668 are actually highly relevant to all the tool selections we wanted to investigate. This is for a given model for a given layer and a given dataset. If you retrain this, you might see different results.

Then somebody could say, why do we have to go through all this craziness of sparse autoencoders and training another machine learning model in all these crazy setups? As you can imagine, it's a lot of computation there. This is basically a couple comparisons. If you take the activations and then train a linear model on this, could we then figure out is this tool correct or incorrect? If you compare this and a binary classification here, we get to almost 80% accuracy. It's not bad, but it's also not perfect. Then if you do some just accuracy versus F1 score, that's a little bit lower. Then somebody could say, what happens if we just take those activations with those 2,000 dimensions and we just cluster them? Could we from the cluster then figure out which tool is the correct one? You're better off flipping a coin than actually clustering.

I think that was for us the interesting thing to see with the sparse autoencoders. I'll explain what fuzzing is. We can bridge the gap between interpretability and also having some causality testable features. I just mentioned token-level fuzzing. That was introduced by Eleuther sometime back when they looked into sparse autoencoders for entire prompts. What they did was they took a look at the prompt and then swapped out individual tokens, and then looked at how is the activation affected by swapping out those tokens and how is the end result being affected by that. That's the same concept we provide in our tool case here, in our framework that people can use when they want to evaluate their sparse autoencoders. Then when you look at the individual features and the quality of them, we can see that for the majority of the features they actually correlate really well to what we predicted the outcome to be. Only a small number of them have very poor influence on the overall decision-making. Again, from those 600 features we selected, it felt pretty good. This is heading in the right direction.

Then, let's take a look at causality and those other things. That's always the big question. We started this project where like, can we explain how an agent selected a tool? At some point, we needed to take a look at, can we actually prove causality? Little side note, I'm not a statistician, so I would love to have a better conversation about this with somebody who is more experienced with this. What we have done is looking at the activations. While the activation in this given layer in the model was produced, we then zeroed out the top 10 activations in that given vector. Then we looked at, is the tool selection changing or not? This was our setup. It's a little bit of like wiring and intercepting all the activations and those types of things. Don't worry, through the framework, we provide the other tools where you can replicate that.

The way this works is for our experiment setups here, where we looked at various tools, we were actually able to show that if you do the contrastive ablation, that worked extremely well for a number of tools. There were certain tools where we couldn't prove it, but for the majority of the tools, it actually looked very promising. Just a couple results here, the p-score is very low, so we were pretty happy about this. Through those testing, we were able to show that 23 of those contrast types actually worked. That worked better than randomly flipping. We felt that this is also, again, heading in the right direction. Like, yes, those particular activations, those 10 dimensions we blanked out or zeroed out actually contributed actively to the tool selection.

This was a lot of theory and a little bit of math and all those types of things, but you don't have to do this yourself, and that's why we have the Kiji Inspector, and that's why we open sourced that at Dataiku. What we're trying to provide here with a toolkit and the framework is like, we wanted to provide a model-agnostic framework that everybody else can use in the industry. Companies like Google have published similar frameworks, but they're always very tool specific. For example, Gemma Scope is the explainability tool for Gemma 2 or Gemma 3 or Gemma 4, or there's no Gemma 4 expanded model yet. There is no training pipeline. There's a lot of repos floating around with scripts and everything, but it's not like something you can download and fork and run something end-to-end on your site for your particular models and your particular use cases.

Then we wanted to provide a full production setup. We see a lot of research in those cases, but we hadn't seen a good production setup where people can run vLLMs and also get the activations back. Because in most setups like vLLM or SGLang, you get the response back but those inference tools don't give you the activations of a particular layer back. We provide a patch to vLLM that allows you to do that, and we also give you the containers so you can run this in production. Then as I said, everything is fully open source. We provide Docker containers, there's a PyPI package as you will see, and then all the models we have trained are on Hugging Face. This is only a subset, the list is way longer of what we're providing on Hugging Face. With our large training set of those 1 million data points or 1 million samples and the 500,000 pairs, we recently just trained Gemma 4.

Who knows if Google actually comes out with their sparse autoencoders. We wanted to beat them, and so we have the sparse autoencoders for the Gemma 4 and then for the latest Nemotron models, the Nemotron 3, we also provide the sparse autoencoders. Unfortunately, we don't have infinite compute resources as Google, that's why we have to pick certain layers to support them. If you have specific reasons, and you want a particular layer of a particular model, let us know, we can probably help you there as well.

How would the inference setup look like? If you run for example an agent and says, analyze my Q3 report, you would go through a large language model. Again, it has to be an open-source model, because you have to host that model so you can patch your vLLM version. We're hoping to get this into vLLM at some point so that hosting platforms like Baseten and others can provide those features as well. Then, you not just get the response back but you also get the activation vector for a given layer for your response. Then that goes into your sparse autoencoder. From your 2688 dimensions, you would then go up to 10,000 dimensions. Remember most of the dimensions are actually zero. Then you can take a look at the top features that are active in this large vector, and then you can take a look at those indices and figure out what are the themes you have determined during the training itself.

Then you can take those themes and put them back into a large language model as an explanation. Now somebody might ask, what's the difference now between doing all of this and chain of thought? The key difference is this information piece was directly derived from the activation during the model when that token was generated. It is not chain of thought where it first goes through some reasoning steps and then tries to execute. In chain of thought it could say like, here are two things I want to do, and then it executes 15 other things. There's no connection between those two steps. Here, there's the direct connection between the activation at a given layer. It goes into the sparse vector, and then we have the connection to the feature map we generated during the training.

Now the actually fun part starts. In Hugging Face, you can define what we call forward hooks. When the model is being executed, in Hugging Face the model is not compiled so you can easily hook into the execution, and say, give me the vector of a given layer for that given input. Then, we can grab the layer from here. When it's being executed, we can then actually ship it back to the response and send it to the user. I can show you another setup we have where you can also work with compiled models so you get a better performance. Then you run the inference, you retrieve the vector, and that is your activation. You're ready to go to use your sparse autoencoder. If you use one of the models we already support, you can then use our Kiji Inspector. We followed the Hugging Face setup. You can say like, from pre-trained, you mention the base model and under the hood we figure out like, what sparse autoencoder it needs to download.

We go to the correct repo, and then we use the correct model for the correct layer. Under the hood we convert this into the correct feature vector and then also do the lookup of the features to the themes. When you run SAE describe, that's how you get the description and not just a random vector. This is how it looks like, and I will show you this, again, but this is a little bit better readable. You see all the indices up here, they basically tell you what indices is the top five the ones that are firing. You see the number one it says unknown. What does it mean? It means like during the training, that feature in that feature vector was not of high importance and we haven't described that. Maybe we need more training data or maybe we need to tweak the training process. The interesting thing is that when we look at the second feature that was firing, it was actually something related to dishwasher gasket issues.

Seems relevant to the prompt we have. If it would fire on something completely unrelated here then there would be a good sign to go back and say like, maybe there's something going on in the model or maybe my prompt is incorrect or something else happening. Those are the things you can then see from the inspection and the data we provide through the package.

Let me show you here a little demo of how this would work and how you can actually use this in production. Again, this is the same code that I showed you earlier where we just stepped through. I pre-ran this in a Colab notebook. If you want to follow along you can go to our GitHub repo. The quick start example works in a free Colab. If you want to use a larger model you have to pay for the bigger GPUs nowadays. This is still giving you an overview of how this works under the hood. Here's a truncated information on the slide. You see some more information, and we also provide the bottom examples. Basically, here you see all the things that are least related to that request. Then you can go down, and you can turn this into a description and you can see what the confidence level is.

Here's another thing that I think could be really interesting for folks. As I mentioned at the beginning, we provide patches for vLLM. Here in this case is like you can also execute the whole thing in vLLM. When you do vLLM generate, you can then also get the same vectors back with the explanations. We tied this all together in vLLM. Then we have another interesting example I think that is a use case where we're stepping through a larger agent setup. Instead of going through the code I want to show you how the result could look like, and maybe that gives you a feeling of how you can use this in your product. We built the standalone demo of like, this is your home repair agent. It tells you if something is broken, can you fix it yourself? Should you call somebody else? It could potentially look up YouTube videos of how to fix it.

In order to make sure that we know what the agent is doing, for every agent step, we then also look up what the sparse autoencoder features are. Here in this particular case, this was the dishwasher example, it relates to a machine handling water I would think, washing machines, and there's something like old machine troubling. At least we know that the agent is heading in the right direction when it made the decision of like a dishwasher is leaking in this particular case. You can do this for every different tool call. This one is completely empty, it's a good example, because when we trained this there was not a tool call in the training set at all for YouTube videos. For us it will be a good sample of like, we need to add more real-world examples in our training set. I showed you this example. There's a couple more, there's a left example there as well where we show this in a live demo, you can follow along what the agent is doing in the frontend while the agent is figuring out what is actually happening. It's pretty fun to look at.

What are the particular use cases you can use for your applications and where you could use the Kiji Inspector. One thing is like you could figure out what an agent misbehavior would be. Anything that is like, has it picked the wrong tool, as I showed you earlier in the examples, that is a something. You can do it for audit compliance. Some companies looking at this and figuring out, it's like, if we have another track record, traces is one thing but explainability is another thing. When we do traces, we basically see what tool has been selected but we still can't explain why that tool was selected. Here we generate another set of logs and figuring out why the agent has particularly selected this tool that is shown in the traces. Then we can do validate of prompt engineering. If you're not quite sure, like you want to optimize your prompt for particular goals and you don't want to do this iterative loop, you can then also investigate like how is that tool responding to your given prompt based on the activations.

Then obviously monitoring production drift. If your data changes, let's say you test your agent with a set of prompts, you watch those activations, and then over time you can see if those activations change. That is a really good indication that the data that is going through that agent has changed. Maybe you should take a look at that as well.

Just to summarize this, what are the key takeaways? We have the chance to prove that sparse autoencoders can work to explain why the agent made a certain decision. We showed how the token-level fuzzing works, and as part of the package we can prove that tweaking those prompts lead to different activations. I also showed the causal evidence of the tool selection is affected by zeroing out certain activations in the model itself. Then we did some comparison with construction only baseline, meaning, because it's a decoder and there's a loss effect, if we take this out, then we can actually show that there's a causal effect in the sparse autoencoder.

I want to let you go with a couple limitations and also pointing out some future work. As I said, you do need the model itself. It doesn't work with closed source models. Hopefully at some point they give us similar tools on there, and that would be fantastic. The training is pretty compute intensive, especially if you want to create your own datasets. If you want to use the tool and you want to create your own training sets, come talk to us. We can share some more tricks and tips of how to run this effectively. As I mentioned earlier, it is a synthetic dataset. If anybody wants to use this and has some ideas of what is missing in the dataset and where should we go in terms of making it more real-world replicable, then let us know. We would love to collaborate on that as well.

There's a future work here. We want to support more open-source models and provide those models from the start through Hugging Face. Something that is on mind is currently Qwen. More multi-layer experiments. Currently everything is based on single layers. It could be really interesting if you take a layer from the first third and then a layer from the last third, and then combine those and see what actually happens. Then another interesting idea we had was like what happens if you do cross-model transfer. Basically, you train on a Gemma model. You take those vectors. You learn certain features. Is there something we can generalize then if we go to another model and so we see certain patterns. That is all future work. We haven't touched this yet. If anybody wants to collaborate on this let me know. Everything is fully open source. We live from contribution from others. This is not our project. It's a community project.

Participant 1: Is there anything that stops this from being applied to something by the training, of course, beyond tool calls. For example, if we were looking at safety alignment. The reason being that at least from the results of the causal inspection that you did, it seems to be possible to do some kind of steering after you train the model. Do you have any insight on any ways that we could possibly change something like this for alignment and then use that for active steering after deployment.

Hannes Hapke: I think there's nothing that I would say that it's not possible. One of the things we're looking into is the security aspects of like, can we detect malicious attacks in those activations? Yes, I think that's possible. I think from the research I showed earlier when I showed the clustering versus linear classification versus the sparse autoencoder, it was visible to me. I think to me that's sort of the proof that if you just look at their pure activations you can't figure out what is going on. You do need the step through the sparse autoencoder. Yes, nothing is limited to just a tool call. For us, it was like a feasible project scope. The team is pretty small, so for us it felt feasible. Yes, totally.

Participant 2: Do you have any real-world examples where using your approach gave you a different understanding of why a tool was selected versus using chain of thought tells?

Hannes Hapke: Yes, we have a bunch of anecdotal examples. We haven't summarized them yet into something scientific that we say here's my prompt and here's my analysis. Chain of thought was maybe a bit abstract. Then in the features, we could see like, this is actually looking for a particular problem. For example, this dishwasher repair thing, it picked water damage on an electrical equipment or something. It felt more precise than the actual chain of thought. There's a little caveat. The sparse autoencoder we trained for those examples, they were domain specific. Meaning that we were focusing on a very particular specific domain and that's what we built the training set for. There was a little bit of an unfair advantage. Also, it changes with model size. If you use a smaller model like the Gemma E4B, I think those interpretability tools have a benefit of it. Those were the two things where you could see the difference between the chain of thought versus the explainability tool.

Participant 2: For those who are stuck with the closed source proprietary models, could you imagine surrogate models working ok enough? Do you think that the closed and open-source models are similar enough with why they would make certain choices?

Hannes Hapke: I can't speak for OpenAI and others. I would think the models are bigger than what we see in the open-source world obviously. I think you have maybe a better chain of thought experiments. That's an interesting question. We should compare different prompts and run them through a large Qwen model versus a large like OpenAI 5.5, and then look at the thinking steps, and see, are they comparable or not? Generally, we will never see this technology in closed source models, because, A, I think all the companies are walking back their logics now, because through the logics you could figure out model internals. This is even more like internals. They never want to share this. The other thing is also like, yes, it's proprietary modeling. They don't want to really open source that or share that.

#9961. Most affairs don't matter except to the people involved. Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen's blunder will rock the world

In the aftermath of Jensen Huang's resignation, not only may the AI bubble pop, but the world economy is in some peril

It's a story as old as time. Billionaire nerd boy meets girl. Girl is later suspected of being a spy. News at 11. Oh, and it's also been reported that he was having an affair with one of his direct-report employees. When Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a "romantic" blunder, he doesn't do it halfway.

The boss of the world's most valuable company – well, it was until recently, anyway – publicly resigned yesterday, November 12, as CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately. We don't know if he jumped or if he was pushed.

He left after admitting to having an affair. Although he never named an affair partner, one of the affairs was reported to be with Alice Huang, AKA Huang Le. She's head of the Chinese company Megaspeed, which was an Nvidia partner. Megaspeed is accused of being a front for China's government that was used to transfer Nvidia chips to China, although this hasn't been proven. Some US officials also suspect [PDF] she's working for Chinese intelligence, although the DoJ said it hasn't yet reached a conclusion about this. The final nail in Jensen's coffin came when The New York Times reported he had also allegedly had an affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell. Jeeze, guy!

In the aftermath, Nvidia's  CFO, Colette Kress, was appointed interim CEO. She won't, I suspect, be in the job for long. CFOs are not CEOs. The jobs aren't remotely the same.  In most companies, Huang would be replaced by the COO. That can't happen here. Nvidia doesn't have a COO. Both inside and outside of Nvidia, Huang is seen as Nvidia, and Nvidia as Huang.

These days, billionaire CEOs are perceived as God-kings who know all and rule all. Much more often than not, that's BS.

That isn't the case with Nvidia. Huang co-founded Nvidia on April 5, 1993. He was appointed CEO on day one, and he never left the job. At first, the company staggered forward. When it released the GeForce 256 in 1999, which it marketed as the first GPU, it started on its path to becoming the chip manufacturer of choice for PC gamers. It still is today.

That's a great niche, but it doesn't make a company a trillion-dollar business. No, the path to that dizzying height came when, in 2006, Nvidia unveiled CUDA. This programming architecture opened its GPUs' parallel-processing capabilities to scientific and other non-graphics workloads. From there, CUDA would become the foundation for most high-performance and AI computing.

Huang was at the center of it all. He still was until now. At KubeCon North America, the trade show for Kubernetes, used in well over half of all AI projects, I spoke to many Nvidia employees. There were two things they all mentioned. First, they were in a state of shock. Maybe the top brass and government officials both in China and the US knew Huang was fooling with fire; the developer rank-and-file folks I spoke to hadn't had a clue. The second was that every month, Huang held an all-hands meeting where, instead of a per-forma corporate pep rally, he answered questions from everyone and gave them real answers. He knew his technology well and actually led his company instead of just impressing gullible stock buyers.

Nvidia can't replace him. It really can't. I'm reminded of when John Sculley forced Steve Jobs out at Apple in 1985. If you're not old enough to remember, Apple did fine for a while, but then by the mid-90s, it lost its way. Apple got its mojo back, and started its rise to being one of the world's top companies only after Jobs came back in 1996.

The big difference, of course, is that Huang's not coming back. I heard many people say that Huang was "too big to fail." True, morality no longer matters much in the US – see Trump's kleptocracy – but this is different. Huang betrayed not just his wife, but his board, employees, and stockholders. If, as some suspect, the board knew full well what was going on, they should be tossed out too, but that's a story for another day.

Oh, and as for Trump's suggestions that Apple's former CEO Tim Cook should become Nvidia's CEO? Give me a break.

Now the question of the day is: how can Nvidia recover from this blow? I don't think it can. I used to say that I didn't know where the AI companies were going, but I was sure that so long as capital kept flowing into Big AI, Nvidia was the one company you could count on that would make money. I think I was wrong.

What does that mean? In the short term, Nvidia stock, after dropping 14 percent in early trading on Thursday, is down "only" five percent. Despite all the Sturm und Drang over Huang's departure, the NASDAQ is actually, when I wrote this, up. Even Nvidia's bonds are holding steady.

Amazon and Google, which have their own horses in the AI TPU races, are hoping, of course, that Nvidia's misfortune will help them lever open the AI hardware market. In these early hours, I don't see that happening.

Frankly, I'm amazed at how stockowners are shaking off Huang's resignation. The AI fever dream, for now, is continuing unabated.

That said, can this go on? This irrational exuberance rests on the belief that, no matter what happens, AI will continue to rule the stock market. Eventually, though, the bubble may pop, and that could put some strain on the global economy. For now, people are ignoring how bad this blow is, or perhaps they're not aware of it.

In a few years, I expect Huang's affair will be seen as the first needle in the AI bubble. ®

#9960. Thinking of ACE? We Can Do It with Fewer Tokens

ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories. The difference is what they do with what they learn — and that decides the token bill.

Give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge. It mis-paginates an API, resolves the wrong person, or returns a value when none was asked for. The model knows the APIs; what it hasn't internalized is how to use them reliably. That's learnable from the agent's own history.

Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here). Both are a form of agentic memory — turning an agent's past trajectories into reusable lessons and feeding them back at inference time, no weight updates, no human labels. They even agree on the hard part. Where they part ways is delivery.

A note on words, because the two systems name things differently: we'll call the raw thing an agent learns a lesson. ACE organizes its lessons into one comprehensive, evolving playbook; we consolidate ours into individually retrievable guidelines. Same lessons, two containers.

ACE names the failure modes precisely: brevity bias — optimization collapsing toward short, generic instructions — and context collapse — a model asked to rewrite its whole context each step summarizing the detail away. Its answer is to keep a rich, itemized playbook, with a helpful/harmful counter on every bullet, and let the model distill relevance at read time.

We reach the same conclusion from the other direction. Every distinct guideline keeps a support count — how many independent episodes produced it — and we never summarize the store down to a handful of rules. A lesson five different tasks discovered is a different object from one that appeared once, and both are worth keeping.

So on the core question — should you compress an agent's hard-won lessons into a tidy summary? — ACE and ALTK-Evolve give the same answer: no. Count them, don't collapse them. ACE's per-bullet counters and our support counts are two spellings of the same idea.

Two places: how the memory is built, and how it's delivered — and it's the delivery difference that shows up in the token bill.

Consolidation (how the store is built). ACE grows one playbook through a Generator → Reflector → Curator loop, applying incremental delta updates and de-duplicating by embedding. We cluster near-duplicate lessons and merge within a cluster, support-conserving — when several lessons merge, the survivor inherits their combined count, so the store shrinks without losing the record of how much experience backs each guideline. We also extract typed guidelines — strategy, recovery, and optimization — with causal attribution and provenance back to the source trajectory, and at subtask granularity, so a lesson learned on one app can transfer to another.

Delivery (what reaches the model at inference). This is the one that drives the numbers. ACE injects the comprehensive playbook on every step, the same way regardless of model or task. We treat delivery as a dial, not a constant: a small fixed core of high-support guidelines, extended per task with a handful selected for the task at hand (cosine or LLM-guided, priority-weighted) — or, when a model has the headroom to use it, the full consolidated set. The same lessons are available to both agents; the difference is that ACE always sends all of them, and we send however many a given model can actually use.

On AppWorld, with the same base ReAct agent, running both systems in-house:

On the strong model we're better on both metrics at ~40% of ACE's inference cost. On the weak model we edge ACE 56.0 to 54.8 — close enough that we call it a tie on accuracy (a repeat run of ours landed at 54.8, matching ACE almost exactly, which is within this benchmark's run-to-run noise) — at about one-seventh the cost.

A fair word on cost: ACE's own efficiency story is about building its context cheaply. Ours is on a different axis — serving it. Retrieving a few guidelines per task instead of injecting the whole playbook on every step is where the tokens go, and it's the direct consequence of the delivery difference above.

Where does the accuracy come from? The by-difficulty breakdown tells two different stories:

Figure 1. Post-memory Task Goal Completion by difficulty, ours vs. ACE. On DeepSeek-V3.2 (right) we win Easy, Hard, and Overall; ACE only edges Medium. On gpt-oss-120b (left) ACE leads easy and medium, but per-task selection wins the hard tasks — and the aggregate. Each system improves from its own no-memory baseline (see the by-difficulty reference tables under Method notes below).

The two models tell different stories. On gpt-oss-120b, ACE's full playbook has the edge on Easy and Medium — there's enough of the task solved by generic instruction-following that a comprehensive prompt helps more than it distracts. But on Hard tasks, where the model has to pick the right lesson rather than wade through all of them, curated retrieval pulls ahead — and that's the tier that decides the aggregate. On DeepSeek-V3.2 the story flips: the stronger model absorbs ACE's full playbook well enough to edge us on Medium, but we lead Easy, Hard, and Overall — with more capacity to spare, more lessons (delivered our way) keep helping instead of crowding each other out.

We give each model its best configuration — the full consolidated set for the strong model, selective retrieval for the weaker one, because a large context overwhelms a weaker model rather than helping it. (Exactly how much to inject, and how it scales across the capability spectrum, is the focus of our follow-up post.)

Both systems refuse to compress an agent's hard-won experience into a tidy summary — that part, we agree on. The difference is whether delivery is fixed or calibrated: ACE sends the whole playbook every step no matter what; we send however much of the guideline set a given model can actually use. That calibration is what bought the numbers above — same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of ACE's inference cost — and on the weaker model, it was the difference between guidance that helped and guidance that got in the way.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld test_normal, 168 tasks. A ReAct code agent (each step writes Python; the environment returns the output). TGC = Task Goal Completion; SGC = Scenario Goal Completion, which requires every variant of a scenario to pass. Memory is mined from train/dev only; results are single runs (pass@1), as is standard on this benchmark.

The ACE numbers are our own runs of the ACE agent, evaluated in-house on the same AppWorld splits and the same base models as ALTK-Evolve (DeepSeek-V3.2 and gpt-oss-120b). The ACE paper reports on a different base model (DeepSeek-V3.1), so running it ourselves keeps the comparison controlled for model and harness. Both systems are the same ReAct agent and differ only in the prompt template — which is why the two no-memory baselines differ (72.0 vs 79.8 TGC); we don't rest the comparison on that baseline gap, only on the claims a prompt tweak can't touch: same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of the tokens.

DeepSeek-V3.2 — by difficulty (baseline → +memory): the two systems start from different no-memory baselines (79.8 vs 72.0 TGC overall) because of the prompt-template difference above.

#9957. Solving the fox game

Christoffer Stjernlöf posted about the Fox Game, an old Norse asymmetric board game (seemingly also called “halatafl”) where twenty sheep try to outsmart two foxes and get to the other side. His AI uncovered some interesting insights, but left the question open as of whether the foxes or the sheep actually win with perfect play (the general sentiment in his family was that winning with the foxes was easy). This was too tempting for me to leave on the table, so I set out to make a strong solve.

Since I don't know this game myself, I've stayed with the rules he describes even when they differ from e.g. Wikipedia (in particular, I do not use forced fox jumps, or multi-jumps); the only real change is that I don't have a 40-move draw rule, any position that is a forced win for one of the sides would be a win no matter how long it would take. (I consider this just an implementation detail in his AI, although morally, I consider a draw a loss for the sheep.) You might want to read his post to get the full rules, because I'm not going to repeat them here.

The results first: The sheep win with perfect play, even with only 19 sheep (remove one on the flank), or 18 if they are allowed to go first. Even with only 9 sheep (the minimum possible that isn't an instant win for the foxes), the sheep can force a draw right from the start. With one fox, 11 sheep suffice for a forced win. (The draw margin is seemingly so large because one fox can just camp in the last spot in the pen, and it's hard to force it away without getting harassed by the other fox, unless you have lots of sheep.)

The rest is about the implementation. I'll skip over a lot of wrong turns, and unsurprisingly, there were a lot of bugs to iron out, but hopefully, it got to a good place in the end. :-) I started out trying to make something very simple, and it worked for the first few cases, but then things got more complicated than I would have liked in the end. Still only at ~1000 lines of code, though, with no dependencies.

The board has 33 squares. I tried a few different ways of represent the state of the game, and ended up on a simple bitboard representation: There's a 64-bit bitmap representing where there are sheep, and another bitmap representing where there are foxes. Since there's plenty of room in there, I use a spare bit to represent side-to-move. This is compact (which mattered a lot earlier on, but not as much later), easy to iterate over, and has little redundancy, so it's easy to keep valid. You need fast 64-bit population count and bit-scan instructions, but a) that's common now everywhere, and b) I decided fairly early that I wanted to require BMI2 anyway.

The bit order mostly doesn't matter; I just started at top-left and went from there. All it really influences is square iteration order. There's a small tweak in that I store the right half of the board mirrored (reverse x order) for symmetry purposes; more on that below.

I just typed in every possible move from every square into an array, then verified by generating some SVGs that I hadn't made any typos (I had). In retrospect, I should have done something more automated; it would have been less painful.

The moves for sheep are just “you can go to X, Y or Z”. The moves for foxes are “you can go to X or Y, or you can go to Z if there's a sheep at W (which will be eaten)”. The move generator mostly just looks up the source square and tests every move. For the sheep, I make an easy test using bitboards; for the foxes, I could probably do something similar, but the jump moves proved a bit tricky (even with PEXT/PDEP) and I didn't end up using it.

This is the part that really determines the geometry of the board (apart from debugging display). Everything else is pretty much geometry-agnostic.

There's a little over 2^41 possible board states (this includes some illegal positions as well as some situations that could never arise during actual gameplay, such as a fox being stuck at C1 with a row of sheep ahead of it), and I want to remember all of them. With that many positions, I figured I needed a fairly compact representation. I needed to store that a position could be sheep win, fox win or a draw, and then there was a fourth “invalid” state that was useful for internal reasons, so that maps exactly to two bits per position. (A tablebase intended for distribution could be compressed to less using the usual tricks of entropy coding, skipping half of the positions, or similar.)

This means we need to give a number to every possible position, ideally one with no collisions and no holes. I learned about combinatorial number systems which fit the bill exactly; given e.g. “we have 33 squares and 15 pieces”, it gives a dense mapping of positions from board to ID (ranking) and the opposite (unranking). (I made some fairly fast ranking and unranking algorithms, which may or may not have been novel, but it turned out I didn't actually need fast unranking after some other optimizations.) There are some extra complications in that there are two types of pieces, but you can solve them in a number of ways.

On a macro level, I store everything with 9 sheep and 1 fox first, then 9 sheep and 2 foxes, 10 sheep and 1 fox, and so on. This gives beautiful locality (a single move can never remove more than one sheep, and only extremely rarely more than one fox), allowing me to just mmap everything and let the kernel deal with it, even though I only had 256GB of RAM and the total set was larger (329,870,110,455 bytes after the symmetry optimizations below).

mmap is almost never the right answer, but again, I was trying to go for simplicity. It certainly brought me pain, though, and perhaps some more explicit I/O would have been better.

The board is left-right symmetric (with an odd number of columns, so that there is a middle column that is neither “left” nor “right”). I had hoped to just ignore this, but eventually the gains became too important to ignore, so I conceded.

The basic idea is that I ranked the board twice, both as itself and mirrored (mirroring is just a couple of masks and shifts, given my representation), and picked the key that was the smaller as canonical. This reduced the number of positions I needed to look at to a bit over 50%, as expected, but it does nothing to the storage/RAM requirements; the new rank is not dense and the “illegal” (non-canonical) positions are spread out a bit all over the place (although of course near the low and high ends of values, it works much better).

As a tweak, I chose to compute all 33+281 canonical fox positions and renumbered using those placements as an assumption. This slashes ~95% of the waste, which is good enough; you can still rank a nonconical position if the foxes are symmetric about the center (or if there's only one fox and it's in the middle!), though.

You can improve on this by making the macro-splitting finer; instead of having a chunk for e.g. “10 sheep, 2 foxes”, you could have one with “5 sheep in left, 0 foxes in left, 1 sheep center, 1 fox center, 4 sheep in right, 1 fox in right” and demand that there are more sheep in left than right. However, you still get problems when the number is balanced, you'd need finer splitting etc.. The gains are small enough that I didn't see the point in doing this, and it tends to be a place where it's easy to introduce bugs.

I imagined calculating the exact number of positions up to symmetry would be an interesting exercise somehow, but I suppose it just immediately falls to Burnside's lemma as soon as you know how to count positions at all.

Now that we have positions and moves and a way to store results, we want to know how to find the result for the starting position (and ideally also all other positions).

My first attempt just did a depth-first search, caching as it went. This worked for the earlier stages but was generally a disaster; it ran out of stack easily (even with 8 GB—eight gigabytes of stack), and had problems with figuring out loops. (It didn't loop infinitely, but was prone to declaring loops where one side could break out of the loop by winning. I had a nasty hack to fix that, but it didn't really feel good.)

What I did instead was propagating results one step at a time. For each possible position:

If from a given position you know you can immediately win (e.g., the sheep reach the pen, or the fox eats the last relevant sheep), mark it as such.

If you can, in one move, reach a known-won position, mark your position as won (for the side to move). Similarly, if you can only reach known-lost positions, mark your position as lost.

Repeat #2 over and over again until you no longer have changes.

This was simple but still inefficient; I typically needed 40–80 passes for each chunk (where a chunk is something like “all positions with 15 sheep, 2 foxes”). However, it was super-easy to parallelize; I have 64 cores and could just hand out reasonable independent sub-chunks, you don't even need locking or atomic operations on the result set.

The correct way of doing this is retrograde analysis (replace #2 with doing backwards moves) and I assume this would have made the calculation roughly ten times as fast. But I only needed ~36 hours for the actual run (plus numerous pre-runs that failed for various reasons!), so I never got to this. After all, I wanted something simple to begin with.

Since I only store win/draw/loss (WDL) for each position (also known as a “bitbase” in chess tablebases), it's not easy to know what the fastest way to win is; just that “this move does not mess it up, the other side still can't force a draw”. However, in practice, you could just do reasonable-looking moves that don't regress the position, and take forward moves whenever you can (i.e., do sheep pushes if that still wins).

I made a simple alpha-beta searcher that tries to get win distances using the bitbase as a guide, which was a really fun challenge! It can find wins when they're perhaps ~20 ply (10 moves for each side) away, depending a bit on how narrow the win is (if there are only a few ways to win, it will obviously have to search a much smaller tree). Ultimately, though, alpha-beta for finding exact mate scores is just a losing game, since even perfect move ordering will only give you a sqrt() improvement over pure minimax.

Perhaps making DTZ (distance-to-zeroing, referring to zeroing the draw move counter in e.g. chess) bases would be possible without breaking the bank on storage space; I would assume that usually, you can force some sort of progress pretty fast, at least as the sheep.

I made a very rudimentary interface to the database; the UI isn't very nice, and it largely relies on hovering (which doesn't work all that well on mobile) but I didn't want a polished game-player, just to know the answer. :-) You can try it out at https://sheep.sesse.net/, although I don't envision keeping it up forever. Perhaps someone can gain new insight from it and become an expert player, although strong solves are rarely very insightful in themselves due to the brute-force nature. At least we've conclusively settled (again, under this ruleset!) that the sheep win with perfect play.

Earlier, I would publish the source, but these days, the only ones who would be reading it would be the AI beast (fox?), and I'm not really so interested in that. :-) I'm definitely open to answering questions if anyone should have them; contact information at my home page as usual.

#9956. Introducing OlmoEarth embeddings: Custom embedding exports from OlmoEarth Studio for downstream analysis

📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth | 📊 Documentation: https://docs.olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings | 💻 Learn more about OlmoEarth: https://allenai.org/olmoearth

OlmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models. The source code and model weights are publicly available alongside the research paper, so the community can inspect exactly how these embeddings are generated.

Embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration. Locations with similar surface characteristics end up with similar vectors; locations that differ land far apart. OlmoEarth embeddings have shown strong performance in our own benchmarking and in independent evaluations. The exported Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) are lightweight and easy to share. Choose your area of interest, time range, encoder variant, resolution, and imagery sources via the Studio UI or API, and get back a COG you can use however you like. If your application requires higher performance, Studio also supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

Custom-computed embeddings are now available for users of OlmoEarth Studio. Reach out if you're interested in gaining access. Instructions for using the publicly available OlmoEarth models to compute your own embeddings are available here.

Global structure in OlmoEarth embeddings from seasonal Sentinel-2 imagery across 1.1M samples. Colors indicate 15 k-means clusters in a PCA-reduced embedding space.

Computing embeddings follows the same workflow as any other prediction in Studio. First configure a model and run it, and then download the results. Several parameters tailor the output:

Different visualization options applied to the same embedding raster.

Studio delivers a COG with one band per embedding dimension. Vectors are stored as signed 8-bit integers (int8). Values range from -127 to +127, with -128 reserved for nodata. To recover floating-point vectors, see dequantize_embeddings in olmoearth_pretrain.

Because everything is computed on demand rather than pulled from a pre-computed global archive, your embeddings reflect exactly the conditions you care about. You can generate monthly embeddings to capture seasonal dynamics, not just annual snapshots.

The examples below all use OlmoEarth-v1-Tiny (192-dim) embeddings at 40-meter resolution with Sentinel-2 L2A composites (annual for most examples; monthly for change detection). Tiny is a lightweight encoder but still highly performant; for your own applications, you can swap it for a larger variant at the cost of higher compute and storage.

Pick a query pixel, extract its embedding, and compute cosine similarity against every other pixel. The result is a heatmap showing where the landscape looks most and least like your query pixel.

This query sits near the Merced urban center in California. Urban fabric and road corridors light up coherently while agricultural parcels stay dark. The model distinguishes built-up surfaces from cropland without any labels.

Switching the query to a small agricultural window, we define the query vector as the mean of the embedding vectors over that window, then pull Sentinel-2 imagery at the highest- and lowest-similarity locations to see what the model treats as similar and dissimilar.

The most similar patches (0.89 and above) are all agricultural parcels with irrigated fields. The least similar (around zero) are an airport with surrounding bare ground, a reservoir with dry terrain, and arid rangeland. No training data, no labels, just a dot product in embedding space.

Similarity search tells you "where is it like this?" but sometimes you need discrete labels across a region. Because the representations are already rich, a simple linear classifier can produce a wall-to-wall land-cover map from very few labeled pixels.

To test this, we labeled just 60 pixels (20 per class) over Ca Mau, Vietnam, a coastal mangrove region. Using ESA WorldCover 2021 as the label source for three classes (mangrove, water, other), we randomly sampled 20 pixels per class, trained a logistic regression with per-feature standardization, and predicted every pixel in the region.

From 60 labeled pixels, the classifier produces a coherent map with weighted F1 = 0.84. Mangrove stands, tidal channels, and open water are delineated across the entire region. The classifier saturates quickly: increasing from 30 to 300 labels barely changes accuracy, because the embeddings are doing most of the heavy lifting.

The core of the analysis is a few lines of Python:

This is a linear probe, a standard evaluation for foundation models. The fact that a logistic regression over 192 dimensions recovers land-cover boundaries from so few labels means the Tiny encoder has organized these ecological distinctions during pretraining. Larger variants (Base, 768-dim) encode even richer representations.

If you have ground-truth polygons, field survey points, or a coarse existing map, you can train a similar classifier and produce a wall-to-wall map for your own region of interest.

Because Studio can generate embeddings at any temporal resolution (monthly through annual), you can compare two time periods directly to identify where surface conditions have changed. Below, we computed monthly Sentinel-2 embeddings for the same region in September 2023 and September 2024 and measured per-pixel cosine distance. The Park Fire (July-September 2024) burn scar in Butte County, California lights up immediately.

No labels or training required—just two embedding COGs and a few lines of Python.

Sometimes you have no query location or reference labels. You just want to understand what structure exists in the embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a clean way to do this: reduce to three dimensions, map to R/G/B, and display as a false-color image. Similar embeddings get similar colors automatically.

Flevoland, in the Netherlands, is a reclaimed polder landscape with a regular grid of agricultural parcels. The PCA false-color image reproduces those boundaries with high fidelity. Different crop types, water bodies, and urban areas each get distinct hues. The embedding has internalized landscape structure without ever being told what a parcel or crop is.

This kind of unsupervised view is a quick way to see what structure the model has picked up across your area of interest.

Similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA exploration are simple operations on standard raster data that run in seconds. The power comes from the embeddings: learned representations that compress earth observation data into vectors capturing rich information about each location from many sensors and millions of training examples.

Custom embedding exports are available now. Create a project, configure an embeddings model, and compute your embeddings. The exported GeoTIFF works with any geospatial tool: QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, or your own scripts. For end-to-end code reproducing the examples in this post, see the embeddings tutorial, which includes working code for similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA visualization. To get hands-on without any local setup, try the Colab notebook.

The examples in this post all use frozen embeddings with no task-specific training. Embeddings are a great entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they enable fast, cost-effective generation of results, work well in resource-constrained environments, and are easy to share. For applications that require higher performance, OlmoEarth Studio also supports SFT, training a task-specific model head on your own labels, which typically outperforms linear probes on frozen features.

While we are always working to improve our pretraining approaches, it's important to check the quality of the embeddings for your use case using some of the techniques described above. Performance also depends on the quality of the input imagery—persistent cloud cover, atmospheric artifacts, or missing observations in the composite period can affect the resulting vectors.

Sentinel-2 L2A imagery from the European Space Agency, accessed via Microsoft Planetary Computer. ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 for mangrove reference. The global clustering visualization uses OlmoEarth-v1-Base (768-dim) with seasonal Sentinel-2 composites at patch size 8, instance-level embeddings over 1.1M pretraining samples.

#9955. Another Linux kernel developer steps back from some duties due to overload

You can probably guess what he blames for the excessive workload

Arm's Lorenzo Stoakes isn't quitting Linux kernel development, though he's stepping back from some of the patch-review work he used to handle.

Stoakes is a principal software engineer at Arm and he's a busy chap. Aside from writing the forthcoming book The Linux Memory Manager, in his CV [PDF], he says:

"I hold four maintainerships: memory mapping, memory mapping (locking), memory mapping (madvise) – essentially the entirety of the userland API to memory management – and the reverse mapping which connects physical to virtual memory."

Even so, he plans to soon be doing a little less. Earlier this week he posted an email to the Linux kernel mailing list to say that he was planning to drop some of his workload.

"Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain. […] Apologies for doing this, but given the current trends I'd like to do something to make my inbox a little more manageable."

As it happens, this came just the day after the Paramount Penguin himself said that he saw signs that the AI patch tide was "starting to turn."

"I am retaining my maintainerships and have no plans on giving those up, I just want my inbox to be less horrendous.

"And yeah, AI is part of the reason; in general, it's gone from 'once a week' to 'daily' to 'half of what I see in review'.

"But the AI wave is hitting [memory management] across the board, really."

"I have a habit of burning myself out over weekends and evenings – you can see my involvement on a thread talking about that here - which gives you a sense of my views if you read back through that thread."

At the Open Source Summit last month, the Reg FOSS desk joined the "Ask the Expert" session with Greg Kroah-Hartman, and he too expressed worrying sentiments:

"The onslaught of the LLM-generated patches… we don't have enough people to review them all… We need more reviewers. We don't have enough. All of the maintainers are burnt out, and we have been for ten years."

"I want to go down to two Long Term Support releases – four, maximum. Six is too many. We're too busy. We don't have the manpower. It’s crazy."

On Red Hat's model of offering 10 years of support for products with a given version of the kernel:

"Debian does it right. Debian and Yocto run the world. I've argued for years that the RHEL and SLES model is broken. That's why I don't work for SUSE any more." ®

#9954. What We Learned by Reproducing 2,200 papers from ICML

Back in July, we ran a hackathon where more than 1,200 community members brought their own coding agents and tried to reproduce the papers published at ICML 2026, claim by claim. In 19 days, participants published 6,816 Trackio logbooks reproducing 2,226 papers, about a third of the conference 🤯

In this post, we're sharing what we learned from running this hackathon, and what it suggests about the role humans will play when agents are doing the research experiments.

Questions about how reproducible AI research really is are older than the current AI wave. But these questions are exacerbated by scale. ICML 2026 received 23,918 submissions and accepted 6,352 papers, roughly double the previous year, continuing an exponential trend that is at least partly driven by AI agents making it faster to run experiments and write them up.

Reviewing capacity has not doubled along with it. Reviewers at most conferences are volunteers who may not have the time or expertise to fully review a paper. Here is a review of one accepted ICML 2026 spotlight paper, in the reviewer's own words:

"My low confidence score is because I did not check all the proofs carefully."

Note that this paper got strong scores and a spotlight. Keep it in mind, because we will come back to this exact paper later in the post, and to what happened when we finally did check the proofs carefully.

What has changed, though, is that the same technology driving the flood of submissions can also help us keep up with it. Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Pi can now read a paper, write the code, launch the experiments, and report back on what they found. Checking a paper carefully used to cost a reviewer a weekend; an agent can attempt it in an afternoon, in parallel, thousands of times over.

So the question we wanted to ask was: if we actually re-examined a major conference at scale, and tried to reproduce every paper, what would we find?

Rather than audit papers ourselves, we opened it up to the whole community, with all the diversity of agent frameworks, compute budgets, and scientific taste that brings. From July 15 to August 2, 2026, the ICML 2026 Open Reproductions challenge worked like this:

Participants received $20 in Hugging Face compute credits to run experiments on HF Jobs; across the challenge, participants launched 2,962 cloud jobs. Where a full reproduction was impossible, for example when a paper's dataset was proprietary or its checkpoints unreleased, participants ran toy reproductions on synthetic data mimicking the original's properties.

Here is what a finished reproduction looks like:

By the numbers, this hackathon was probably the largest attempted reproduction of a scientific conference:

Aggregating the claim-level verdicts per paper:

51% of examined papers (1,103) had at least one claim independently verified. Of those, 266 papers were fully reproduced, with every extracted claim verified, and 632 more were partially reproduced with nothing falsified. In total, 3,978 individual claims were confirmed with real experiments.

23% of examined papers (496) had at least one claim falsified or contested. That includes 49 papers where all claims were falsified and nothing could be verified, and, maybe most interestingly, 242 papers where independent reproduction teams reached opposite verdicts on the same claims. Reproducibility is not binary; it is adversarial.

The remainder sat in the middle: 502 papers with toy-scale evidence only, and 280 where nothing could be established either way (missing artifacts were the most common cause).

Some papers came through the gauntlet looking great, and the community's best logbooks are worth reading in their own right:

35 participants formally claimed they had falsified something. We adversarially re-verified every claimed falsification: re-reading the paper, re-reading the logbook, and re-deriving the math or re-implementing the experiment from the paper's own text.

A few of the confirmed falsifications, linking to the logbook that found it:

The paging paper from the introduction. The reviewer who did not check the proofs carefully? The paper, "Towards Optimal Robustness in Learning-Augmented Paging," claims its algorithm achieves robustness Hk+O(1)H_k + O(1)Hk​+O(1). One participant's logbook measured the additive term growing like 0.38ln⁡k0.38 \ln k0.38lnk and located the exact step of the proof that breaks. Our own re-implementation extended the sweep to k = 1,024 and confirmed the growth at roughly nine sigma. The true robustness is Hk+Θ(log⁡k)H_k + \Theta(\log k)Hk​+Θ(logk).

A theorem that falls after step 224. "Attention's forward pass and Frank-Wolfe" proves that token particles collapse to the origin whenever the origin starts inside their convex hull. Three independent teams found counterexamples, with violations first appearing at t = 224, ~3,800, and 6,416 steps, which neatly explains why everyone else "verified" the claim: finite-horizon checks stop too early. The cleanest counterexample is stated in exact rational arithmetic, so there is no floating-point ambiguity to hide behind. The authors confirmed the same day and are working on a fix.

Theory written for one loss, results produced by another. In "Self-Distillation Enables Continual Learning," the paper's central equation and its entire theory section analyze reverse KL divergence, but the released code's default, which per the authors produced all the paper's results, computes forward KL. The logbook that caught it also failed to reproduce the paper's headline +4pp result under the authors' own code and data. The authors have already uploaded a clarified version to arXiv.

An evaluation diluted by padding. In "Do Transformers Need Three Projections?", a participant discovered that ~66% of evaluated label positions were EOS padding tokens that train to near-zero loss, deflating perplexity roughly threefold. The abstract's "3.1% quality cost for 50% cache reduction" becomes roughly 9.4% once corrected.

🚨 False falsifications. Sometimes we found flaws in an attempted reproduction. One logboook claimed dramatically, "the paper's method is 2x slower than the baseline"; this turned out to be an arithmetic bug in the reproduction: per-trajectory time compared against per-batch-of-50 time. Correctly normalized, the participant's own data confirms the paper's claimed 8x speedup.

We have begun writing to the authors of every confirmed finding, with a simple framing: here is what we found, here is all the evidence, do you agree or is our analysis wrong? The early responses have been very positive:

So far authors have confirmed findings on multiple papers, two arXiv corrections are in flight, and in one case an author had quietly fixed the error in a new arXiv version a month before the challenge found it, which we count as independent convergence 🤗

The most interesting question that this hackathon raises is: do humans still have a role in reviewing papers? We think so, for several reasons:

Pure agent execution hits real limits. Agents got stuck in local loops, misread scale-dependent behavior (several "verified" verdicts on the paging paper came from checks that stopped before the log-k growth became visible), and occasionally built an entire falsification on top of a units mismatch. The challenge's most reliable results came from workflows where a human was steering: re-pointing the agent, questioning an assumption, or deciding that an experiment's premise was wrong before burning a week of compute on it.

Some evaluation is irreducibly human, for now. Our human-in-the-loop winner is the clearest example. The paper claimed stable image generation under extreme quantization. Numerical metrics said "no collapse"; whether the images were actually usable was a perceptual question. The agent built a purpose-built review UI, and the human personally judged all 128 image pairs, with the annotations committed to the repo and the agent validating their consistency afterward. The published agent trace captures the whole exchange, down to the participant asking how the review tool works and coming back with "I have gone over the pairs and put the csv in the repo, please check."

So what are our roles as human reviewers? We think it is to manage intelligence effectively. Much like a professor or principal investigator (PI) sets up an environment where grad students can do good work, with compute, harnesses, data access, and targeted feedback at the right moments, the participants who got the most out of their agents were the ones who built the right environment and asked the right questions, then let the agents do the running.

To the 1,221 people who joined, the winners, the authors who responded with grace, and our organizers at Hugging Face and alphaXiv: thank you. Every logbook, verdict, trace, and artifact from the challenge is public, starting from the challenge Space. We think this is the largest open, claim-by-claim audit of a machine learning conference to date, and we would love for it not to hold that record for long.

Stay tuned for future reproduction events. 🤗

It was interesting to reproduce one of the ICML accepted papers using these tools.This analysis from the hackathon was particularly insightful, and agent-based reproducibility has the potential to become a de facto standard for strengthening the credibility of claims in ML conferences. It could also serve as a valuable pathway toward refining autonomous scientific discovery, revealing not only where agents succeed, but also where they fail, providing important insights into their limitations and how human-agent collaboration can be improved.

I have been working on a complementary experiment at https://ReproducibleAIList.org, though not the same scale. We've been taking models from Chip Huyen's GoodAIList.com and having a clean-room agent try to reproduce each one from scratch using the code repos (not the papers).

One other difference: every attempt runs under roar (python package roar-cli), which passively captures provenance rather than relying on code instrumentation like Trackio or W&B. That gives us the actual lineage of code, data, environment and artifacts, automatically producing an AI-BOM and a roar reproduce path others can independently repeat.

It was a great demonstration of how agent-assisted research can make independent reproduction and auditing accessible with relatively modest compute.
